It includes challenging benign cases in which actions resemble risky ones but are consistent with the task and its authorization. It also provides paired trajectory versions to test whether auditors detect the same risks more reliably when the trajectory is shortened or missing information is supplied. Most samples are drawn from real production trajectories, with scenarios manually selected and adapted to preserve realistic tasks and risks that could plausibly arise during execution.

authors.name: Zipeng Ye, Shenyu Dai, Yong Xie, Kun Wang, Jiyang Guan, Zhikai Chen, Jiaqi Weng, Jialing Tao, Hui Xue

papers.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
papers.summary: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.60. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

authors.name: Yang Zhou, Krish Agarwal, Zhuoming Chen, Zerui Wang, Zhenyu Zhang, Wenshuang Li, Xinpeng Wei, Zhichen Zeng, Jingyu Liu, Jue Wang, Sen Wu, Ziheng Jiang, Zhen Dong, Han Cai, Binhang Yuan, Ying Sheng, Ce Zhang, Bo Li, Beidi Chen

papers.title: InertiaMPDD: Multimodal Personalized Depression Detection via Emotional Inertia-Inspired Dynamics Modeling
papers.summary: Multimodal depression screening estimates risk from speech, visual behavior and language. Current methods mainly predict labels, with limited evidence of departures from a non-depressed reference. Recording-level supervision also leaves fine-grained emotional dynamics unannotated. Motivated by emotional inertia, the persistence of affect, InertiaMPDD learns healthy next-state patterns using a world-model-inspired latent predictor. Using pretrained multimodal representations, it predicts from observed history and context. Reference deviation, residual decay rate and a Jacobian spectral descriptor form reference-derived emotional dynamics descriptors, evaluated as candidate proxy biomarkers for standalone screening and personalized decision correction. Across five cohorts from four datasets, fusion reaches 98.41% F1 on D-Vlog and 84.98% on LMVD. Standalone descriptors outperform fixed additive fusion on MPDD but discriminate weakly on AVEC2014. These findings distinguish reference informativeness from fusion benefit and reveal context-dependent utility.

authors.name: Changzeng Fu, Songyang Wang, Chang Gao, Xinyi Zhang, Peilin Li, Mo Meng, Jiarui Wu, Mingze Li, Hongwei Ding, Shiqi Zhao, Yong Li, Lang He

papers.title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps. We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively. We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

authors.name: Qijia Zhuang, Yanyin Gou, Wenbin Ma, Yuxiang Ren

papers.title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
papers.summary: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies further show that the 4-km forecasts retain coastal gradients and localized concentration maxima that are weakened by coarse-grid averaging. These results demonstrate the potential of observation-driven deep learning for high-resolution forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a variability at the near-global scale.

authors.name: Yong Jiang, Zheng Jiang, Gaowei Zhang, Zengzhou Hao, Suixiang Shi, Chi Zhang, Wei Wang

papers.title: Typing Matters: Muscle, Language and Typing Behaviour in Live Keystroke Decoding from sEMG
papers.summary: Surface electromyography (sEMG) from the wrists can recover typed text without a keyboard. It is usually posed as a signal-inference problem: characters are read out of the muscle signal and character error rate is reported offline. We argue that this framing removes most of the problem. The decoder is constrained simultaneously by the muscles, by the language being typed, and by typing behaviour such as typos, corrections, backspaces and line breaks, and a usable system must predict keys live while the hand keeps moving. Existing systems fall short on two counts: (1) they process sEMG in fixed windows and carry nothing from one window to the next, discarding context accumulated over a session, and (2) they lack any understanding of the linguistic structure that drives typing, so every keystroke is inferred from the muscle signal alone. We propose a fully causal, zero-lookahead sEMG typing decoder built on a state space model (SSM), in which a single model decodes a whole session without windowed partitions, conditioned on what has already been typed. We achieve this by fusing a traditional typing decoder with an efficient autoregressive language model, instilling both sEMG and linguistic understanding in one model. To train such a model for per-character typing rather than whole-word text, we introduce a retokenization method that rewrites ordinary prose as human-like typing, with keystrokes, typos, backspaces and line breaks included, converting WikiText into a large typing corpus where none existed. Our model, having never seen a single sEMG-to-character transcript in typing, achieves a state-of-the-art character error rate of 25.13% on emg2qwerty's cross-user benchmark, a 5.4% relative improvement over the previous best with 6.7 times fewer parameters, while running strictly causally with no future context.

authors.name: Abhilash Durgam, Nyle Siddiqui, Mubarak Shah, Qiushi Fu

papers.title: Ensemble Modeling for Time Series Forecasting: an Adaptive Robust Optimization Approach
papers.summary: Accurate time-series forecasting is critical for many problems involving temporal data. Ensemble modeling is a well-established technique that leverages multiple predictive models to improve accuracy and robustness, since a single predictor's performance can vary widely due to shifts in the underlying data distribution. This paper proposes a new methodology for building robust ensembles of time series forecasting models. Our approach uses Adaptive Robust Optimization (ARO) to construct a linear regression ensemble whose model weights adapt over time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through synthetic experiments covering eight disturbance scenarios, from no drift to abrupt regime shifts, and real-world applications, including air pollution management, energy consumption forecasting, and tropical cyclone intensity forecasting. In the real-world applications, our adaptive ensembles outperform the best ensemble member in hindsight by 16-26% in root mean square error (RMSE) and 14-28% in conditional value at risk at the 15% level and improve over the other ensemble methods we compare on most metrics. In the synthetic experiments, they have lower mean RMSE than a rolling-ridge comparator in seven of the eight scenarios, significantly in four, while an abrupt regime shift that first appears after model selection remains a limitation.

authors.name: L\'eonard Boussioux, Henry Mao, Dimitris Bertsimas

papers.title: Integrating Fairness and Model Pruning Through Bi-level Optimization
papers.summary: Deep neural networks achieve high predictive performance but often require substantial computational and storage resources, which motivates model compression techniques such as neural network pruning. Conventional pruning methods, however, can introduce or amplify algorithmic bias and produce disparate outcomes across demographic groups. We study fair model pruning, which seeks sparse models that satisfy fairness criteria while maintaining predictive performance. We characterize fairness using both group accuracy disparity and differences in compression-induced accuracy degradation across demographic groups. We propose a framework that jointly optimizes pruning masks and model weights under fairness constraints, thereby integrating accuracy and fairness into the compression process. We formulate fair pruning as a constrained bi-level optimization problem and derive an efficient optimization procedure. Experiments across multiple datasets, predictive tasks, model architectures, and sparsity levels show that our framework improves the trade-off among fairness, accuracy, and training efficiency relative to the baseline pruning strategies. Compared with the strongest evaluated baselines, BiFP maintains competitive accuracy and fairness while requiring more than 94% fewer training iterations in the real-world experiments.

authors.name: Yucong Dai, Gen Li, Feng Luo, Xiaolong Ma, Yongkai Wu

papers.title: Could Mobile AI be Exploited?: Understanding the Exploitations of Trust and Ethics Gap in On-Device Small Language Models
papers.summary: In this paper, we present a very first study to investigate trust and ethical implications of on-device artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on small language models (SLMs) amenable for personal devices like smartphones. While on-device SLMs promise enhanced privacy, reduced latency, and improved user experience compared to cloud-based services, we posit that they might also introduce significant risks and vulnerabilities compared to their on-server counterparts. As part of our study, we conduct a systematic evaluation of the state-of-the-art on-devices SLMs, compared to their on-server counterparts, using well-established trust and ethics frameworks. Our results illustrate that on-device SLMs are significantly less trustworthy and lacks ethical safeguards, specifically demonstrating more stereotypical, unfair, privacy-breaching and harmful content generation behavior. Further, these risks of on-device SLMs could be exploited through Open Knowledge (OkNow) Attacks, and we demonstrated them using potentially unethical vanilla prompts, to which the on-device SLMs answer with valid responses without any filters and without the need for any jailbreaking or prompt engineering. These responses can be abused for various harmful and unethical scenarios like: societal harm, illegal activities, hate, self-harm, exploitable phishing content, disinformation and many others.

authors.name: Kalyan Nakka, Jimmy Dani, Nitesh Saxena

papers.title: quanda: An Interpretability Toolkit for Training Data Attribution Evaluation
papers.summary: Training data attribution (TDA) methods estimate the influence of individual training samples on a model's predictions, offering a principled lens for interpreting neural networks. Despite rapid methodological progress, TDA evaluation remains scattered across papers and rarely reproducible, making fair comparison between methods challenging. We introduce quanda, a Python toolkit that standardizes TDA evaluation. quanda features a comprehensive collection of evaluation metrics and ready-to-use benchmarks spanning image classification, text classification, and language modeling, alongside a uniform interface for integrating diverse TDA implementations. We showcase quanda through a comparative study of existing TDA methods and find that no approach excels uniformly across metrics, with clear trade-offs between ground-truth faithfulness and downstream task performance. By consolidating the tooling around TDA, quanda equips the community to evaluate attribution methods rigorously and reproducibly. The toolkit is thoroughly tested, documented, and available as an open-source library on PyPI and at https://github.com/dilyabareeva/quanda.

authors.name: Dilyara Bareeva, Galip \"Umit Yolcu, Anna Hedstr\"om, Niklas Schmolenski, Thomas Wiegand, Wojciech Samek, Sebastian Lapuschkin

papers.title: Hallucination Mitigation using Agentic AI Natural Language-Based Frameworks
papers.summary: Hallucinations remain a significant challenge for Generative AI, undermining trust in AI systems and their reliability. This study investigates how orchestrating multiple specialized AI agents can mitigate hallucinations, with a focus on systems that use Natural Language Processing (NLP) for agent interaction. We design a pipeline that feeds 310 prompts, purposefully crafted to induce hallucinations, into a front-end agent; its outputs are reviewed and refined by second- and third-level agents that detect unverified claims, add explicit disclaimers and clarify speculative content. We introduce four novel Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) - Factual Claim Density, Factual Grounding References, Fictional Disclaimer Frequency and Explicit Contextualization Score - aggregated into a Total Hallucination Score (THS) and assessed by a dedicated fourth-level evaluator agent. Inter-agent context is carried by the Open Floor Protocol (OFP, formerly OVON, Open Voice Network), whose structured JSON messages let each reviewer pass its assessment of hallucination likelihood, and the reasons behind it, to the next stage. Across the 310 prompts, THS improves by a mean of -0.131 per prompt from the front-end agent to the final reviewer (Cohen's d = 2.38), with lower scores on 302 of 310 prompts. The gain is carried mainly by explicit disclaimers and contextualization, making speculative content more transparent and clearly demarcated from factual claims. The results show that multi-agent orchestration with structured, NLP-based exchange of meta-information can substantially strengthen the epistemic framing of AI-generated responses and improve their explainability.

authors.name: Diego Gosmar, Deborah A. Dahl

papers.title: ResBench: Benchmarking LLM-Generated FPGA Designs with Resource Awareness
papers.summary: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are widely used in modern hardware design, yet writing Hardware Description Language (HDL) code for FPGA implementation remains a complex and time-consuming task. Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising tool for HDL generation, but existing benchmarks for LLM-based code generation primarily focus on functional correctness while overlooking hardware resource usage. Furthermore, current benchmarks offer limited diversity and do not fully represent the wide range of real-world FPGA applications. To address these shortcomings, we introduce ResBench, the first resource-focused benchmark explicitly designed to distinguish between resource-optimized and inefficient LLM-generated HDL code. ResBench consists of 56 problems across 12 categories, covering applications from finite state machines to financial computing. Our open-source evaluation framework automatically tests LLMs by generating Verilog code, verifying correctness, and measuring resource usage. The experiments, which primarily analyze Lookup Table (LUT) usage, reveal significant differences among LLMs, demonstrating ResBench's capability to identify models that generate more resource-optimized FPGA designs.

authors.name: Ce Guo, Tong Zhao

papers.title: Breaking the Silence: A Dataset and Benchmark for Bangla Text-to-Gloss Translation
papers.summary: Gloss is a written approximation that bridges Sign Language (SL) and its corresponding spoken language. Despite a deaf and hard-of-hearing population of at least 3 million in Bangladesh, Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) remains largely understudied, with very limited prior work on Bangla text-to-gloss translation and no publicly available parallel dataset at the time of this work. To address this gap, we construct the first publicly available Bangla text-to-gloss dataset, consisting of 1,000 manually annotated and 4,000 synthetically generated Bangla sentence-gloss pairs, along with 159 expert human-annotated pairs used as a test set. Our experimental framework performs a comparative analysis between several fine-tuned open-source models and a leading closed-source LLM to evaluate their performance in low-resource BdSL translation. GPT-5.4 achieves the best automatic metric scores, while open-source models perform competitively despite being much smaller. This work introduces the first publicly available expert-annotated Bangla text-to-gloss dataset, benchmark and trained model for Bangla text-to-gloss translation. It also demonstrates the effectiveness of systematically generated synthetic data for addressing challenges in low-resource sign language translation.

authors.name: Sharif Mohammad Abdullah, Abhijit Paul, Shubhashis Roy Dipta, Zarif Masud, Shebuti Rayana, Ahmedul Kabir

papers.title: OpenClassGen: A Large-Scale Corpus of Real-World Python Classes for LLM Research
papers.summary: Existing class-level code generation datasets are either synthetic (ClassEval: 100 classes) or insufficient in scale for modern training needs (RealClassEval: 400 classes), hindering robust evaluation and empirical analysis. We present OpenClassGen, a large-scale corpus of 324,843 Python classes extracted from 2,970 engineered open-source projects. Each entry pairs a human-written class with its corresponding skeleton, which comprises class and method signatures with associated docstrings, and is enriched with 27 static code metrics covering complexity, coupling, cohesion, and inheritance properties. Unlike prior benchmarks that require repository-level context resolution, OpenClassGen provides self-contained class skeletons that serve as complete generation specifications. We demonstrate the corpus's utility by evaluating three LLMs (GPT-o4-mini, Claude-4-Sonnet, Qwen-3-Coder) on a curated, executable subset of 300 classes, enriched with test suites achieving 58% branch coverage. Results show strong semantic similarity (CodeBERTScore-F3: 0.89) but moderate functional correctness (pass rate: 0.33), with substantial variance across models. This variance, along with diverse class characteristics, confirms that OpenClassGen enables meaningful differentiation of LLM capabilities. The dataset supports diverse use cases, including fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, difficulty modelling, and failure mode analysis. The complete dataset and curation scripts are publicly available at https://zenodo.org/records/18409150.

authors.name: Musfiqur Rahman, SayedHassan Khatoonabadi, Emad Shihab

papers.title: Simple yet Effective Semi-supervised Knowledge Distillation from Vision-Language Models via Dual-Head Optimization
papers.summary: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a practical solution for addressing data scarcity challenges by leveraging unlabeled data. Recently, vision-language models (VLMs), pre-trained on massive image-text pairs, have demonstrated remarkable zero-/few-shot performance that often surpasses SSL approaches due to their exceptional generalization capabilities. This gap motivates us to question: how can we effectively harness the powerful generalization capabilities of VLMs into task-specific models? Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a natural framework for transferring VLM capabilities, but we identify that it suffers from gradient conflicts between supervised and distillation losses. To address this challenge, we propose Dual-Head Optimization (DHO), which introduces dual prediction heads for each distinct signal. We observe that DHO mitigates gradient conflicts, enabling improved feature learning compared to single-head KD baselines, with practical benefits of minimal computational overhead and test-time hyperparameter tuning without retraining. Extensive experiments across 15 datasets show that DHO consistently outperforms KD baselines, often outperforming teacher models with smaller student models. DHO also achieves new state-of-the-art performance on both in-distribution ImageNet semi-supervised learning and out-of-distribution generalization across ImageNet variants. Code and model checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/erjui/DHO/tree/main.

authors.name: Seongjae Kang, Dong Bok Lee, Hyungjoon Jang, Sung Ju Hwang

papers.title: Benign Overfitting of Two-Layer ReLU Networks in Fixed Dimension through Localized Initialization
papers.summary: Benign overfitting occurs when a model fits noisy training data exactly and still generalizes well. We establish this behavior for finite-width two-layer networks with the standard ReLU activation, trained by gradient flow in fixed dimension. Our data-independent initialization combines Gaussian weights with neurons initially active only on shrinking spherical caps. For uniform spherical inputs and any fixed bounded conditional response law, training and excess risks vanish in probability uniformly over all sufficiently late times. The parameters also converge, with probability tending to one, to an interpolating limit whose excess risk vanishes in probability. We use one schedule depending only on sample size and dimension. Our proof connects the network to a kernel flow whose limit combines ridge regression with localized spikes that fit the training residuals. We give explicit sample-size, width and training-time bounds.

authors.name: Junhyung Park, Patrick Bloebaum, Shiva Prasad Kasiviswanathan

papers.title: Learning-based Autonomous Oversteer Control and Collision Avoidance
papers.summary: Oversteer, wherein a vehicle's rear tires lose traction and induce unintentional excessive yaw, poses critical safety challenges. Failing to control oversteer often leads to severe traffic accidents. Although recent autonomous driving efforts have attempted to handle oversteer through stabilizing maneuvers, the majority rely on expert-defined trajectories or assume obstacle-free environments, limiting real-world applicability. This paper introduces a novel end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving approach that tackles oversteer control and collision avoidance simultaneously. Existing E2E techniques, including Imitation Learning (IL), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and Hybrid Learning (HL), generally require near-optimal demonstrations or extensive experience. Yet even skilled human drivers struggle to provide perfect demonstrations under oversteer, and high transition variance hinders the accumulation of sufficient data. Hence, we present Q-Compared Soft Actor-Critic (QC-SAC), a new HL algorithm that effectively learns from immature demonstration data and adapts rapidly to new conditions. To evaluate QC-SAC, we introduce a benchmark inspired by real-world driver training: a vehicle encounters sudden oversteer on a slippery surface and must avoid randomly placed obstacles ahead. Experimental results show that QC-SAC attains near-optimal driving policies, significantly surpassing state-of-the-art IL, RL, and HL baselines. Hardware-in-the-loop simulation (HILS) validation with physical steering hardware further demonstrates that QC-SAC can operate beyond a software-only simulation, providing an intermediate validation step toward real-vehicle implementation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that achieves safe autonomous control of vehicles in oversteer while simultaneously avoiding obstacles.

authors.name: Seokjun Lee, Seung-Hyun Kong

papers.title: But what is your honest answer? Aiding LLM-judges with honest alternatives using steering vectors
papers.summary: LLM-as-a-judge is widely used as a scalable substitute for human evaluation, yet judges are least reliable on subtle dishonesty such as sycophancy and manipulation, where a judge scoring a response in isolation lacks a reference point. We introduce Judge Using Safety-Steered Alternatives (JUSSA), a framework that reduces this evaluator uncertainty using the assessed model's own internal representations. An honesty-promoting steering vector, optimized from a single training example, generates a contrastive alternative against which each response is judged. On a new manipulation dataset with human-validated response pairs, JUSSA improves AUROC for both GPT-4.1 (0.893$\rightarrow$0.946) and Claude Haiku (0.859$\rightarrow$0.929) judges. The gains concentrate almost entirely on the pairs a judge would otherwise misrank. They reverse once a judge has saturated a task and for the weakest judge we test, so contrastive evaluation helps most when a judge is capable enough to use the reference but has not yet saturated the task. A layer-wise analysis further locates steering effectiveness in the middle layers, where model representations of honest and dishonest prompt processing diverge. Our work demonstrates that steering vectors can serve as tools for evaluation rather than for improving model outputs at inference, opening a new direction for white-box auditing.

authors.name: Leon Eshuijs, Archie Chaudhury, Alan McBeth, Ethan Nguyen

papers.title: Data-Driven Exploration for a Class of Continuous-Time Indefinite Linear--Quadratic Reinforcement Learning Problems
papers.summary: We study reinforcement learning (RL) for a class of continuous-time stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) control problems, where volatilities depend on both states and controls while states are scalar-valued and there are no running control rewards, the last feature also leading to the so-called indefinite LQ controls. We propose a model-free, data-driven exploration mechanism that adaptively adjusts entropy regularization by the critic and policy variance by the actor. Unlike the constant or deterministic exploration schedules employed in the existing literature, which require extensive tuning for implementations and ignore learning progress during iterations, our adaptive exploratory approach boosts learning efficiency with minimal tuning. Despite its flexibility, our method achieves a sublinear regret bound that matches the best-known model-free results for this class of LQ problems, which were previously derived only with fixed exploration schedules. Numerical experiments demonstrate that adaptive explorations accelerate convergence and improve regret performance compared to the non-adaptive model-free and model-based counterparts.

authors.name: Yilie Huang, Xun Yu Zhou

papers.title: Symbolic Branch Networks: Tree-Inherited Neural Models for Interpretable Multiclass Classification
papers.summary: Symbolic Branch Networks (SBNs) are neural models whose architecture is derived directly from an ensemble of decision trees. Each root-to-parent-of-leaf decision path is mapped to a hidden neuron, while the matrices W1 (feature-to-branch) and W2 (branch-to-class) encode the structural relationships induced by the teacher ensemble. This provides an explicit correspondence between teacher branches and neural components, enabling feature-level and branch-level interpretation while retaining the flexibility of gradient-based optimization. The primary configuration studied in this work trains the teacher-derived feature-to-branch matrix W1 through gradient-based learning while keeping the branch-to-class matrix W2 fixed; this configuration is denoted SBN1,0. Across 29 multiclass tabular datasets, this configuration improves upon the teacher ensemble on 28 of 29 datasets, increasing mean accuracy from 84.0% to 87.9%. For reference, XGBoost and TabPFN achieve mean accuracies of 87.3% and 91.3%, respectively, on the same datasets. A one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on dataset-level mean accuracies indicates a statistically significant improvement of SBN1,0 over the teacher ensemble (p=4.71x10-7). Beyond predictive performance, SBN provides an explicit structural basis for interpretation. Global feature importance can be derived from the teacher-induced feature-to-branch connectivity, while individual predictions can be traced to selected branch-neurons, their associated features, and their class contributions. An analysis across ten independently constructed teacher ensembles shows consistent predictions for a selected instance but only partial stability in its local feature rankings.

authors.name: Dalia N\"oth-Rodr\'iguez

papers.title: Are Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) Suitable for Imbalanced Data Classification?
papers.summary: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) parameterize each connection as a learnable univariate B-spline, offering native feature-level interpretability. Whether this locality helps or hinders under class imbalance, where minority sparsity may leave spline edges without enough local observations to update reliably, remains unexamined. We evaluate KANs against capacity-matched Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) and XGBoost across ten imbalanced tabular datasets under three conditions: native class distribution, Focal Loss, and SMOTE-Tomek resampling, within a parameter-parity, two-phase framework. Under the native distribution, KAN spline activations collapse in minority-sparse regions, showing stronger majority-class bias than the matched MLP. Focal Loss yields negligible improvement, as it reweights gradients without providing the localized observations needed for discriminative curvature. Conversely, SMOTE-Tomek resampling lets spline activations recover structured minority-class representations, achieving the best cohort-wide rank and a large, statistically significant gain over unmitigated KANs, though not over resampled baselines. KAN's native spline interpretability directly reveals these dynamics via learned activation profiles, proving representational change rather than threshold recalibration without post-hoc attribution. However, these interpretability gains incur substantially higher training overhead than a parameter-matched MLP across all conditions, with no strategy-dependent latency reduction. Thus, KANs are conditionally suitable for imbalanced tabular classification: effective and interpretable with data-level resampling, yet costly relative to simpler alternatives without it.

authors.name: Pankaj Yadav, Vivek Vijay

papers.title: A Disease-Centric Vision-Language Foundation Model for Precision Oncology in Kidney Cancer
papers.summary: The non-invasive assessment of renal masses remains a critical challenge in urologic oncology, where diagnostic uncertainty frequently causes overtreatment. Here, we develop RenalCLIP, a vision-language foundation model for precision oncology in kidney cancer. Utilizing 27,866 computed tomography scans from 8,809 patients across diverse multi-center cohorts, we employ a two-stage pre-training strategy to align domain-specific visual and textual representations. RenalCLIP achieves enhanced performance and generalizability across ten core clinical tasks, spanning anatomical assessment, diagnostic classification, and survival prediction, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art general-purpose foundation models. Furthermore, RenalCLIP demonstrates strong data efficiency in diagnostic classification, achieving peak baseline performance using only 20% of the training data. The model also exhibits robust zero-shot diagnostic capabilities, effective image-text retrieval, and high-quality medical report generation. Our findings establish RenalCLIP as a powerful, generalizable tool to enhance diagnostic precision, refine prognostic stratification, and personalize the management of renal masses.

authors.name: Yuhui Tao, Zhongwei Zhao, Zilong Wang, Xufang Luo, Feng Chen, Kang Wang, Chuanfu Wu, Xue Zhang, Shaoting Zhang, Jiaxi Yao, Xingwei Jin, Xinyang Jiang, Yifan Yang, Dongsheng Li, Lili Qiu, Zhiqiang Shao, Jianming Guo, Nengwang Yu, Shuo Wang, Ying Xiong

papers.title: AgriChrono: A Longitudinal Dataset and Benchmark for Novel-View Synthesis of Field-Grown Crops
papers.summary: Reliable 3D reconstruction of field-grown crops is hindered by thin, overlapping structures, wind-driven foliage motion, and changing illumination. Yet longitudinal field datasets and standardized novel-view synthesis (NVS) benchmarks remain scarce. We present an integrated framework for robotic acquisition, dataset construction, NVS evaluation, and agricultural scene reconstruction. AgriChrobot enables web-based teleoperation and repeated multi-view capture along crop rows. Using this platform, we introduce AgriChrono, a longitudinal canola dataset collected over approximately one month, comprising 160 recording sessions, four RGB streams, two depth maps, and estimated camera poses. We define seven NVS scenarios spanning four times of day and three acquisition dates, and benchmark 15 NeRF- and Gaussian Splatting-based methods. In addition to whole-image metrics, we assess fine-detail reconstruction within manually annotated canola regions using gradient- and edge-based metrics. Our results show that strong whole-image scores do not guarantee faithful reconstruction of thin, overlapping crop structures. To address this gap, we propose AgriSplat, which relaxes visibility filtering during initialization and reallocates model capacity through contribution-based pruning and budgeted reinvestment in sub-threshold candidates ranked by existing gradient statistics. After reallocation, asymmetric directional supervision penalizes insufficient contrast along reference image-gradient directions. Relative to Octree-GS, AgriSplat improves mean crop-region gradient-energy ratio from 0.506 to 0.847 and edge F-score from 0.712 to 0.797 across seven scenarios, while also improving whole-image PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. These contributions provide a dataset, benchmark, and method for systematic crop reconstruction under field conditions.

authors.name: Jaehwan Jeong, Tuan-Anh Vu, Mohammad Jony, Shahab Ahmad, Md. Mukhlesur Rahman, Sangpil Kim, M. Khalid Jawed

papers.title: A Survey on Cloud-Edge-Terminal Collaborative Intelligence in AIoT Networks
papers.summary: The proliferation of Internet of things (IoT) devices in smart cities, transportation, healthcare, and industrial applications, coupled with the explosive growth of AI-driven services, has increased demands for efficient distributed computing architectures and networks, driving cloud-edge-terminal collaborative intelligence (CETCI) as a fundamental paradigm within the artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) community. With advancements in deep learning, large language models (LLMs), and edge computing, CETCI has made significant progress with emerging AIoT applications, moving beyond isolated layer optimization to deployable collaborative intelligence systems for AIoT (CISAIOT), a practical research focus in AI, distributed computing, and communications. This survey describes foundational architectures, enabling technologies, and scenarios of CETCI paradigms, offering a tutorial-style review for CISAIOT beginners. We systematically analyze architectural components spanning cloud, edge, and terminal layers, examining core technologies including network virtualization, container orchestration, and software-defined networking, while presenting categorizations of collaboration paradigms that cover task offloading, resource allocation, and optimization across heterogeneous infrastructures. Furthermore, we explain intelligent collaboration learning frameworks by reviewing advances in federated learning, distributed deep learning, edge-cloud model evolution, and reinforcement learning-based methods. Finally, we discuss challenges (e.g., scalability, heterogeneity, interoperability) and future trends (e.g., 6G+, agents, quantum computing, digital twin), highlighting how integration of distributed computing and communication can address open issues and guide development of robust, efficient, and secure collaborative AIoT systems.

authors.name: Jiaqi Wu, Jing Liu, Yang Liu, Lixu Wang, Zehua Wang, Wei Chen, Zijian Tian, Richard Yu, Victor C. M. Leung

papers.title: Autonomous Learning From Success and Failure: Goal-Conditioned Supervised Learning with Negative Feedback
papers.summary: Learning from reward functions and imitation learning of demonstrations are the two principal approaches for training autonomous systems that interact with an environment through action and observation. Both, however, require human specification for each behaviour to be acquired, a problem for long-lived self-adaptive systems whose goals and operating conditions cannot be fully anticipated at design time. Recently, Goal-Conditioned Supervised Learning (GCSL) through self-imitation has been proposed as a self-supervised alternative: by strategically relabelling goals, agents can derive policy insights from their own experiences. Despite its successes, this framework presents two notable limitations: (1) learning exclusively from self-generated experiences can exacerbate the agents' inherent biases; (2) the relabelling strategy allows agents to focus solely on successful outcomes, precluding them from learning from their mistakes. To address these issues, we propose GCSL with Negative Feedback (GCSL-NF), which evaluates each trajectory twice: positively with respect to relabelled goals, and correctively with respect to the goal originally intended. The corrective target comes from a similarity function learned contrastively from trajectory-induced neighbourhood relations, so that neither a reward function nor a geometric distance needs to be specified. Our experiments show that GCSL-NF overcomes limitations imposed by agents' initial biases, increasingly benefits from negative feedback as learning progresses, and matches or surpasses GCSL- and HER-based methods. By reducing reliance on prespecified reward functions, the proposed approach is particularly relevant for self-adaptive autonomous systems, where adaptation objectives may be diverse, changing, or difficult to engineer.

authors.name: Zeqiang Zhang, Fabian Wurzberger, Gerrit Schmid, Sebastian Gottwald, Daniel A. Braun

papers.title: Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Asset-Liability Management
papers.summary: This paper proposes a novel approach for Asset-Liability Management (ALM) by employing continuous-time Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a linear-quadratic (LQ) formulation that incorporates both interim and terminal objectives. We develop a model-free, policy gradient-based soft actor-critic algorithm tailored to ALM for dynamically synchronizing assets and liabilities. To ensure an effective balance between exploration and exploitation with minimal tuning, we introduce adaptive exploration for the actor and scheduled exploration for the critic. Our empirical study evaluates this approach against two enhanced traditional financial strategies, a model-based continuous-time RL method, and three state-of-the-art RL algorithms. Evaluated across 200 randomized market scenarios, our method achieves higher average rewards than all alternative strategies, with rapid initial gains and sustained superior performance. The outperformance stems not from complex neural networks or improved parameter estimation, but from directly learning the optimal ALM strategy without learning the environment.

authors.name: Yilie Huang

papers.title: Space Group Conditional Flow Matching
papers.summary: Inorganic crystals are periodic, highly-symmetric arrangements of atoms in three-dimensional space. Their structures are constrained by the symmetry operations of a crystallographic \emph{space group} and restricted to lie in specific affine subspaces known as \emph{Wyckoff positions}. The frequency an atom appears in the crystal and its rough positioning are determined by its Wyckoff position. Most generative models that predict atomic coordinates overlook these symmetry constraints, leading to unrealistically high populations of proposed crystals exhibiting limited symmetry. We introduce Space Group Conditional Flow Matching, a novel generative framework that samples significantly closer to the target population of highly-symmetric, stable crystals. We achieve this by conditioning the entire generation process on a given space group and set of Wyckoff positions; specifically, we define a conditionally symmetric noise base distribution and a group-conditioned, equivariant, parametric vector field that restricts the motion of atoms to their initial Wyckoff position. Our form of group-conditioned equivariance is achieved using an efficient reformulation of \emph{group averaging} tailored for symmetric crystals. Importantly, it reduces the computational overhead of symmetrization to a negligible level. We achieve state of the art results on crystal structure prediction and de novo generation benchmarks. We also perform relevant ablations.

authors.name: Omri Puny, Yaron Lipman, Benjamin Kurt Miller

papers.title: Chance-constrained Flow Matching for High-Fidelity Constraint-aware Generation
papers.summary: Generative models excel at synthesizing high-fidelity samples from complex data distributions, but they often violate hard constraints arising from physical laws or task specifications. A common remedy is to project intermediate samples onto the feasible set at each sampling step. However, repeated projection can disrupt the learned sampling dynamics because this feasible set is defined for clean samples rather than noisy intermediate states. Thus, recent studies first estimate clean samples and then project them to the feasible set, but this increases algorithmic complexity and accumulates errors across steps. To address these issues, this paper proposes Chance-constrained Flow Matching (CCFM), a training-free method that formulates constraint enforcement during sampling as stochastic optimization while retaining the hard-constraint feasibility guarantee of projection-based methods. By avoiding direct projection of noisy intermediate states onto the clean-sample feasible set, CCFM mitigates the distributional distortion. Unlike approaches that first estimate and project clean samples, CCFM avoids complex multi-stage procedures. Experiments show that CCFM outperforms current state-of-the-art constrained generative models in modeling complex physical systems governed by partial differential equations, molecular docking problems, and physics-informed motion generation, delivering superior feasibility and fidelity.

authors.name: Jinhao Liang, Yixuan Sun, Anirban Samaddar, Sandeep Madireddy, Ferdinando Fioretto

papers.title: Feedback Forensics: A Toolkit to Measure AI Personality
papers.summary: Some traits making a "good" AI model are hard to describe upfront. For example, should responses be more polite or more casual? Such traits are sometimes summarized as model character or personality. Without a clear objective, conventional benchmarks based on automatic checks struggle to measure such traits. Evaluation methods using human feedback such as Chatbot Arena have emerged as a popular alternative. These methods infer "better" personality and other desirable traits implicitly by ranking multiple model responses relative to each other. Recent issues with model releases highlight limitations of these existing opaque evaluation approaches: goblin-obsessed, sycophantic and generally over-the-top personalities have resulted in model rollbacks and extensive media coverage. Despite these known issues, limited public tooling exists to explicitly evaluate model personality. We introduce Feedback Forensics: an open-source toolkit to track AI personality and related behavioural traits, both those encouraged by human (or AI) feedback, and those exhibited across AI models trained and evaluated on such feedback. Feedback Forensics is adaptive and can automatically find new traits appearing in models. We demonstrate the toolkit's usefulness in two steps: (A) first we analyse the personality traits encouraged in popular human feedback datasets including MultiPref, PRISM and data from Chatbot Arena; and (B) then use our toolkit to analyse how much popular models exhibit such traits. We release (1) our Feedback Forensics toolkit alongside (2) a web app tracking AI personality in popular models and feedback datasets and (3) the underlying annotation data, see https://github.com/rdnfn/feedback-forensics.

authors.name: Arduin Findeis, Timo Kaufmann, Eyke H\"ullermeier, Robert Mullins

papers.title: Formally Verified Certification of Unsolvability of Temporal Planning Problems
papers.summary: We present an approach to unsolvability certification of temporal planning. Our approach is based on encoding the planning problem into a network of timed automata, and then using an efficient model checker on the network followed by a certificate checker to certify the output of the model checker. Our approach prioritises trustworthiness of the certification: we formally verify our implementation of the encoding to timed automata using the theorem prover Isabelle/HOL and we use an existing certificate checker (also formally verified in Isabelle/HOL) to certify the model checking result.

authors.name: David Wang, Mohammad Abdulaziz

papers.title: Readers Prefer Outputs of AI Trained on Copyrighted Books over Expert Human Writers
papers.summary: The use of copyrighted books for training AI has sparked lawsuits from authors concerned about AI generating derivative content. Yet whether these models can produce high-quality literary text emulating authors' voices remains unclear. We conducted a preregistered study comparing MFA-trained writers with three frontier models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) writing up to 450-word excerpts emulating 50 award-winning authors' styles. In blind pairwise evaluations by 28 MFA-trained readers and 516 college-educated general readers, AI text from in-context prompting was strongly disfavored by MFA readers for stylistic fidelity (OR=0.16) and quality (OR=0.13), while general readers showed no fidelity preference (OR=1.06) but favored AI for quality (OR=1.82). Fine-tuning ChatGPT on authors' complete works reversed these results: MFA readers favored AI for fidelity (OR=8.16) and quality (OR=1.87), with general readers showing even stronger preference (fidelity OR=16.65; quality OR=5.42). Both groups preferred fine-tuned AI, but the writer-type X reader-type interaction remained significant (p=0.021 for fidelity; p<10^-4 for quality), indicating general readers favored AI by a wider margin. Effects are robust under cluster-robust inference and generalize across authors in heterogeneity analyses. Fine-tuned outputs were rarely flagged as AI-generated (3% vs. 97% for prompting) by leading detectors. Mediation analysis shows fine-tuning eliminates detectable AI quirks that penalize in-context outputs, altering the nexus between detectability and preference. While not accounting for effort to transform AI output into publishable prose, the median fine-tuning cost of $81 per author represents a 99.7% reduction versus typical writer compensation. Author-specific fine-tuning enables non-verbatim AI writing preferred over expert human writing, providing evidence relevant to copyright's fourth fair-use factor.

authors.name: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Jane C. Ginsburg, Paramveer Dhillon

papers.title: EDVD-LLaMA: Explainable Deepfake Video Detection via Multimodal Large Language Model Reasoning
papers.summary: The rapid development of deepfake video technology has not only facilitated artistic creation but also made it easier to spread misinformation, which is increasingly difficult to identify. Traditional deepfake video detection (DVD) methods face issues such as a lack of transparency in their principles and insufficient generalization capabilities to cope with evolving forgery techniques. This highlights an urgent need for detectors that can identify forged content and provide verifiable reasoning explanations. This paper proposes the explainable deepfake video detection (EDVD) task and designs the EDVD-LLaMA multimodal, a large language model (MLLM) reasoning framework, which provides traceable reasoning processes alongside accurate detection results and trustworthy explanations. Our approach first incorporates a Spatio-Temporal Subtle Information Tokenization (ST-SIT) to extract and fuse global and local cross-frame deepfake features, providing rich spatio-temporal semantic information input for MLLM reasoning. Second, we construct a Fine-grained Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (Fg-MCoT) mechanism, which introduces facial feature data as hard constraints during the reasoning process to achieve pixel-level spatio-temporal video localization, suppress hallucinated outputs, and enhance the reliability of the chain of thought. In addition, we build an Explainable Reasoning FF++ benchmark dataset (ER-FF++set), leveraging structured data to annotate videos and ensure quality control, thereby supporting dual supervision for reasoning and detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EDVD-LLaMA achieves outstanding performance and robustness in terms of detection accuracy, explainability, and its ability to handle cross-forgery methods and cross-dataset scenarios. Compared to previous DVD methods, it provides a more explainable and superior solution.

authors.name: Haoran Sun, Chen Cai, Huiping Zhuang, Kong Aik Lee, Lap-Pui Chau, Yi Wang

papers.title: A Survey of Data Agents: Emerging Paradigm or Overstated Hype?
papers.summary: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has spurred the emergence of data agents, autonomous systems designed to orchestrate Data + AI ecosystems for tackling complex data-related tasks. However, the term "data agent" currently suffers from terminological ambiguity and inconsistent adoption, conflating simple query responders with sophisticated autonomous architectures. This terminological ambiguity fosters mismatched user expectations, accountability challenges, and barriers to industry growth. Inspired by the SAE J3016 standard for driving automation, this survey introduces the first systematic hierarchical taxonomy for data agents, comprising six levels that delineate and trace progressive shifts in autonomy, from manual operations (L0) to a vision of generative, fully autonomous data agents (L5), thereby clarifying capability boundaries and responsibility allocation. Through this lens, we offer a structured review of existing research arranged by increasing autonomy, encompassing specialized data agents for data management, preparation, and analysis, alongside emerging efforts toward versatile, comprehensive systems with enhanced autonomy. We further analyze critical evolutionary leaps and technical gaps for advancing data agents, especially the ongoing L2-to-L3 transition, where data agents evolve from procedural execution to autonomous orchestration. Finally, we conclude with a forward-looking roadmap, envisioning proactive, generative data agents. A curated companion repository is available at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/awesome-data-agents.

authors.name: Yizhang Zhu, Liangwei Wang, Chenyu Yang, Xiaotian Lin, Boyan Li, Wei Zhou, Xinyu Liu, Zhangyang Peng, Tianqi Luo, Yu Li, Chengliang Chai, Chong Chen, Shimin Di, Ju Fan, Ji Sun, Nan Tang, Fugee Tsung, Jiannan Wang, Chenglin Wu, Yanwei Xu, Shaolei Zhang, Yong Zhang, Xuanhe Zhou, Guoliang Li, Yuyu Luo

papers.title: Beyond Synthetic Benchmarks: Evaluating LLM Performance on Real-World Class-Level Code Generation
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly from well-studied function-level code generation to emerging repository-level approaches, yet this progression reveals a critical gap: class-level code generation, which is the fundamental building block connecting individual functions to complete repositories, remains systematically underexplored. Understanding class-level capabilities is a prerequisite to repository-level success, as current approaches cannot distinguish whether failures stem from basic implementation deficiencies or sophisticated context management issues. We introduce RealClassEval, a benchmark derived from real-world open-source repositories, comprising 400 classes divided into seen and unseen partitions based on model training cutoffs. Our systematic evaluation across seven state-of-the-art LLMs reveals fundamental limitations masked by synthetic benchmarks: while LLMs achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks, they attain only 25 to 34% on real-world classes, with minimal distinction between seen and unseen codebases. Notably, this performance range converges with concurrent work using rich natural language descriptions and repository context, suggesting that specification complexity cannot overcome core implementation bottlenecks. Documentation provides marginal improvements (1 to 3%), while retrieval augmentation yields greater gains (4 to7%), specifically with incomplete specifications. Error analysis reveals AttributeError, TypeError, and AssertionError dominate 84% of failures, with distinct patterns between synthetic (logic-focused) and real-world (object-oriented) scenarios. These findings establish the diagnostic foundation necessary for advancing both fundamental LLM capabilities and sophisticated repository-level approaches, while providing actionable guidance for production deployment strategies.

authors.name: Musfiqur Rahman, SayedHassan Khatoonabadi, Emad Shihab

papers.title: SEPS: Semantic-enhanced Patch Slimming Framework for fine-grained cross-modal alignment
papers.summary: Fine-grained cross-modal alignment aims to establish precise local correspondences between vision and language, forming a cornerstone for visual question answering and related multimodal applications. Current approaches face challenges in addressing patch redundancy and ambiguity, which arise from the inherent information density disparities across modalities. Recently, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have emerged as promising solutions to bridge this gap through their robust semantic generation capabilities. However, the dense textual outputs from MLLMs may introduce conflicts with the original sparse captions. Furthermore, accurately quantifying semantic relevance between rich visual patches and concise textual descriptions remains a core challenge. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Semantic-Enhanced Patch Slimming (SEPS) framework, which systematically addresses patch redundancy and ambiguity. Our approach employs a two-stage mechanism to integrate unified semantics from both dense and sparse texts, enabling the identification of salient visual patches. Additionally, it leverages relevance-aware selection with mean value computation to highlight crucial patch-word correspondences, thereby improving cross-modal similarity assessment. Comprehensive experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO datasets validate that SEPS achieves superior performance, surpassing existing approaches by 23\%-86\% in rSum across diverse model architectures, with notable enhancements in text-to-image retrieval scenarios. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/Sweet4tars/seps.git.

authors.name: Xinyu Mao, Junsi Li, Haoji Zhang, Yu Liang, Ming Sun

papers.title: SciEGQA: A Dataset for Scientific Evidence-Grounded Question Answering and Reasoning
papers.summary: Scientific documents contain complex multimodal structures, which makes evidence localization and scientific reasoning in Document Visual Question Answering particularly challenging. However, most existing benchmarks evaluate models only at the page level without explicitly annotating the evidence regions that support the answer, which limits both interpretability and the reliability of evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce SciEGQA, a scientific document question answering and reasoning dataset with semantic evidence grounding, where supporting evidence is represented as semantically coherent document regions annotated with bounding boxes. SciEGQA consists of two components: a **human-annotated fine-grained benchmark** containing 1,623 high-quality question--answer pairs, and a **large-scale automatically constructed training set** with over 30K QA pairs generated through an automated data construction pipeline. Extensive experiments on a wide range of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) show that existing models still struggle with evidence localization and evidence-based question answering in scientific documents. Training on the proposed dataset significantly improves the scientific reasoning capabilities of VLMs. The project page is available at https://yuwenhan07.github.io/SciEGQA-project/.

authors.name: Wenhan Yu, Zhaoxi Zhang, Wang Chen, Guanqiang Qi, Weikang Li, Lei Sha, Deguo Xia, Jizhou Huang

papers.title: Diffusion-based Surrogate Model for Time-varying Underwater Acoustic Channels
papers.summary: Accurate modeling of time-varying underwater acoustic channels is essential for the design, evaluation, and deployment of reliable underwater communication systems. Conventional physics models require detailed environmental knowledge, while stochastic replay methods are constrained by the limited diversity of measured channels and often fail to generalize to unseen scenarios, reducing their practical applicability. To address these challenges, we propose StableUASim, a pre-trained conditional latent diffusion surrogate model that captures the stochastic dynamics of underwater acoustic communication channels. Leveraging generative modeling, StableUASim produces diverse and statistically realistic channel realizations, while supporting conditional generation from specific measurement samples. Pre-training enables rapid adaptation to new environments using minimal additional data, and the autoencoder latent representation facilitates efficient channel analysis and compression. Experimental results demonstrate that StableUASim accurately reproduces key channel characteristics and communication performance, providing a scalable, data-efficient, and physically consistent surrogate model for both system design and machine learning-driven underwater applications. In this work, we focus on sparse underwater channels, and expanding the diversity of the pre-training dataset is expected to further improve generalization to a broader range of underwater propagation environments.

authors.name: Kexin Li, Mandar Chitre

papers.title: Re(Visiting) Time Series Foundation Models in Finance
papers.summary: Financial time series forecasting is vital for trading, portfolio optimization, and risk management but is challenged by noisy, nonstationary, and heterogeneous data. Time series foundation models (TSFMs), inspired by large language models, aim to learn transferable temporal representations. Whether pre-training on massive, diverse datasets enables similar generalization to finance remains an open question. This study provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation of TSFMs in global financial markets using large-scale daily excess-return data. We assess zero-shot inference, fine-tuning, and pre-training from scratch against strong benchmarks. Off-the-shelf TSFMs generally perform poorly, while finance-native pre-training improves long-window gross portfolio performance. Larger pre-training datasets and synthetic augmentation improve selected specifications, particularly at longer input windows. Configuration changes have mixed effects across forecasting and portfolio metrics, and TSFMs do not consistently outperform strong benchmarks. These findings caution against uncritical AI adoption in finance, where insufficient validation can lead to unreliable forecasts and substantial financial losses.

authors.name: Eghbal Rahimikia, Hao Ni, Weiguan Wang

papers.title: A Layered Protocol Architecture for the Internet of Agents
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can learn domain-specific languages such as APIs and tool interfaces, enabling agents that act through standardized protocols like MCP. But LLM context windows cannot grow indefinitely, so scaling beyond individual capacity requires agent collaboration: the "Internet of Agents" (IoA). Current network stacks (OSI, TCP/IP) were designed for data delivery, not semantic coordination, so we propose two new layers: an Agent Communication Layer (L8) that standardizes message envelopes, speech-act performatives, and interaction patterns; and an Agent Semantic Layer (L9) that negotiates a shared context, grounds and disambiguates content against it, and provides consensus primitives for population-scale coordination. On two real datasets and two LLMs, L9's schema-grounded disambiguation improves accuracy on ambiguous requests by 13--72 percentage points over blind guessing, at no added cost when disambiguation is not needed; an ablation shows this gain is schema-specific for open-domain QA but not for structured slot-filling, where the protocol's round-trip structure alone already suffices.

authors.name: Charles Fleming, Luca Muscariello, Vijoy Pandey, Ramana Kompella

papers.title: CrypTorch: Unified PyTorch-based Auto-tuning Compiler for Private Machine Learning Inference
papers.summary: MPC-based ML uses secure multi-party computation (MPC) to execute machine learning (ML) workloads across multiple parties without requiring any party to reveal its private data or model parameters. Our characterization study finds that the performance of state-of-the-art MPC frameworks is often dominated by operator-approximation strategies, where ML operators not natively supported by MPC are replaced with iterative methods or polynomials. These approximations are typically chosen heuristically by each framework and applied globally. As a result, they can be unnecessarily expensive in some cases, yet insufficiently accurate in others. We find that the best approximation choice depends on the context, target framework, and application, making a single globally fixed approximation fundamentally suboptimal. To address this problem, we design CrypTorch, a multi-stage compiler for MPC-based ML that supports multiple MPC frameworks as backends. At the core of CrypTorch is its auto-tuning stage, which extracts cost estimates from the target MPC backend and quality estimates from a proxy PyTorch execution, and uses them to automatically select a set of approximations that maximizes performance while satisfying the given quality constraint. We show that CrypTorch's auto-tuner improves performance across multiple MPC backends by 1.14--1.60x without degrading accuracy, and by 1.17--1.92x with less than 3% accuracy degradation. CrypTorch's unified design also improves programmability and usability by allowing multiple backends to share other common compiler functionality and optimizations. We further show that the auto-tuner extends to a related fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) backend, reducing the number of bootstrapping operations by 1.31--1.65x.

authors.name: Jinyu Liu, Gang Tan, Kiwan Maeng

papers.title: A Survey of Bugs in AI-Generated Code
papers.summary: AI coding systems are increasingly used to help developers write code at scale, improving software development efficiency and boosting productivity. While these models and agents have shown strong performance, concerns persist regarding the quality of the AI-generated code. Although prior work has reported a range of quality issues associated with AI-generated code, these findings remain scattered and lack a systematic synthesis. A comprehensive review is lacking that demonstrates the bug types, patterns, distribution, their correlation with specific AI coding systems, and the remediation strategies proposed to address them. To fill this gap, we conduct a systematic literature review of existing studies on AI-generated code to develop a comprehensive understanding of bugs in the generated code and provide a foundation for future improvements in AI-assisted coding. Our results show that bugs are widespread in AI-generated code, with functional and stability bugs emerging as the most frequently reported categories across the reviewed studies, a substantial proportion of which is attributed to model hallucination. Model size, instruction-following capability, and the quality and diversity of training data are key factors influencing bug occurrence. To mitigate bugs, prompt engineering techniques are widely used; however, certain domain-specific or semantically complex issues remain difficult to resolve automatically and still require human intervention.

authors.name: Ruofan Gao, Amjed Tahir, Peng Liang, Teo Susnjak, Ali Soltanian Fard Jahromi, Foutse Khomh

papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of Embedding Representations for Financial News Sentiment Analysis
papers.summary: Financial sentiment analysis enhances market understanding. However, standard Natural Language Processing (NLP) approaches encounter significant challenges when applied to small datasets. This study presents a comparative evaluation of embedding-based techniques for financial news sentiment classification in resource-constrained environments. Word2Vec, GloVe, and sentence transformer representations are evaluated in combination with gradient boosting on a manually labeled dataset of 349 financial news headlines. Experimental results identify a substantial gap between validation and test performance. Despite strong validation metrics, models underperform relative to trivial baselines. The analysis indicates that pretrained embeddings yield diminishing returns below a critical data sufficiency threshold. Small validation sets contribute to overfitting during model selection. Practical application is illustrated through weekly sentiment aggregation and narrative summarization for market monitoring. Overall, the findings indicate that embedding quality alone cannot address fundamental data scarcity in sentiment classification. Practitioners with limited labeled data should consider alternative strategies, including few-shot learning, data augmentation, or lexicon-enhanced hybrid methods.

authors.name: Joyjit Roy, Samaresh Kumar Singh

papers.title: From Evidence to Judgment: Trace-Augmented Reasoning under Conflicting Evidence
papers.summary: Retrieved documents often disagree, contain outdated information, or fail to support any answer, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have no reliable way to decide which documents to trust. We treat this as a reasoning problem and test it separately from answer generation. We release 943 training and validation examples and a disjoint 736-example benchmark, and fine-tune four language models to write a structured think trace before answering: the model judges each document, infers the conflict pattern, and writes a grounded answer or a justified refusal. Our evaluation framework, CATS (Conflict-Aware Trust Score), scores grounded refusal, behavioural adherence, factual grounding, and single-truth recall; a human study validates factual grounding and single-truth recall (kappa=0.78 and 0.79). The think trace improves the answer/refuse decision: under all three prompts, untuned models score at most 0.429 Refusal F1 (F1 with refusal as the positive class) and trace-tuned models at least 0.826. On the answerable examples a model answers, factual grounding under the 40-word prompt is at most 0.11 for untuned and 0.86-0.88 for trace-tuned models. Cutting the prompt from 1,965 words to 40 leaves trace-tuned scores within the benchmark's measurement noise (+/-0.034). Answer-only fine-tuning trails trace supervision on every metric under the minimal prompt.

authors.name: Shubham Mishra, Atharv Sharma, Dhruv Kumar, Harsh Sharma

papers.title: VeruSAGE-Bench: A Benchmark Suite for Rust System Verification
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive capability to understand and develop code. However, their capability to rigorously reason about and formally prove the correctness of software systems remains in question. Current benchmarks for formal proof generation focus on isolated tasks, typically algorithmic-style problems utilizing basic data structures. We curate a new benchmark suite for system-level proof generation, VeruSAGE-Bench, which consists of 849 proof tasks extracted from eight open-source Verus-verified Rust systems, covering operating systems, storage systems, memory allocators, and more. These tasks are much more complicated than those in previous benchmarks, containing on average more than 20x the formal specification (in Lines of Code) and requiring a much broader array of verification techniques. We evaluate six LLMs on VeruSAGE-Bench (o4-mini, GPT-5, Sonnet 4, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, Qwen3.5), and demonstrate that different models and agentic setups lead to vastly different success rates and costs. We also show that the best models possess impressive capability in writing correctness proofs and hence should inspire new ways of developing trustworthy software. Meanwhile, some difficult tasks in VeruSAGE-Bench stress even the best model, forcing long reasoning time (over an hour on the hardest tasks, 15.3 min per task on average), high token cost (USD 13.65 per task on average), and proof failures, which we hope will guide future improvements in models and agents. This is particularly true for a harder no-lemma version of VeruSAGE-Bench, where the helper lemmas written by human experts are removed: there, the best model proves only 41% of the tasks from the hardest project, at USD 96 per task.

authors.name: Chenyuan Yang, Natalie Neamtu, Chris Hawblitzel, Jacob R. Lorch, Shan Lu

papers.title: MHRC-Bench: A Multilingual Hardware Repository-Level Code Completion benchmark
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on code completion in general-purpose programming languages, but existing repository-level benchmarks focus almost exclusively on software code and largely overlook hardware description languages (HDLs). We present \textbf{MHRC-Bench}, consisting of \textbf{MHRC-Bench-Train} and \textbf{MHRC-Bench-Eval}, the first benchmark for multilingual hardware code completion at the repository level with functional evaluation. MHRC-Bench covers three major hardware design coding styles and annotates each completion target with code-structure-level and hardware-oriented semantic labels derived from concrete syntax tree (CST) analysis. Post-training billion-scale code LLMs on MHRC-Bench-Train enables smaller open-weight models to outperform much larger general-purpose models under matched context windows. Beyond aggregate accuracy, our analysis surfaces four findings that distinguish hardware from software code completion: \emph{(i)}~performance varies sharply across HDLs, with high-level synthesis (HLS) easiest and VHDL hardest in most settings across functional pass rate, exact match (EM), and edit similarity (ES); \emph{(ii)}~hardware accuracy is non-monotonic in code-structure depth, in contrast with the monotonic depth--accuracy curve known for software; \emph{(iii)}~accuracy plateaus once the input context exceeds 2{,}048 tokens, while software completion continues to benefit from longer context; and \emph{(iv)}~certain repository-level retrievers tuned on software underperform a no-retrieval baseline on HDL repositories because their structural and dependency assumptions are violated by hardware code.

authors.name: Qingyun Zou, Jiahao Cui, Nuo Chen, Bingsheng He, Weng-Fai Wong

papers.title: VIOLA: Towards Video In-Context Learning with Minimal Annotations
papers.summary: Generalizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to novel video domains is essential for real-world deployment but remains challenging due to the scarcity of labeled data. While In-Context Learning (ICL) offers a training-free adaptation path, standard methods rely on large annotated pools, which are often impractical in specialized environments like industrial or surgical settings since they require the experts' annotations. To bridge this gap, we introduce VIOLA (Video In-cOntext Learning with minimal Annotation), a label-efficient framework that synergizes minimal expert supervision with abundant unlabeled data. First, to maximize the efficiency of a strict annotation budget, we propose density-uncertainty-weighted sampling. Unlike standard diversity or uncertainty strategies that risk selecting visual outliers, our method leverages density estimation to identify samples that are simultaneously diverse, representative, and informative. Second, to utilize the remaining unlabeled data without noise propagation, we construct a hybrid pool and introduce confidence-aware retrieval and confidence-aware prompting. These mechanisms explicitly model label reliability, retrieving demonstrations based on a composite score of similarity and confidence while enabling the MLLM to adaptively distinguish between verified ground truths and noisy pseudo-labels. Extensive experiments across nine diverse benchmarks using three MLLMs demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms various baselines in low-resource settings, achieving robust adaptation with minimal annotation costs. Project page: https://fujiry0.github.io/VIOLA-project-page/

authors.name: Ryo Fujii, Hideo Saito, Ryo Hachiuma

papers.title: Will It Survive? Deciphering the Fate of AI Agent-Authored Code in Open Source
papers.summary: AI coding agents such as GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex and Devin now open pull requests (PRs) that are merged into open-source projects. Industry reports suggest that AI-assisted code is revised or reverted soon after it is written, which raises the concern that agent code is "disposable". However, little is known about what happens to agent code after it is merged. Knowing how long this code survives, and why it is changed, can help maintainers decide how much review it needs. We performed a survival analysis of the 648,959 lines that 2,794 merged PRs added outside vendored and generated paths in 215 open-source repositories from the AIDev dataset, comparing agent-attributed and human code within the same repositories. Agent-attributed code is not modified sooner than human code. When each PR is weighted equally, agent-attributed lines are modified later (HR = 0.83, 95% CI [0.75, 0.93]). This difference comes from the supervised assistants, mainly Copilot and Codex (HR = 0.76). Code from Devin does not differ from human code over the whole period (HR = 0.95), but among PRs merged after mid-May 2025, code from both the supervised assistants and Devin is modified later. Without PR weighting, the difference is not statistically significant. When agent-attributed code is modified, the intent of the change is similar to that of human code (Cramer's V = 0.080). A file's size and recent changes predict whether agent-attributed code will be modified better than its code tokens do (AUC-ROC 0.78 vs. 0.70), and process features predict when it will be modified only weakly (Macro F1 of 0.31 against 0.25 for a random guess). Our findings suggest that agent code is not disposable, but whether it survives longer than human code depends on the agent, on when the code was merged and on how the comparison is computed.

authors.name: Musfiqur Rahman, Mahi Begoug, Emad Shihab

papers.title: Probing the Trajectories of Reasoning Traces in Large Language Models
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly solve difficult problems by producing reasoning traces before emitting a final response. However, it remains unclear how accuracy and decision commitment evolve along a reasoning trajectory, and whether intermediate trace segments provide answer-relevant information beyond generic length or stylistic effects. Here, we propose a trajectory-probing protocol for evaluating how a reasoning model's predicted answer evolves along a partial reasoning trace. The protocol (1) generates a model's full reasoning trace, (2) truncates it at fixed token-percentiles, and (3) injects each partial trace back into the model, measuring the model's induced answer distribution. We apply the protocol to seven open-source reasoning models (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, gpt-oss-20b/120b, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and Gemma-4-31B-it) across four benchmarks (GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, Omni-MATH-2 and CompMath). The protocol reveals that accuracy and decision commitment generally increase as the percentage of provided reasoning tokens grows, and length, form, and token-identity controls confirm that gains stem from instance-specific semantic content rather than context length or generic reasoning style effects. Furthermore, cross-model probing shows that even stronger models frequently repeat the source model's errors when given its partial reasoning trace, while allowing further reasoning substantially improves recovery.
