This emulator is trained on over 200,000 samples, each consisting of a pair of landslide thicknesses and velocities on a given DEM with a fixed time interval. To constrain the model's physical consistency, we define physics-based loss functions based on mass conservation and the system's kinetic energy loss. The model demonstrates high fidelity across the test dataset, achieving root mean square errors of approximately 0.06 m for thickness and 0.11 m/s for velocity in single-step predictions. In autoregressive rollout, these errors evolved modestly to about 0.21 m and 0.09 m/s after 110 iterations, while greatly improving computational efficiency by more than 50 times.

authors.name: Ye Chen, Lorenzo Nava, Maximillian Van Wyk de Vries, Fawu Wang

papers.title: Cap-Aware Boosting for Green Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting
papers.summary: Accurate forecasting of Green Day-Ahead Market (GDAM) electricity prices is essential for market participants in the Indian power sector. We present a LightGBM-based forecasting framework for Indian Energy Exchange GDAM prices, which clear in 96 fifteen-minute intervals per day. The proposed system explicitly models price-cap behavior by separating capped-price events from normal market conditions. A classification head estimates the probability of the regulatory price cap (Rs 10,000/MWh), while a regression head predicts uncapped prices in logarithmic space. Final forecasts are obtained through probabilistic blending of these components and are accompanied by nine quantile forecasts for uncertainty estimation. Evaluated on 257 trading days between 1 January and 14 September 2026, the model achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 397.9 Rs/MWh and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 9.57%, substantially outperforming a Chronos-2 baseline (583.3 MAE) and a persistence baseline using the previous day's profile (589.1 MAE). We further introduce leak-safe variants that incorporate real-time market signals, unmatched sell volumes, and solar generation proxies. In a recent out-of-sample evaluation, the quantile-clock variant achieved the best short-term performance with an MAE of 789 Rs/MWh during 25-28 October, while the enhanced capped-price model achieved an MAE of 716 Rs/MWh across 21 evaluation days through 16 November. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of regime-aware probabilistic forecasting for high-volatility electricity markets.

authors.name: Shubham Pratap

papers.title: When Feature Representation Changes Local Explanations: A Controlled Comparison of SHAP and LIME under Numerical Discretization
papers.summary: Local feature attributions are computed over a feature representation chosen by an upstream data-engineering step, yet they are read as statements about the underlying quantity. We ask how discretizing one continuous feature changes local KernelSHAP and LIME explanations when the classifier is held fixed, and whether the two explainers respond differently. A random forest is trained on UCI Adult and frozen; age is collapsed onto equi-width or quantile bin representatives (k in {3,5,10}) before the model receives it, and the same 120 held-out instances are explained in every condition across multiple seeds. We show analytically and numerically that for KernelSHAP this is exactly equivalent to explaining the unchanged model at the quantized instance against a quantized background, so the comparison is between two effective inputs rather than a pure explainer effect; for LIME no such equivalence holds. Each attribution change is compared with a seed-noise floor from re-running the explainer on the unchanged condition. KernelSHAP's age attribution exceeds its noise floor in all 6 pre-specified conditions (median ratios 2.4-59, all significant after Holm correction); on the raw scale LIME's exceeds its floor in only 2 of 6 and in the rest is no larger than its own run-to-run variation. SHAP's normalized change exceeds LIME's in every condition (rank-biserial 0.81-1.00), while LIME is 2.5-4.6x less consistent across repeats. Predicted classes change for only 0.8-5.8% of instances and held-out ROC-AUC never falls below 0.9097, yet 45-94% of instances show a large SHAP attribution change with no class flip. Feature-importance rankings barely move (median Spearman >= 0.979, top-3 overlap 1.00). The representation change and the change in effective input cannot be separated within a frozen-model design.

authors.name: Parv Patel (Indian Institute of Technology Palakkad)

papers.title: Determining Concentration from Raman Spectroscopy with Manifold Learning and Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoders
papers.summary: Monitoring of chemical processes is crucial in chemical engineering, motivating sophisticated process analytical technology (PAT). In-line analytics are advantageous, with Raman spectroscopy being an established and reliable tool in various applications, from which many properties can be determined. We recently [Koronaki et al., AIChEJ 2024] proposed determining polymer particle size from Raman spectroscopic data, by combining Diffusion Maps (a manifold learning method) with a Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoder Neural Network. Herein, we extend this workflow to predict liquid concentrations, allowing also for multiple target predictions from the same model. We apply the methods on two datasets consisting of Raman measurements and concentration measurements: one from microgel polymerization and one from citric acid dissociation. The single-target concentration prediction results, where one target is determined from each model at a time, are accurate. Comparing against dedicated methods such as Indirect Hard Modeling (IHM) is not straightforward, due to the different validation strategies and the considered spectra range; nevertheless, it is fair to say that IHM performs slightly better than the proposed workflow. We further compare this approach with other regression methods, such as artificial neural networks, extreme gradient boosting and partial least squares, and the results show that the Conformal Autoencoders achieve higher predictive performance, demonstrating that the workflow can also be used for concentration determination. Finally we find that single-target concentration predictions are more accurate than the multiple target predictions for both case studies.

authors.name: Anna Taka, Eleni D. Koronaki, Ioannis G. Kevrekidis, Eike Cramer, Joern Viell, Alexander Mitsos

papers.title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models
papers.summary: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.

authors.name: Carlo Alberto Barbano, Giovanni Marraffini, Demian Wassermann

papers.title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
papers.summary: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.

authors.name: Ofir Gordon, Lior Dikstein, Paul Balanca, Idan Achituve, Douglas Orr, Hai Victor Habi

papers.title: Anytime-Valid PAC-Bayes Certificates for Adaptive Test-Time Scaling
papers.summary: Test-time scaling systems often choose how much to sample, which prompt to use, and which verifier or aggregation rule to trust after repeatedly inspecting a calibration set. Standard validation error bars are not valid after this adaptive selection. We model a test-time scaling recipe as a randomized predictor with a random cost and prove a time-uniform PAC-Bayes certificate that holds simultaneously over all calibration times, all posterior mixtures over recipes, and all data-dependent stopping rules. Thus the same event covers the recipe search that precedes deployment, not merely the fixed recipe finally reported. For a finite grid of budgets and verifiers, the penalty is the familiar $\log M/n$, which in the worst case no certificate valid after selection can avoid, while non-uniform priors and localized posterior mixtures can give sharper certificates for structured searches. We specialize the result to self-consistency and show a complementary margin law: plurality voting improves exponentially in the sample budget only on examples where the correct answer is the generator's unique mode; otherwise more compute can provably amplify errors. The same margin analysis yields an oracle water-filling law for compute allocation. A synthetic audit quantifies the optimism caused by adaptive budget selection, and a 192-example GSM8K audit using gpt-4.1-mini generations illustrates risk-cost reporting for a real inference pipeline. At scale, with two models on GSM8K and MATH-500, selected-best error bars fall below the out-of-split GSM8K risk in up to 22.5% of random splits at a nominal 5% while the certificate never does, and on the full GSM8K test split it tightens to 0.109 (held-out risk 0.039). The results give a lightweight, distribution-free way to report risk and compute claims for adaptive inference systems.

authors.name: Xiaoyu Li, Jiangxuan Long

papers.title: Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning for Sample Efficient Experimentation
papers.summary: Self-driving laboratories must learn to control a process from tens to hundreds of expensive experiments, too few for deep reinforcement learning (RL). We learn the Q-function directly with a Gaussian process (GP), which avoids learning the dynamics, and show that the GP posterior supplies the learning rate of Q-learning. If each Bellman target is treated as a noisy measurement of the Q-function, the learning rate that minimises the mean squared error is the Kalman gain, and applying it to every observed transition is equivalent to GP regression. Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning (HGPQ) sets the noise variance of each target with a heteroscedastic GP, which learns how unreliable the targets are across the states and inputs. Targets from noisy operating conditions, or from regions where the value function has large gradients, then move the estimate less than targets from low-noise regions, so HGPQ learns quickly where the data are reliable without being misled where they are not. For kernel value iteration with per-target variances that are assigned when a target is collected, we prove a high-probability bound on the error of the value estimate, uniform over the explored region. Pooled over five simulated benchmarks, which include a chemical reactor and a bioprocess, HGPQ approaches the best return found by any method in fewer episodes than GP, kernel and deep RL baselines.

authors.name: Maximilian Bloor, Max Mowbray, Calvin Tsay, Ehecatl Antonio del Rio Chanona

papers.title: The Price of Choosing Examples: Context Overfitting in Adaptive In-Context Learning
papers.summary: In-context learning is usually analyzed as if the examples in the prompt were sampled before the learner is chosen. In deployed systems they are not: examples are retrieved, filtered, re-ranked, edited, and repeatedly tested after seeing the query and the data store. We formalize this gap by treating prompt construction as adaptive data analysis through a conditional stochastic-kernel calculus. Our main quantity is the context capacity, the mutual information or approximate max-information between the data store and the final prompt transcript. For any frozen in-context learner and any adaptive context pipeline with capacity $\kappa$, we prove a finite-sample context generalization bound of order $\sqrt{\kappa/k}$, where $k$ is the number of selected examples whose losses form the reported score. We prove a matching lower bound, whose constant is exact when $\log k\ll\kappa\ll k$, and derive two PAC-Bayesian retrieval rules: a first-order Gibbs rule that charges data-dependent candidate gates their prior mass, and a self-normalized second-order rule. On Banking77 with 64 retrieval recipes and two model families, the certificates hold in all 24,000 resampled selection events, and from 64 (Qwen2.5-7B) or 128 (GPT-4.1-mini) reused validation queries the Gibbs rule certifies a risk below the zero-shot error in over 99% of validation draws. Finally, we instantiate the theory for Bayesian linear in-context regression, including an order-statistics analysis of query-aligned top-$k$ Gaussian retrieval. The results separate context quality from context certification: longer or more relevant contexts improve risk only when the procedure used to choose them is stable enough for selected-context evidence to transfer.

authors.name: Xiaoyu Li, Jiangxuan Long

papers.title: Classical structural priors improve neural molecular representations in molecule language models
papers.summary: Classical molecular similarity is central to chemical information systems, yet molecule-language models trained on paired structure-text data do not necessarily organize molecular embeddings according to graded structural relationships. Here we introduce Structure-Aware Guided Alignment (SAGA), a training-only regularizer that uses Centered Kernel Alignment to align neural molecular representations with fingerprint-based Tanimoto similarity, without adding parameters or requiring fingerprints at inference. In MolCA and Atomas, SAGA improves molecule-text retrieval, shifts non-exact retrieval toward closer structural analogues, and increases average scaffold-split property-prediction performance, while molecular description and text-to-molecule generation are improved or preserved in single-run ablations. These results show that established chemoinformatics priors can make molecule-language representations more chemically faithful while retaining their multimodal utility.

authors.name: Donghyeok Lee, Sangkwon Park, Munyoung Chang, Sungroh Yoon

papers.title: The Price of Not Planning: Parallel Sampling Depth Peaks at the Reconstruction Threshold
papers.summary: Masked diffusion models sample the tokens of one round independently. Planned decoders first generate a coarse plan, then fill in the tokens in parallel. We ask when a plan saves rounds, how many it saves, and how fine it must be. We study this on broadcast trees: the leaves are the tokens, the internal nodes are the plan, and the edge correlation $\theta$ sets how strongly tokens depend on the plan. Errors are measured by the forward Kullback-Leibler divergence $\varepsilon$, and the lower bounds hold for every deterministic value-adaptive rule, also with learned conditionals. We show that a decoder without the plan needs of order $\min\{n,(n/\varepsilon)^{\alpha}\}$ rounds below the reconstruction threshold, where $\alpha=\log b/(4\log(1/\theta))$ rises to $1/2$ at the threshold, and that the exponent stays below $1/2$ above it (binary channel: $0.02\le\theta\le0.98$). With the plan, $\log_b n+1$ rounds suffice. In the binary model below the threshold, a plan with units of $m$ tokens needs of order $\log_b(n/m)+\min\{m,(n/\varepsilon)^{\alpha}\}$ rounds, so it gives logarithmic depth exactly when $m$ is logarithmic. A plan therefore helps most near the threshold, and only if its units are small. Exact divergence computations in the Gaussian model with up to $2^{20}$ leaves confirm these exponents below the threshold.

authors.name: Chuling Wen, Weijie Liang, Jian Lu

papers.title: Deep Learning for Physicists: From Linear Regression to Reasoning Models
papers.summary: These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly. The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students. The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

authors.name: Masanori Hanada

papers.title: Wavelet-Energy-Driven Dynamic Patching for Time Series Forecasting
papers.summary: Patch-based transformers tokenise a time series into fixed-size, uniform windows, which commits the model to a single temporal resolution even though real signals are multi-scale. The discrete wavelet transform (DWT) is a natural alternative because it decomposes a signal across scales. A growing body of work makes the wavelet filter learnable, on the assumption that a more flexible wavelet forecasts better. That assumption has rarely been tested in isolation, because a single reported improvement usually credits three things at once. These are the use of any multi-resolution decomposition, the choice of wavelet and training the filter. We introduce a forecaster that turns a learnable-DWT per-scale energy map into variable-length patches by merging adjacent windows that share a dominant scale. Three findings follow. First, most of the improvement is there before any filter is learned. A frozen wavelet beats a fixed-patch baseline on eight of the nine datasets by 1.5% to 7.8%, and on four of them it recovers all of the gain. Traffic is the one exception, where it is 1.2% worse. Second, learning the filter gives a further improvement on only some datasets. It helps on three of the nine datasets and makes Traffic 2.7% worse. Third, having variable-length patches helps, but exactly where their boundaries fall does not. A fixed-size uniform grid, even with its patch size tuned per task, is worse than our variable-length patches on 27 of 36 settings. Recomputing the boundaries from the learned filter at every step, rather than caching them once, never helps. The improvement in wavelet-based forecasting comes from the multi-resolution structure and the variable-length patches it induces, not from making the wavelet learnable. In practice, start from any valid wavelet, cache the patch boundaries once and treat training the filter as a per-dataset decision rather than a default.

authors.name: Syed Hafiz Bin Salim Alsree, Stephen Roberts, Stefan Zohren

papers.title: TEMPO: Regime-Aware Operator Learning with Locally Adapted POD Bases
papers.summary: Operator learning approximates the solution map of a parametric partial differential equation from data, enabling fast prediction at new parameter values without repeated simulation. The dominant approach fits a single global low-rank basis, typically a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), to all solution snapshots. This fails when the snapshots span qualitatively different solution shapes, from smooth diffusive profiles to near-discontinuous shocks. We propose TEMPO (Trajectory Expectation-Maximization Mixture of POD Operators), a two-phase framework for regime-aware operator learning. In the offline phase, TEMPO recovers latent regimes via expectation-maximization, fitting a dedicated linear or nonlinear basis to each discovered regime. In the online phase, a gating network and per-regime branch networks are trained jointly, routing new inputs to the regimes at inference. We test TEMPO on Burgers' flow, Sod shock tubes, Coanda flow, Darcy flow, Navier-Stokes flow and the heterogeneous Helmholtz equation. With 64 total POD modes, TEMPO gives 18.61% test error on Burgers', compared with 19.61% for global POD. It also gives lower errors on Coanda and Helmholtz.

authors.name: Rodion Akinzhala, Alexander Terentyev, Alexey Golubev, Yury Maximov

papers.title: Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion for Decomposable Generative Models
papers.summary: Generative model pre-training typically optimizes a model as a whole without explicitly organizing its parameters for selective reuse. Decomposable pre-training instead learns reusable components for downstream adaptation while retaining strong generative performance. However, existing knowledge diversion methods incur substantial parameter overhead through weight factorization and rely on fixed component assignments to induce specialization, potentially compromising in-distribution generation quality. We therefore propose Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv), which learns how generative knowledge is shared and specialized for effective generation and selective downstream reuse. SGKDiv constructs Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels, preserving native computational structure without SVD-based reparameterization. Calibrated condition-wise routing combines a shared usage prior with conditional adjustments, while complementary regularization shapes their allocation, diversity, and magnitude. Together, these designs replace predefined component assignments with adaptively learned and explicitly regulated knowledge specialization. Experiments across diverse model and training settings demonstrate better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines, alongside stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.

authors.name: Yucheng Xie, Fu Feng, Jing Wang, Xin Geng, Yong Rui

papers.title: Federated TD Learning in Heterogeneous Environments with Average Rewards: A Two-timescale Approach with Polyak-Ruppert Averaging
papers.summary: Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) provides a promising way to speedup training in reinforcement learning when one has access to multiple edge devices that can operate in parallel. Recently, it has been shown that even when these edge devices have access to different dynamic models---such as cars or robots with differing system configurations---an optimal convergence rate that has a linear speedup proportional to the number of devices is achievable. However, this result requires that the algorithm's stepsize be chosen in a manner that depends on the unknown model parameters. Also, it applies only to a discounted setting, which has been argued to fit episodic tasks better than continuing control tasks. In this paper, we obtain finite-time bounds for heterogeneous FRL with average rewards. We show that optimal convergence rate and linear speedup are achievable even with a universal stepsize choice, independent of the underlying dynamics. To achieve our result, we modify the existing one-timescale FRL method to a novel two-timescale variant that additionally incorporates iterate averaging. We remark that this idea also extends to other settings already studied in the literature, such as the homogeneous FRL or the heterogeneous case with a discounted cost function.

authors.name: Ankur Naskar, Gugan Thoppe, Abbasali Koochakzadeh, Vijay Gupta

papers.title: Learning What Pairs Miss for Higher-Order Multimodal Alignment
papers.summary: Contrastive learning beyond two modalities now scores the whole tuple with multilinear products, volumes, and fusion heads, critics that can represent the joint distribution. In practice these critics still behave like bags of pairs. Their negatives break at least two of the three pairs, a single pairwise check rejects them, and when most samples can be solved by pairs the higher-order term receives almost no gradient. To solve this problem, we propose CHORD (Contrastive Higher-Order Residuals with Decoys), which trains a residual against decoys drawn from a calibrated pairwise model, negatives that the pairwise model finds plausible, so that rejecting them often needs all three modalities. Drawing decoys costs one inner-product query over a memory bank, and the optimal residual is the log-ratio between the data and the pairwise model, so the decoy loss also bounds what that model misses. On M3-Mix, where one in ten training samples needs all three modalities, our CHORD improves accuracy on those samples by 21.2 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines. CHORD also gives the best two-to-one results on every real dataset, and its residual improves other retrievers without retraining.

authors.name: Kunyu Zhang, Shenghui Feng, Xiangjie Shi, Zeqing Wang, Yingxu Wang

papers.title: MegNIST, A Benchmark for Non-Invasive Inner Speech Decoding
papers.summary: MegNIST is a benchmark dataset for developing and evaluating machine learning methods for inner speech decoding from magnetoencephalography (MEG). The dataset comprises 12,000 trials of a single participant imagining speaking the digits zero through nine, recorded across four sessions. Each trial contains 306-channel MEG recordings sampled at 250 Hz, preprocessed using signal space separation, filtering, and downsampling. Data are provided as pre-defined training (10,000 trials), validation (1,000 trials), and test (1,000 trials) splits, with entire experimental runs assigned to each split to preserve temporal independence. The dataset is available in both BIDS format for neuroimaging analysis and as serialised tensors for machine learning workflows. Baseline classification results demonstrate that imagined digits can be decoded significantly above chance. Standardised splits, validated baselines, example code, and a PyTorch-compatible loader in the pnpl Python library enable straightforward integration with machine learning frameworks, lowering barriers for researchers to rapidly develop and benchmark inner speech decoding methods for non-invasive brain-computer interfaces.

authors.name: Teyun Kwon, Pratik Somaiya, Gereon Elvers, Francesco Mantegna, Anna Camera, Sven Braeutigam, Mark Woolrich, Oiwi Parker Jones

papers.title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning
papers.summary: Modeling large multi-agent systems poses challenges for trajectory inference and parameter identification, as network size and coupling increase computational demands and partial observations require reconstructing unobserved states. We propose MAS-PINN, a neural-network architecture with a tailored training algorithm for a physics-informed learning framework that leverages the network topology and the agents' similarity to reduce computational and memory costs of simulating and identifying multi-agent systems. Its architecture represents agent trajectories through shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients. Training alternates between learning features, fitting coupled trajectories, and estimating physical parameters. A matrix-free update exploits local interactions to fit trajectories without forming large global matrices. Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka--Volterra networks, and R\"ossler oscillators show improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including inference in large systems and identification under partial observations or unknown topology, alongside substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.

authors.name: Yulun Wu, Nicola Bastianello, Karl Henrik Johansson, Matthieu Barreau

papers.title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
papers.summary: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.

authors.name: Matteo Fischetti

papers.title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
papers.summary: The electronic Schr\"odinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at $K=10$, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.

authors.name: Minchan Jeong, J. Jon Ryu, Se-Young Yun, Gregory W. Wornell

papers.title: Reading or Remembering? Measuring Temporal Contamination in Language Models
papers.summary: Language models are now used to read central-bank text for economic forecasting, but most were trained on text written after the documents they read. A model reading a 2021 FOMC statement may already know that inflation rose in 2022, so part of its apparent skill can be memory of the outcome, a temporal form of test-set contamination. We measure this memory on FOMC statements and minutes from 2000 to 2026 by comparing modern open models with chronologically consistent models, which are trained only on text from before a fixed date. Asked about past GDP outcomes given only a date, models that cannot know the answer still reach an AUC of up to 0.64 from priors on dates and eras, so chance is the wrong baseline. Against these memory-free models on the same questions, most modern models recall which years had strong growth. Membership-inference scores sort documents by era and document type rather than by whether a model saw them, as exact counts in an open pretraining corpus show. In real-time nowcasts, every lookahead premium we estimate on US GDP is smaller than the forecast comparison can detect at macroeconomic sample sizes, and none on GDP or inflation survives correction for multiple testing. Lookahead audits should therefore measure memory directly against memory-free models on the same items.

authors.name: Arunkumar V, Gangadharan G. R., S. Senthilkumar

papers.title: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
papers.summary: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.

authors.name: Van Tuan Nguyen, Agathe Guilloux

papers.title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
papers.summary: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.

authors.name: Steve Rhyner, Yubo Gao, Stefan de Lasa, Sankeerth Durvasula, Nandita Vijaykumar

papers.title: Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging
papers.summary: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colon\Sigma^\star\to\Sigma$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/\delta))/\epsilon)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $\Sigma$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|\Sigma|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/\delta))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.

authors.name: Awni Altabaa, John Lafferty, Omar Montasser

papers.title: Quantifying the added value of human forecaster discussions for tropical cyclone intensity prediction
papers.summary: The National Hurricane Center routinely releases Tropical Cyclone Discussions that offer insights into its tropical cyclone forecasts. This study examines the added value of these discussions for intensity forecasting beyond a set of numerical predictors. For 637 Atlantic and eastern North Pacific tropical cyclones from the 2002-2023 hurricane seasons, we analyze the discussion text and its combination with 13 hurricane environmental predictors from SHIPS and ERA5 10-meter wind fields, for forecasting intensity changes at lead times of 24 to 120 hours using three modeling methods. In one approach, an end-to-end deep learning framework for the text shows that the discussions alone offer comparable value for 24-hour intensity forecasts to the SHIPS predictors. Adding discussion information to the SHIPS predictors in an ensemble of five such models reduces the mean absolute error of 24-hour maximum sustained wind forecasts for 2022-2023 cyclones from 9.89 to 8.90 kt, with a confidence interval that excludes zero when whole storms are resampled. The ERA5 wind fields have a minor effect on mean absolute error in wind predictions, and model rankings differ across predicted variables, lead times and model types. We provide prediction intervals for these forecasts, whose coverage falls below the 90% target during rapid intensification. Analysis of the text shows that words related to intensity and intensity change (such as intensify, weaken, eyewall and category) are important for the model predictions. This retrospective study shows the added value of the forecasters' discussions and suggests that multi-modal learning can help understand the predictive contribution of expert human judgment. The reanalysis data differ from real-time analyses, and the discussions are issued at least three hours after the valid time of the other inputs, so these results should not be interpreted operationally.

authors.name: Ilia Azizi, Frederick Iat-Hin Tam, Marc-Olivier Boldi, Val\'erie Chavez-Demoulin, Tom Beucler

papers.title: Parkinson's Disease Freezing of Gait (FoG) Symptom Detection Using Machine Learning from Wearable Sensor Data
papers.summary: Freezing of gait (FoG) is a special symptom found in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). Patients who have FoG abruptly lose the capacity to walk as they normally would. Accelerometers worn by patients can record movement data during these episodes, and machine learning algorithms can be useful to categorize this information. Thus, the combination may be able to identify FoG in real time. In order to identify FoG events in accelerometer data, we introduce the Transformer Encoder-Bi-LSTM fusion model in this paper. The model's capability to differentiate between FoG episodes and normal movement was used to evaluate its performance, and on the Kaggle Parkinson's Freezing of Gait dataset, the proposed Transformer Encoder-Bi-LSTM fusion model produced 92.6% accuracy, 80.9% F1 score, and 52.06% in terms of mean average precision. The findings highlight how Deep Learning-based approaches may progress the field of FoG identification and help PD patients receive better treatments and management plans.

authors.name: Mahmudul Hasan

papers.title: Giving Meaning to Movements: Challenges and Opportunities in Expanding Communication by Pairing Unaided AAC with Speech Generated Messages
papers.summary: Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) technologies are categorized into two forms: aided AAC, which uses external devices like speech-generating systems to produce standardized output, and unaided AAC, which relies on body-based gestures for natural expression but requires shared understanding. We investigate how to combine these approaches to harness the speed and naturalness of unaided AAC while maintaining the intelligibility of aided AAC, a largely unexplored area for individuals with communication and motor impairments. Through 18 months of participatory design with AAC users, we identified key challenges and opportunities and developed AllyAAC, a wearable system with a wrist-worn IMU paired with a smartphone app. We evaluated AllyAAC in a field study with 14 participants and produced a dataset containing over 600,000 multimodal data points featuring atypical gestures--the first of its kind. Our findings reveal challenges in recognizing personalized, idiosyncratic gestures and demonstrate how to address them using Transformer-based large machine learning (ML) models with different pretraining strategies. In sum, we contribute design principles and a reference implementation for adaptive, personalized systems combining aided and unaided AAC.

authors.name: Imran Kabir, Sharon Ann Redmon, Lynn R Elko, Kevin Williams, Mitchell A Case, Dawn J Sowers, Krista Wilkinson, Syed Masum Billah

papers.title: No Convergence in Learned Eavesdropping-Detection Dynamics for BB84 Quantum Key Distribution
papers.summary: In prior work we showed that a reinforcement-learning eavesdropper can intercept BB84 quantum key distribution while holding the quantum bit error rate below the abort threshold and keeping a usable distillable key. In this paper we ask whether an equally adaptive learning detector can close this stealth window. We cast the interaction as an alternating best-response game between a tabular eavesdropper and a tabular threshold-adapting detector. We measure exploitability, which is the detection rate and distillable key fraction achieved by a fresh attacker best-responding to the final detector. Across three learning rules (Q-Learning, SARSA, Double Q-Learning), three channel-noise levels, and a uniform false-alarm discipline, the dynamics do not settle out to twenty rounds. The exploitability does not approach a fixed point, and its round-to-round swings do not decay. Two controls, one retraining the attacker against a frozen defender and one retraining the defender against a frozen attacker, show that the swings on each side match the variance of the best-response procedure itself. The dynamics fluctuate at the scale of best-response variance rather than converging, with neither player settling to a fixed response. The behavior is noise-dependent, and the stealth window stays open at the low noise where practical QKD operates. The defender contains the attacker on average at intermediate noise without the contest settling, and at high noise the channel rather than the learned policy suppresses the attack. As a candidate mechanism we examine a last-mover information asymmetry, supported by significant anti-persistence at intermediate noise and consistent with best-response noise at low noise. The results suggest that a learned detector cannot be certified from any single round, and that closing the window calls for breaking the information structure rather than out-adapting the attacker.

authors.name: Ramon Jose C. Bagunu

papers.title: Internal Verdicts Track Evidence: A Template-Controlled Neutrosophic Reading of Epistemic States in Large Language Models via the Jacobian Lens
papers.summary: For twenty-five years, neutrosophic logic has assigned independent degrees of truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) to epistemic states that classical and fuzzy semantics cannot express. Previous applications measured these components on outputs: answers, judgments, expert evaluations. This paper reports, to our knowledge, the first neutrosophic reading of components inside the internal representations of a large language model. Using the recently released Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B, we project intermediate-layer readouts onto lexicons of support, refutation, and hedging, obtaining layer-wise (T, I, F) profiles under conflicting evidence, first-person false belief, and factual control (n = 20 each). A first battery yielded three striking signatures: a surge of refutation mass under conflict, sustained indeterminacy under false belief, and an apparent "verdict collapse" before the output layer. A second, template-controlled battery showed that all three, as initially stated, were largely artifacts of prompt grammar: matched templates with agreeing evidence inflate the same lexicon masses, true beliefs elicit the same hedging, and the model verbalizes its verdict when allowed to generate. What survives the controls is stronger than what died: the neutrosophic verdict balance B = log10(F) - log10(T) tracks evidence polarity under identical templates (about 3 orders of magnitude of separation, Cohen's d = 2.3-2.5, p < 10^-6 in 9 of 9 layers; paired Wilcoxon: median difference +2.4 orders, 19/20 items, p = 3.8x10^-6) and residually discriminates false from true first-person beliefs. We argue that the independence of the neutrosophic components is what keeps the common-mode channel observable, making both the measurement and its self-correction possible, and we distill the two-battery design into a reusable protocol for auditing language model internals with lens-based readouts.

authors.name: Maikel Yelandi Leyva-Vazquez, Alexis Matheu Perez, Florentin Smarandache

papers.title: Physics-informed and event-aware forecasting of ammonia emissions in aerobic chicken manure composting bioreactors: A PINN-PatchTST-GPR framework with symbolic dynamic extraction
papers.summary: Predicting ammonia (NH3) concentrations during aerobic chicken manure composting provides critical feedforward signals for intelligent aeration. However, the concurrence of long-term biochemical evolution and intermittent forced-aeration pulses poses significant modeling hurdles across steady baselines, transient surges, and risk quantification. Existing data-driven models lack physical consistency, while mechanistic kinetic models struggle with environmental disturbances. To bridge this gap, we propose PINN-PatchTST-GPR, a physics-informed neuro-symbolic forecasting framework. Validated on a 28-day composting campaign across six vertical bioreactors, the framework couples a channel-independent PatchTST backbone with macroscopic kinetic constraints, dynamic physical bounds, and a Gaussian process regression (GPR) event specialist. Multi-channel sensor streams drive discrete differential equation residuals and non-negativity bounds, strictly ensuring physical plausibility. A block-split conformal prediction module yields nominal 90% distribution-free prediction intervals, while PySINDy and PySR extract low-complexity symbolic equations for quiescent and surge regimes. The model achieves an overall RMSE of 0.8256 +/- 0.0132 ppm, R2 of 0.9817 +/- 0.0006, Epeak of 1.6793 +/- 0.0725 ppm, and Etime of 0.7 +/- 0.2 min. For uncertainty quantification, it attains PICP90 of 99.792 +/- 0.047%, MPIW of 6.951 +/- 0.128 ppm, and IS0.1 of 6.968 +/- 0.128 ppm. Symbolically, PySINDy yields an RMSE of 0.4624 +/- 0.0758 ppm (R2 = 0.9896), while PySR yields 2.4084 +/- 0.0864 ppm (R2 = 0.9523). Biologically, the 20-min aeration strategy minimizes cumulative NH3 emissions. Overall, PINN-PatchTST-GPR harmonizes global forecasting, localized transient responsiveness, and risk quantification for precision composting.

authors.name: Lanbin Wei, Haiyong Weng

papers.title: Ensemble Bounds for Pairwise Dissimilar Decomposition of Deterministic Datasets
papers.summary: In this paper, we study reduced similarity decompositions of \emph{deterministic} datasets using redundancy graphs and obtain \emph{ensemble} bounds for the minimum size of such constrained decomposition. We consider batch decompositions that reduce similarity \emph{across} batches and use the Lov\'asz local lemma to obtain bounds for the minimum size of a decomposition with a given pairwise dissimilarity. We then consider unique batch decomposition with a given relaxation parameter and obtain upper and lower ensemble bounds for the minimum size. Throughout, we use Binomial random graphs to obtain the desired ensemble bounds, by conditioning on the number of similar \emph{pairs} of data points.

authors.name: Ghurumuruhan Ganesan

papers.title: FlashREINFORCE: Critic-Free Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL for Agentic Language Models
papers.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but removes the variance-reducing group baseline, making updates noisier and more prone to instability on stale, variable-length trajectories. We present FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, one-pass framework built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. These components preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. In our experiments, FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at a policy lag of approximately four updates. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks, outperforming the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 percentage points with half the rollouts (256k versus 512k). Python-tool experiments extend to the 30B MoE model Qwen3-30B-A3B, with stable training at policy lag eight. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FlashREINFORCE maintains tool use where GRPO stops making tool calls and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

authors.name: Jian Hu, Yifan Zhang, Hao Zhang, Binfeng Xu, Shaokun Zhang, Hongqing Peng, Zhiding Yu, Pavlo Molchanov, Jan Kautz, Yi Dong

papers.title: Domino: Joint Unmasking via First-order Markov Chain for Few-Step Masked Diffusion
papers.summary: Masked diffusion models generate a sequence by revealing masked positions over many denoising steps. A few-step sampler has to reveal many positions at once, but the standard reverse kernel draws them independently and primarily ignores the conditional dependence between tokens revealed in the same step. We propose a novel framework called Domino, which models this dependence with a first-order Markov chain over the revealed positions, given the current state. The first revealed position keeps the posterior of a pre-trained masked diffusion model (MDM), and each subsequent position follows a transition given the token of its predecessor. Notably, the resulting step is normalized by construction, contains the factorized step in MDMs as a special case, and has a likelihood in closed form. We implement the Domino transitions via a lightweight module on the hidden states of a pre-trained MDM denoiser with only 2.6% parameter overhead and train by keeping the MDM denoiser frozen. Our extensive evaluations across text, molecules, and images show that Domino lowers the few-step generative perplexity of MDMs by a factor of 1.7 to 3.8 on One Billion Word (LM1B), WikiText-103, and OpenWebText at nearly unchanged sample entropy. It also raises the validity of few-step molecule samples by 1.5x. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/domino.git

authors.name: Mansoor Ahmed, Lilia Chebbah, Jenny Dinh, Murray Patterson, Hemanth Venkateswara

papers.title: Random matrix discrepancy -- CLuP algorithm and parametric RDT approach
papers.summary: We study information-theoretic and algorithmic aspects of random matrix discrepancy in proportional regime. The problem amounts to finding $\kappa=\min_{\x\in\mB^n}\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bar{A}_i\x_i\|_2$, where $\bar{A}_i\in\mR^{d\times d}$ is a collection of $n$ iid GOE matrices, $\mB^n$ are vertices of the unit cube in $\mR^n$, and $\alpha=\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac{n}{d^2}$ is a proportionality constant. Strong progress is made in several directions: (i) We develop a Random duality theory (RDT) framework and utilize its a lifted variant to establish lower bounds on $\kappa$, which precisely match the bounds obtained via the first moment in [81]. (ii) To address analytical challenges, we propose a negative Hopfield model as a proxy for implementation of a fully lifted RDT. On the 2nd lifting level, this model fits remarkably well between the information-theoretic lower bounds from [81] and the algorithmic upper bounds from [38]. (iii) On the 3rd and 4th lifting levels, parametric RDT concepts predict a sizeable computational gap for lower $\kappa$ values in the proxy model. Extending proxy information-theoretic fitting to algorithmic suggests a similar computational gap for matrix discrepancy in low $\kappa$ regime, aligning with [73]. (iv) We design a Controlled Loosening Up (CLuP) algorithm for matrix discrepancy. Its performance strongly matches our analytical results -- closely approaching information-theoretic predictions in lower $\alpha$ ranges (indicating a small or nonexistent computational gap) and following the proxy model's algorithmic predictions in higher $\alpha$ ranges (indicating a sizeable computational gap). Both the information-theoretic and algorithmic predictions match the corresponding phenomenologies of the symmetric binary perceptron (SBP) vector analogue in the entire $\alpha\in(0,\infty)$ range [1,2,14,31,51,92,111].

authors.name: Mihailo Stojnic

papers.title: Robust-GCD
papers.summary: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) classifies an unlabeled pool that contains both known and novel classes, given labels for the known classes only. Existing GCD methods assume that every un- labeled image is clean, but unlabeled data collected in the wild is often degraded by blur, sensor noise and compression artifacts. We formalize the setting in which an unknown fraction of the unlabeled pool is corrupted by an unknown operator as Degraded Generalized Category Discovery (D-GCD). To tackle it, we propose Robust-GCD, a framework that estimates the corruption directly from the unlabeled pool and uses the estimate to build labeled anchors for known classes and pseudo-anchors for novel classes inside the corrupted region of feature space. A trust curriculum controls how much the unlabeled pool is trusted while the anchors take hold, and a paired alignment loss keeps a clean image and its corrupted twin close in feature space. Across five datasets and multiple corruption families, Robust-GCD recovers between 43% and 96% of the All accuracy that SimGCD loses under contamination, and more than 60% on four of the five datasets, with the largest gains on the corrupted images themselves.

authors.name: Daniel Wang

papers.title: Different Timescales, Different Signals: Multimodal Landmark-Visibility Prediction in a Long-Term Webcam Network
papers.summary: Scenic visibility is not a single forecasting problem: planning a trip months ahead, deciding whether to go outside today, and judging whether tomorrow will be clear rely on different information. Using a year-scale multimodal archive of Mount Fuji webcams and meteorological observations, we identify a clear hierarchy across timescales. Seasonal climatology provides useful long-range guidance, webcam imagery is the strongest same-day observation (AUC 0.95), and the numerical forecast valid on the target day carries most of the day-specific signal one to three days ahead. Revealing this hierarchy requires evaluation that respects the dependence among cameras observing the same regional weather state: permissive splits substantially overstate multi-day performance, while date-grouped and forward-in-time evaluation reduce the apparent contribution of the current scene and current weather. On 6,575 camera-days, the current visual summary provides no measurable one-day gain once the target-day forecast is available. The remaining opportunity lies at shorter horizons, where the present visual representation discards cloud geometry and motion. These results recast scenic visibility prediction as a multi-timescale sensing problem rather than a single multimodal forecasting task.

authors.name: Bryceton Bible, Hairong Qi, Masahiro Toyoura

papers.title: TyphoonWorld: A Residual Token World Model for Probabilistic Forecasting of Typhoon Imagery
papers.summary: A satellite forecast of a typhoon should give a low-error picture of the next two days, together with an ensemble whose members are coherent fields and whose spread responds to the storm at hand. A small direct regression network already gives the lowest squared error on held-out storms, so a generative model has to earn its cost through the part of the future that the regression smooths away. We present TyphoonWorld, a discrete-token world model that generates only that part. Conditioned on tokens of the regression forecast, the latest frames and the best-track state at forecast time, it samples residual fields lead by lead, and members add these residuals to the regression center. We compare it under one protocol with per-pixel Gaussian networks, a diffusion model of the same residuals, residuals from other storms and an unconditional token world model, on 276 forecast windows from 46 held-out storms of Digital Typhoon. TyphoonWorld matches the squared error of the regression, lowers the CRPS of the area colder than 220 K, a direct measure of deep convection, by 14 to 39% against every other ensemble, and ties its spread to forecast error as closely as the Gaussian network, with a correlation of 0.78 across windows. It uses 56% of the parameters of the unconditional world model.

authors.name: Xiaoyu Chen, Tianyi Li, Xuanyi Zhang

papers.title: Hybrid quantum learning for imbalanced blood-cell classification: domain adaptation and classifier design
papers.summary: Limited annotated data, class imbalance, and morphological similarity make white blood cell classification challenging. We benchmark hybrid variational quantum classifier heads against an affine baseline on 821 microscopy images across seven morphological classes. Using ImageNet-initialised ResNet34 backbones and repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation, we first compare direct transfer with intermediate adaptation on MLL23, a larger peripheral blood cell microscopy dataset. To guide the head comparison, we explore different encoding strategies, variational depth, and the number of independent circuit blocks. We then compare the classifier performance using the affine head and two hybrid heads across multiple random seeds, under a shared training and evaluation protocol. For this comparison, all backbones share the same MLL23-adapted initialisation. Intermediate adaptation increases mean macro-F1 across all four affine-head fine-tuning configurations. The largest gain occurs with a frozen backbone, where macro-F1 rises from $0.685$ to $0.786$, a relative improvement of approximately $14.7\%$. The shallow two-block hybrid head achieves a mean pooled out-of-fold macro-F1 of $0.865 \pm 0.010$, compared with $0.879 \pm 0.008$ for the affine head. The corresponding balanced accuracies are $0.886 \pm 0.008$ and $0.889 \pm 0.010$, respectively. In the architectural exploration, the two-block hybrid head achieves the highest macro-F1 and balanced accuracy among the evaluated hybrid configurations, while the effect of encoding varies across the considered metrics. Our results help guide the design and evaluation of hybrid classifier heads for imbalanced microscopy by linking architectural choices to overall performance and class-specific precision-recall trade-offs.

authors.name: Gabriele D'Angeli, Cyrill Aebischer, Eryk Schiller, Gianluca Nicchiotti, Su Fong Chien, J\'er\^ome Extermann, Enrico Pomarico

papers.title: Quantum-inspired orthogonal adapters for certifiably robust medical image classification
papers.summary: Medical image classifiers require not only high accuracy but also reliable predictions under small input perturbations. Certified robustness provides mathematical guarantees of prediction stability, but preserving these guarantees when adapting pretrained models to new tasks remains challenging. We propose a fine-tuning approach based on quantum-inspired orthogonal butterfly layers that preserves the Lipschitz bounds of pretrained certified networks. Inspired by quantum circuits of reconfigurable beam splitters, these layers preserve orthogonality by construction using only $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ trainable parameters. Their structured design enables efficient classical implementation and offers a path toward future quantum implementations with logarithmic circuit depth under suitable connectivity assumptions. Controlled experiments on MNIST and MedMNIST demonstrate improved certified robustness compared with conventional alternatives and, in the DermaMNIST transfer, greater resistance to the tested attacks than low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We then apply it to trichoscopic image classification for alopecia diagnosis and alopecia areata activity assessment. By adapting a certified ImageNet-pretrained network, butterfly fine-tuning achieves approximately twice the certified accuracy of conventional fine-tuning and LoRA, with comparable classification accuracy on the same backbone and data split and similar empirical resistance to the tested adversarial attacks. Larger robustness guarantees, including certificates covering certain image-processing transformations, can be obtained at the cost of reduced accuracy. These results highlight the potential of quantum-inspired butterfly layers for parameter-efficient adaptation of medical image classifiers while preserving the mathematical guarantees underlying certified robustness.

authors.name: Olga Tsurkan, Laia Domingo, Victoria Orlova, Asel Sagingalieva, Iris Zalaudek, Raffaele Dante Caposiena Caro

papers.title: Trajectory-Based Bayesian Discovery of a Host-Pathogen Model from Quasi-Steady-State Observations
papers.summary: System identification of nonlinear dynamical systems becomes challenging when the measured data come from a nearly settled state. We study this situation in the case of a bistable host-pathogen interaction model with a cubic term, whose seven true mechanisms are hidden among twenty candidate terms. The data are from one noise-free trajectory on a quasi-steady-state observed window and the initial state. In this situation, classical sparse identification approaches fail to identify the correct mechanisms as the candidate library becomes ill-conditioned along the quasi-steady-state trajectory. To address this, we propose an alternative approach in which sparse Bayesian learning and $\ell_{0}$ iterative hard thresholding with pursuit provide a good start, and a two-swap climb on the Bayesian evidence of the candidate ODE solutions recovers the true model. Our results show successful model recovery, i.e., correct identification of its support and accurate estimation of its coefficients, as validated by exhaustive scoring.

authors.name: Reymart Salcedo Lagunero, Andreas Langer, Cordula Reisch

papers.title: Multi-Assay Antibody Developability Prediction with Shared Structure-Language Representations
papers.summary: Early assessment of antibody developability is critical in drug discovery, but computational approaches remain limited by the scarcity of experimental data. We explore two strategies for working within that limit. First, we designed per-residue physicochemical descriptors encoding the local structural environment, including new terms such as directional charge asymmetry and screened electrostatic potential. These feed a convolutional network, combined with protein language model (PLM) embeddings in a two-stream architecture: the two are encoded and predicted independently and merged only at the prediction stage. Second, a shared trunk with per-assay heads passes information between related assays. Both are implemented in the Multi-Assay Developability Model (MADM) and evaluated on eight assays: HIC, heparin affinity (HAC), AC-SINS, and polyspecificity ELISA against BVP, dsDNA, insulin, ovalbumin and soluble membrane proteins (SMP), with labels from 29 open sources. Structural descriptors match or exceed PLM embeddings (AbLang2, ESM2) on several assays; combining the streams gives a small but consistent gain in accuracy and reduces seed-to-seed variance. Multi-assay training raises Spearman rho for ovalbumin and SMP by about 0.1, where assays correlate and share sequence space. Under cluster-split cross-validation the strongest results are for HAC, ovalbumin, insulin, SMP and HIC (rho = 0.70-0.82); AC-SINS, BVP and dsDNA are weaker (0.50-0.55). In these three, sequence clusters largely coincide with data source, so a held-out fold measures transfer to differently calibrated measurements as well as to new sequences. On the 80-antibody GDPa3 hold-out, performance falls by rho around 0.1 for all but SMP (0.22). Transfer to the VHH panel of Ginkgo GDPa5 gives comparable results, and scFv validation against binary SMP labels yields F1 = 0.89, AUC = 0.95.

authors.name: Daria B. Kokh

papers.title: Exstill: The Most Efficient Single-Chip Processor for the Next Token
papers.summary: Generating a token with a language model requires a fixed amount of arithmetic, whose energy sets a floor beneath any hardware. For Qwen3-1.7B at a 16K-token context, gate-level measurements at 5 nm place this floor at 0.89 mJ per token, yet an NVIDIA B300 spends 391-1,120x that. The excess is the price of generality, software layers, programmable hardware and moving weights and key-value (KV) caches from external memory, and it widens with each process generation. We present a co-design approach that brings token generation close to this floor and then lowers the floor itself, optimizing silicon and model together in a gate-level search loop. Fixing one model architecture in the datapath, with weights still loadable, and holding weights and every conversation's KV cache on-die, a pre-silicon 5 nm design brings an unchanged Qwen3-1.7B token to 3.4x its floor. Co-designing the model with the circuits at fixed quality lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and the token to 0.52 mJ, 1.8x the new floor and less than the baseline model's arithmetic alone, while on-die capacity grows from one user to twelve. Against a measured B300 serving the same twelve users, the design decodes each user's tokens 110x faster at 690x lower energy. To show that one fixed architecture can serve, as a co-processor, the latency-critical workloads around a frontier model, we introduce Polyglot-DC (1.7B and 4B, each with its own design), specialized for each job by distillation and task-specific training into its own weights. As a drafter it speeds single-user speculative decoding of large open models by up to 6.6x at the maximum reasoning effort. Its guard returns multilingual verdicts in a millisecond or less, within a point of the strongest open guard. Its agent and financial-reasoning models lead comparable open models on established benchmarks, with a reasoning turn falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds.

authors.name: Valavan Manohararajah, Vithursan Thangarasa

papers.title: Quantifying Membership Inference Risks in Genomic Data Sharing: The Role of Attacker's Auxiliary Information
papers.summary: Genomic data sharing is essential for biomedical research but introduces significant privacy risks, including membership inference attacks, in which an adversary determines whether a specific individual's data was used in a study. Existing privacy protections are typically applied after a release format has already been chosen, leaving researchers without a principled method to assess dataset-specific risk beforehand. We propose a server-assisted, principal component analysis-based pre-release auditing framework that maps genomic data into a shared low-dimensional space, applies epsilon-local differential privacy via the Laplace mechanism with a formally derived sensitivity for principal component analysis scores, and estimates membership inference attack power at a controlled 5% false-positive rate using a distance-threshold attack. A membership-neutrality diagnostic based on Unbiased Reconstruction Robustness is reported alongside attack power, precision, and recall. Experiments using the openSNP and 1000 Genomes Project datasets across multiple dimensionalities and privacy budgets show that separation between the researcher's dataset and public auxiliary data in principal component analysis space is a dominant determinant of attack success, exceeding the effect of perturbation level alone. Comparison against a genome-wide association study-style likelihood ratio test baseline further contextualizes the measured risk. This framework enables researchers, data repositories, and institutional review bodies to quantify dataset-specific membership inference risk before genomic data publication, supporting more informed and privacy-aware biomedical data-sharing decisions.

authors.name: Maryam Ghasemian, Lynette Hammond Gerido, Erman Ayday

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Clustering Algorithm and Parameter Selection for Collaborative Population Stratification Using Distributed PCA
papers.summary: We propose a privacy-preserving selection layer for collaborative population stratification workflows, enabling an honest-but-curious server to recommend a strong clustering algorithm-hyperparameter configuration from privacy protected shares. Instead of using a fixed workflow such as PCA followed by K-Means with a preset number of clusters, the framework compares multiple clustering methods and parameter settings under privacy constraints. To avoid relying on a public reference basis, we construct a shared low-dimensional representation through a distributed-PCA (DPCA) procedure in which each party computes local top-$r$ principal-component information and the server aggregates only low-rank summaries to recover a global basis. Building on this representation, the framework supports three LDP-protected pipelines: PCA then Noise, Noise then PCA, and Noise-Only. The server evaluates clustering methods and parameter settings using internal validation metrics and recommends a top-performing configuration from the perturbed data; this step is pure post-processing. Experiments on openSNP and 1000 Genomes show that the server-side selection layer reliably identifies strong settings from LDP-protected data. Across both datasets, the PCA-based pipelines outperform Noise-Only in clustering utility, communication cost, and runtime, and show lower membership-inference attack (MIA) power at small privacy budgets. Overall, they provide the best utility--scalability trade-off in our setting.

authors.name: Maryam Ghasemian, Lynette Hammond Gerido, Erman Ayday

papers.title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.

authors.name: Tianhua Tao, Akshita Bhagia, Dirk Groeneveld, Pete Walsh, Tyler Romero, Yashas Samaga, Jacob Morrison, Iz Beltagy, Taira Anderson, Noah A. Smith, Hannaneh Hajishirzi

papers.title: Accelerating Atomistic-Continuum Simulations of Multilayer 2D Materials with Functional Principal Component Analysis-Based Machine Learning
papers.summary: Atomistic-continuum simulations of complex wrinkling deformations in large-area multilayer two-dimensional (2D) materials are computationally expensive. To accelerate these simulations, this work presents a machine-learning (ML) framework that first constructs a low-dimensional representation of the deformation field, then learns the deformation in this reduced space. Dimensionality reduction of deformed 2D membranes is challenging because of the extremely high dimensionality of discretized deformation fields, the need to preserve surface continuity and prescribed geometric constraints, the stochastic nature of wrinkling patterns, and the limited availability of training data. We address these challenges using two-dimensional functional principal component analysis (FPCA). The proposed FPCA representation reduces deformation fields containing millions of degrees of freedom to latent spaces with only tens of dimensions while preserving the continuity of the deformed surface. In addition, prescribed homogeneous boundary constraints are satisfied exactly through an appropriate choice of basis functions in the FPCA representation. A neural network is then trained to predict the principal components from the system and loading parameters. The resulting ML-predicted deformation fields are used as high-quality initial configurations for the atomistic-continuum solver, which subsequently performs energy minimization to obtain equilibrium solutions. The framework is demonstrated for multilayer graphene subjected to uniaxial compression, biaxial compression, and combined biaxial compression and simple shear. For the most computationally intensive large-strain cases, the proposed approach achieves speedups of at least 6.8 times while converging to final energies comparable to, and in some cases lower than, those obtained using conventional atomistic-continuum initialization.

authors.name: Jonathan Oleson, Abhishek Keripale, Shashank Pathrudkar, Susanta Ghosh

papers.title: Taking Band-Limited Maximum Likelihood to High Dimensions: Linear Memory, the Parametric Rate, and a Self-Tuning Cut-off
papers.summary: Band-limited maximum likelihood (BLML) estimates a density as the square of a band-limited function. The estimate is non-negative, and when the square root of the true density is band-limited its error falls at the parametric rate $n^{-1}$. Its algorithm bins the data, which is fast only in one or two dimensions: from three on every point has its own bin, the kernel system is dense, and memory grows as $n^2$, 40 GB at $10^5$ points. Whether the rate survives in higher dimension, where kernel estimators slow down, had not been tested. We study dense data, densities that fill their space, not data near a low-dimensional manifold. We show that the binned equations are the stationarity condition of a strictly convex objective and minimise it by block coordinate descent without forming the kernel matrix: memory is linear in $n$, a sweep costs $O(n^2 d)$ and a fit takes about ten, and one A100 GPU fits $10^6$ points in eight dimensions in about ten minutes. On band-limited truths the error then decays as $n^{-1}$ in every dimension we tested, up to eight, while the slopes of kernel estimators flatten from -0.67 to -0.28, and it is 2 to 18 times lower than a neural spline flow's. A streaming fit learns the cut-off, BLML's only tuning parameter, from analytic gradients of the held-out likelihood, for about the cost of one more fit. On real data BLML is the strongest nonparametric estimator we tested: it leads kernel and nearest-neighbour estimators on electricity prices by 0.27 to 0.47 nats per hour, and a tuned kernel estimator on the full POWER and GAS benchmarks by 0.39 and 1.58 nats per point, placing it between early and recent normalizing flows. It loses on densities with a kink.

authors.name: Rahul Agarwal, Ankit Agarwal

papers.title: Averaged-Cost Control with Shared Feedback under Model Uncertainty
papers.summary: This paper studies the shared-feedback design problem for finite-horizon averaged-cost control under model uncertainty represented by a joint law over the model parameter and initial state. One feedback map is shared across all realizations and uses only time and the current state as online inputs.
