The learning is that gated search around the prior. In two pre-registered analyses, on synthetic data whose 20 hidden truths were sampled from that typed space, the learner at 30 records per party was non-inferior, within 2 points, to all seven tuned baselines (a confined gradient learner, Ditto, FedRep, federated averaging, two pooled networks and pooled boosted trees), scoring 96.6% against 91.7% for the unchanged rule; a descriptive greedy ablation with no prior, over a separate space, scored 84.0%. In a third registered test, typed edits over a network trained on shared records beat that network alone by +5.4 points and the same edits over the published rule by +3.1; oracle-tuned fine-tuning and Ditto matched it at 30 records. An acceptance body recomputes each edit from its declaration and writes it into units reserved for that party, so by construction an edit changes no decision about any other subject, withdraws exactly, discloses at most log2 of the typed space's size in bits, and the artefact can hide nothing beyond its declared values; timing is not covered. We report where it loses: truths shared by all parties, relaxations, ten records, a pre-stated gate criterion that failed in both runs, and a language model given the records that decided about as accurately on one draw. On a rule-only base, a table of owned exceptions makes the same decisions.

authors.name: John J. O'Hare

papers.title: Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation as an Optimization Constraint for Continual Learning
papers.summary: Regularization-based continual learning reduces catastrophic forgetting by penalizing changes to parameters that mattered for earlier tasks. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), a standard instance, weights its quadratic penalty by the empirical Fisher, usually justified as approximating loss curvature. We instead derive the penalty from what training on a new task should preserve. In this formulation, Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC), new training must keep chosen functionals of learned behavior unchanged, and the local approximation of this constraint is the stored penalty. We show that EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each old sample's loss. The derivation exposes a flaw: EWC weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so samples the model fits well barely contribute, although later training can still forget them. Improved EWC (IEWC) instead penalizes how far each old output moves off its loss level set, rather than how much its loss changes, which removes this weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR, a classification-specific correction. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, removing this weighting alone raises ImageNet-R accuracy over EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07). More broadly, CLOC turns the design of continual-learning penalties into a choice of what to preserve, from which a principled penalty follows by derivation.

authors.name: Davide Wiest

papers.title: "It's Just a Small Weapon": What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models
papers.summary: Developers train models to follow a consistent character using methods like Model Spec Midtraining (Li et al., 2026), which have been hypothesized to make alignment more robust and generalize broadly. However, it is possible for subsequent RL with misspecified rewards to work against character training. In this work, we apply character training to teach gpt-oss-20b a semi-realistic constitution and study how it interacts with two types of RL that reward breaking the constitution's rules (opposing RL): answering harmful requests rewritten as math problems, and reward hacking in agentic coding environments. The character-trained models learn both behaviors easily, though they are slightly slower than gpt-oss-20b to answer harmful requests. Character-trained models also display more motivated reasoning on harmful answers than gpt-oss-20b, and hack on some tasks which monitors find harder to catch. Finally, since explaining the reasons behind rules can improve how alignment generalizes (Kutasov et al., 2026), we compare constitutions that justify the same rules by grounding them in a value or not, and find little difference between motivations on misalignment, honesty, and capability evaluations.

authors.name: Mohammad Omar Khursheed, Thomas Morris, Fabien Roger

papers.title: LoCoJAX: Host-Local Coordination for Small-Model RL on TPUs
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly targets small language models, and executing these workloads efficiently across multiple accelerators requires effective coordination. On TPUs, Pathways-based RL uses a single controller to coordinate computation across hosts. This execution model is effective for large models, but its coordination computational costs are harder to amortize when small models repeatedly invoke short computations. To characterize these computational costs, we sweep dense models from 0.6B to 405B parameters on TPU v7x under a decode-heavy workload and measure how host and network computational overhead vary with model size. At 0.6B, host orchestration occupies 36% of step time and network communication 2%, whereas for large models, estimated network computational costs dominate the non-compute time. Motivated by these findings, we present Local Coordination JAX (LoCoJAX), which implements local rollout and reward processing on each TPU host with synchronous global training. In controlled comparisons against a tuned and optimized Pathways baseline on Qwen3-0.6B across three workloads and 8-64 TPU v7x chips, its colocated mode (LoCoJAX-CO) is 1.3-3.6x faster per step; on GSM8K, it completes a step faster on 8 chips than Pathways does on 64. Finally, a Ray-managed disaggregated mode (LoCoJAX-DA) overlaps rollout and training on separate hosts, and placement experiments establish when this overlap compensates for dividing devices and transferring weights: only when rollout dominates the step and receives most of the hosts. On NuminaMath-CoT at 256 chips, giving rollout 75% of hosts cuts step time by about 15% compared with LoCoJAX-CO.

authors.name: Loki Chen, Gregory B. Rehm, Yang Song, Hongye Xie, Ming Lei, Chongyang Bai, Bob Kamma, Mingfu Liang, Kavosh Asadi, Yufei Li, Xi Liu, Jay Xu, Rui Liu, Maziar Sanjabi, Luke Simon, Hamed Firooz

papers.title: On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models
papers.summary: During the supervised learning phase, autoregressive language models are typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training data, which decomposes as a sum of token-level cross-entropies via teacher forcing. This objective is simple and efficient but potentially suffers from so-called exposure bias: a mismatch between the way the model is trained and the way it is used at inference time. Can we instead design sequence-level loss functions that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures, such as greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling? We show that two natural attempts lead to loss functions that are fundamentally flawed: unbounded below. We further show that these two flawed loss functions are intimately connected: using autoregressive Gumbel tricks, the sampling based loss is the expected greedy loss under Gumbel perturbations. Since the pathology stems from the dependence of the decoded sequence on the model parameters, we analyze the update direction obtained by applying a stop gradient on the sampling procedure, leading to a moment matching direction. While it is not the gradient of any loss function, we prove that it defines a valid descent direction in function space for the autoregressive negative log-likelihood. Despite these theoretical insights, the moment matching direction suffers from high variance. We conclude that teacher forcing may well be ``all you need'' for supervised learning of autoregressive models.

authors.name: Mathieu Blondel, Micha\"el E. Sander, Germain Vivier-Ardisson, Tianlin Liu, Vincent Roulet

papers.title: Temporal Regularized Learning: Self-Supervised Learning Local in Space and Time
papers.summary: Self-supervised objectives such as VICReg learn representations by making related inputs similar, while variance and covariance penalties prevent collapse. These penalties are statistics over a batch of samples, so layer-local variants, too, are typically local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), which optimizes a VICReg-style objective one sample at a time with purely local updates: each update uses only the current activity of its own and the preceding layer and a fixed-size running state. Temporally adjacent inputs serve as positive pairs, which makes the objective a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis (SFA). Running estimates of each neuron's mean and variance, together with one lateral matrix per layer, replace the batch statistics; held fixed during differentiation, they turn the gradient into a Hebbian feedforward update and an anti-Hebbian lateral update. We show that a two-layer network trained with batch size one on an MNIST stream of class-homogeneous chunks reaches 96.48% linear-probe accuracy, above random features (95.09%) and classical SFA, and that the temporal order and each loss term contribute to this result. With both locality constraints relaxed, the same objective matches supervised backpropagation. TeReL thus shows that the collapse-preventing statistics of modern self-supervised learning can be held as running state at each neuron, which brings these objectives closer to what brains and neuromorphic hardware can implement.

authors.name: Davide Wiest

papers.title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
papers.summary: Symmetry is a foundational principle of physics: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the coordinate frame, unit system, or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet today's leading neural surrogates lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation), rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs. Because the boundary determines the interior solution, ISLA encodes the posed boundary once into learned slices and evaluates arbitrary interior points independently through a tree-accelerated learned boundary kernel. Inputs are nondimensionalized in scales computed from the boundary, sums over boundary cells are area-weighted quadratures that converge under mesh refinement, and geometry enters only as distances and relative angles to equivariant slice anchors, making the model equivariant to rigid motions and reflections up to optional token subsampling and tree clustering. On AeroZoo, 2,816 3D flows spanning diverse geometries, poses, physical scales, and boundary conditions, ISLA's mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 1.9 and 2.2 times lower than any baseline's. On full AirfRANS, ISLA is second only to an explicit boundary-integral network (GLOBE), with errors at least 1.6 times lower than Transolver's and GeoTransolver's in every field.

authors.name: Peter Sharpe

papers.title: Towards a Theory of Learnability via Debate
papers.summary: Debate has been recently proposed as a training protocol that is hoped to produce more aligned models even as model capabilities scale. The idea is that the human, instead of providing supervision in the form of labels, judges a debate between two models that compete to prove the correctness of opposite labels. It can be shown that functions of a much higher computational complexity can be correctly judged in this way, compared to the complexity of functions that can be directly evaluated using a computationally weak evaluator. This suggests that perhaps debate can be used to teach very complicated functions to models. However, previous work has largely ignored the fact that this is a training protocol, and simply analyzes the game being played between the two debaters for a known judge. We take the first steps towards understanding the learning problem implicit within the protocol, by formulating it as an online learning problem. We show that once we formulate the learning problem precisely, there are cases where the best way to learn given access to a judge is different from running an adversarial debate. This motivates us to define a cooperative version of the protocol, whose learnability we characterize using a combinatorial dimension. We also consider the possibility of the human judge being fallible and occasionally judging the debate incorrectly. We show that a small number of errors in judgement can lead to a large error in learning.

authors.name: Tosca Lechner, Vinayak Pathak, Sivan Sabato, Ruth Urner

papers.title: Storage and Learning phase transitions in the Random-Features Hopfield Model
papers.summary: The Hopfield model is a paradigmatic model of neural networks that has been analyzed for many decades in the statistical physics, neuroscience, and machine learning communities. Inspired by the manifold hypothesis in machine learning, we propose and investigate a generalization of the standard setting that we name Random-Features Hopfield Model. Here $P$ binary patterns of length $N$ are generated by applying to Gaussian vectors sampled in a latent space of dimension $D$ a random projection followed by a non-linearity. Using the replica method from statistical physics, we derive the phase diagram of the model in the limit $P,N,D\to\infty$ with fixed ratios $\alpha=P/N$ and $\alpha_D=D/N$. Besides the usual retrieval phase, where the patterns can be dynamically recovered from some initial corruption, we uncover a new phase where the features characterizing the projection can be recovered instead. We call this phenomena the learning phase transition, as the features are not explicitly given to the model but rather are inferred from the patterns in an unsupervised fashion.

authors.name: Matteo Negri, Clarissa Lauditi, Gabriele Perugini, Carlo Lucibello, Enrico M. Malatesta

papers.title: Faster Algorithms for Structured Linear and Kernel Support Vector Machines
papers.summary: Many machine learning problems are quadratic programs, including Support Vector Machines (SVMs). A general quadratic program has input size $\Theta(n^2)$, and assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), no $O(n^{2-o(1)})$ time algorithm exists when the objective matrix is positive semidefinite (Backurs, Indyk, and Schmidt, NeurIPS'17). SVMs, however, are given by $n$ data points of dimension $d$, often much smaller than $n$, and have only $O(1)$ equality constraints. In this work, we design the first nearly-linear time algorithm for solving quadratic programs whenever a low-rank factorization of the quadratic objective matrix is given, the number of linear constraints is small, the coefficients of the objective and some optimal solution are bounded by $\mathrm{poly}(n)$, and some feasible point has all entries between $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ and $\mathrm{poly}(n)$. For linear SVM on $d$-dimensional data, our randomized algorithm runs in expected time $\widetilde O(nd^{(\omega+1)/2}\log(n/\epsilon))$ when $(d+1)^{\omega-1}\le n$ and the data points have norms at most $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ and margin at least $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, where $\omega<2.258$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Its output satisfies the equality constraint only approximately. For Gaussian kernel SVM, when $d=O(\log n)$, the squared dataset radius is $o(\log n/\log\log n)$ and the dual variables lie in a box $[0,R]^n$ with $R\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$, our randomized algorithm runs in expected time $n^{1+o(1)}$ for any accuracy $\epsilon\ge 1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$. We also prove that, assuming SETH, when the squared dataset radius is $\Omega(\log^2 n)$, $\Omega(n^{2-o(1)})$ time is required on some inputs to reach error $\exp(-\Theta(\log^2 n))$ for the program without the bias term. This improves upon the prior best lower bound in both the dimension $d$ and the squared dataset radius.

authors.name: Yuzhou Gu, Zhao Song, Lichen Zhang

papers.title: Gaussian-Channel Regularity and Distribution Learning with Flow Matching
papers.summary: We study distribution learning by flow matching with linear interpolation from a Gaussian source under Gaussian-channel regularity, a condition on the target distribution. For an integer $r\geq2$, we establish spatial regularity of order $r$ for the population velocity, together with temporal Lipschitz continuity on the full interval and local time analyticity before the terminal time. We use these properties to construct a finite multiscale ReLU sieve with a spatial Lipschitz bound independent of the truncation radius. For an exact minimizer of the empirical flow matching risk over this sieve, we obtain an upper bound on the expected Wasserstein-$2$ error of order $n^{-r/(d+2r)}$, up to a logarithmic factor, where $n$ is the sample size and $d$ is the dimension. The bound includes Euler discretization up to time one, without early stopping. The conditions hold at $r=2$ for targets with strongly convex $C^2$ potentials and two-sided Hessian bounds. They also hold at every fixed order $r\geq2$ for distributions obtained by convolving a law of bounded support with a nondegenerate isotropic Gaussian. For sufficiently large fixed constants defining the target class, we prove a minimax lower bound of order $\max\{n^{-1/2},n^{-(r+1)/(d+2r)}\}$.

authors.name: Yuan Gao, Jian Huang, Yuling Jiao, Shurong Zheng

papers.title: Sfumato Supervision: Learning Instance Segmentation with Noisy Labels
papers.summary: Instance segmentation requires precise object masks, yet both human annotators and promptable models can produce unreliable contours. A high prediction loss near a contour does not necessarily indicate an annotation error: valid edges can also be uncertain. Inspired by Leonardo da Vinci's \emph{sfumato}, which softens transitions between a subject and its surroundings, we introduce \textbf{\texttt{CB-LNL} (Copula-Boundary Learning with Noisy Labels)}. Rather than judging each contour pixel alone, CB-LNL combines foreground evidence inside the mask with background evidence outside it to guide local supervision and annotation repair. We ground this approach in an audit of paired COCO and LVIS annotations, and introduce benchmarks covering human annotations, weak-prompt SAM2 masks, and controlled corruptions in natural and driving scenes. Controlled comparisons show improved training on procedural contour noise and fewer harmful edits than direct teacher-mask replacement. Paired-seed and frozen-prediction evaluations reveal how these benefits depend on the annotation source, supporting separate assessment of category and contour reliability.

authors.name: Moshe Kimhi, Ehud Rivlin, Chaim Baskin

papers.title: Identification and estimation for matrix time series CP-factor models
papers.summary: We propose a new method for identifying and estimating the CP-factor models for matrix time series. Unlike the generalized eigenanalysis-based method of Chang et al. (2023) for which the convergence rates of the associated estimators may suffer from small eigengaps as the asymptotic theory is based on some matrix perturbation analysis, the proposed new method enjoys faster convergence rates which are free from any eigengaps. It achieves this by turning the problem into a joint diagonalization of several matrices whose elements are determined by a basis of a linear system, and by choosing the basis carefully to avoid near co-linearity (see Proposition 5 and Section 4.3). Furthermore, unlike the generalized eigenanalysis-based method which requires the two factor loading matrices to be full-ranked, the proposed new method can handle rank-deficient factor loading matrices. Illustration with both simulated and real matrix time series data shows the advantages of the proposed new method.

authors.name: Jinyuan Chang, Yue Du, Guanglin Huang, Qiwei Yao

papers.title: ExclaveFL: Verifiable Claims for Federated Learning using Exclaves
papers.summary: In federated learning (FL), data providers jointly train a machine learning model without sharing training data. This makes it challenging to provide verifiable claims about the trained model, e.g., related to the employed training data, data sanitization, or training algorithm---a malicious data provider can simply deviate from the correct training protocol without detection. Prior FL training systems have used trusted execution environments (TEEs) to protect the training computation, relying on the confidentiality and integrity of TEEs. TEE confidentiality, however, has been shown to be vulnerable to various attacks, e.g., via side channels. We describe ExclaveFL, a system for training FL models that establishes verifiable claims about models through fine-grained runtime attestation proofs. Since such proofs only require integrity, ExclaveFL generates them using exclaves, which are integrity-only execution environments without software-managed secrets, making them immune to data leakage attacks. ExclaveFL uses exclaves to attest data transformations during FL training, and the runtime attestation proofs then form an attested dataflow graph of the entire training computation. The graph is checked by an auditor to ensure that the trained model satisfies claims, e.g., about the use of data sanitization by data providers or aggregation by the model provider. Since exclaves require minor yet proprietary firmware changes, we evaluate a variant with similar performance but slightly weaker security guarantees on existing AMD SEV-SNP hardware. We show that ExclaveFL introduces less than 12% overhead compared to unprotected FL model training.

authors.name: Jinnan Guo, Kapil Vaswani, Andrew Paverd, Peter Pietzuch

papers.title: Projected gradient methods for nonconvex and stochastic smooth optimization: new complexities and auto-conditioned stepsizes
papers.summary: We present a novel class of projected gradient (PG) methods for minimizing a smooth but not necessarily convex function over a convex compact set. We first provide a novel analysis of the constant-stepsize PG method, achieving a unified iteration complexity for finding an approximate stationary point for convex and nonconvex problems. We then develop an "auto-conditioned" projected gradient (AC-PG) variant that achieves the same iteration complexity without requiring the input of the Lipschitz constant of the gradient or any line search procedure. The key idea is to estimate the Lipschitz constant using first-order information gathered from the previous iterations, and to show that the error caused by underestimating the Lipschitz constant can be properly controlled. We then generalize the PG methods to the stochastic setting, by proposing a stochastic projected gradient (SPG) method and a variance-reduced stochastic gradient (VR-SPG) method, achieving new unified complexity bounds in different oracle settings. We also present auto-conditioned stepsize policies for both stochastic PG methods and establish comparable convergence guarantees.

authors.name: Guanghui Lan, Tianjiao Li, Yangyang Xu

papers.title: Mean--Variance Portfolio Selection by Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms, Regret Analysis, and Empirical Study
papers.summary: We study continuous-time mean--variance portfolio selection in markets where stock prices are diffusion processes driven by observable factors that are also diffusion processes, yet the coefficients of these processes are unknown. Based on the recently developed reinforcement learning (RL) theory for diffusion processes, we present a general data-driven RL approach that learns the pre-committed investment strategy directly without attempting to learn or estimate the market coefficients. For multi-stock Black--Scholes markets without factors, we further devise an algorithm and prove its performance guarantee by deriving a sublinear regret bound in terms of the Sharpe ratio. We then carry out an extensive empirical study implementing this algorithm to compare its performance and trading characteristics, evaluated under a host of common metrics, with a large number of widely employed portfolio allocation strategies on S\&P 500 constituents. The results demonstrate that the proposed continuous-time RL strategy is consistently among the best, especially in a volatile bear market, and decisively outperforms the model-based continuous-time counterparts by significant margins.

authors.name: Yilie Huang, Yanwei Jia, Xun Yu Zhou

papers.title: The Revenue Cost of Inference in Online Assortment Optimization
papers.summary: A seller running an assortment experiment must earn revenue while collecting data to compare future offers. For a regular finite-dimensional parametric choice model and a finite assortment family, we characterize the oracle frontier between expected revenue loss and the largest local first-order variance constant across prespecified revenue comparisons. The oracle benchmark remains finite at zero cost exactly when revenue-maximizing assortments provide information in every target-gradient direction. When costly offers can supply the missing information, we derive the exact leading coefficient of the inverse-budget variance law and the limiting optimal spending shares. A pilot-based procedure reserves reference offers to preserve information and tightens the estimated budget constraint to account for uncertainty. We give conditions for the implemented design's variance criterion to converge to the stabilized oracle value at a fixed budget and reference share. Simulations with synthetic instances and Expedia-calibrated markets show that allocating offers across the full assortment family can improve the precision of revenue comparisons under a common opportunity-cost budget. Additional experiments assess pilot spending, budget protection, and sensitivity to choice-model misspecification.

authors.name: Jierui Zuo, Hanzhang Qin

papers.title: Rectifying Conformity Scores for Better Conditional Coverage
papers.summary: We present a new method for generating confidence sets within the split conformal prediction framework. Our method performs a trainable transformation of any given conformity score to improve conditional coverage while ensuring exact marginal coverage. The transformation is based on an estimate of the conditional quantile of conformity scores. The resulting method is particularly beneficial for constructing adaptive confidence sets in multi-output problems where standard conformal quantile regression approaches have limited applicability. We develop a theoretical bound that captures the influence of the accuracy of the quantile estimate on the approximate conditional validity, unlike classical bounds for conformal prediction methods that only offer marginal coverage. We experimentally show that our method is highly adaptive to the local data structure and outperforms existing methods in terms of conditional coverage, improving the reliability of statistical inference in various applications.

authors.name: Vincent Plassier, Alexander Fishkov, Victor Dheur, Mohsen Guizani, Souhaib Ben Taieb, Maxim Panov, Eric Moulines

papers.title: LiteLMGuard: Seamless and Lightweight On-Device Guardrails for Small Language Models against Quantization Vulnerabilities
papers.summary: The growing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has influenced the development of Small Language Models (SLMs) for on-device deployment across smartphones and edge devices, offering enhanced privacy, reduced latency, server-free functionality, and improved user experience. However, due to on-device resource constraints, SLMs undergo size optimization through compression techniques like quantization, which inadvertently introduce fairness, ethical and privacy risks. Critically, quantized SLMs may respond to harmful queries directly, without requiring adversarial manipulation, raising significant safety and trust concerns. To address this, we propose LiteLMGuard, an on-device guardrail that provides real-time, prompt-level defense for quantized SLMs. Additionally, our guardrail is designed to be model-agnostic such that it can be seamlessly integrated with any SLM, operating independently of underlying architectures. Our LiteLMGuard formalizes deep learning (DL)-based prompt filtering by leveraging semantic understanding to classify prompt answerability for SLMs. Built on our curated Answerable-or-Not dataset, LiteLMGuard employs ELECTRA as the candidate model with 97.75% answerability classification accuracy. The on-device deployment of LiteLMGuard enabled real-time offline filtering with over 85% defense-rate against harmful prompts (including jailbreak attacks), 94% filtering accuracy and ~135 ms average latency. These results demonstrate LiteLMGuard as a lightweight robust defense mechanism for effectively and efficiently securing on-device SLMs against Open Knowledge Attacks.

authors.name: Kalyan Nakka, Jimmy Dani, Ausmit Mondal, Nitesh Saxena

papers.title: Forests for Differences: Beyond Parametric Difference-in-Differences
papers.summary: This paper introduces the Difference-in-Differences Bayesian Causal Forest (DiD-BCF), a novel non-parametric model addressing key challenges in DiD estimation, such as staggered adoption and heterogeneous treatment effects. DiD-BCF provides a unified framework for estimating Average (ATE), Group-Average (GATE), and Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). By structuring separate regression forests for cohort-specific levels, common untreated trends and treatment effects, the model directly embeds conditional parallel trends and no-anticipation restrictions into Bayesian nonparametrics. We establish non-parametric identification and integrated treatment effect consistency of the exact treatment effect posterior distribution. Extensive simulations demonstrate DiD-BCF's superior performance over established benchmarks, particularly under non-linearity, selection biases, and effect heterogeneity. Applied to U.S. minimum wage policy, the model uncovers significant conditional treatment effect heterogeneity related to county population, insights obscured by traditional methods. DiD-BCF offers a robust and versatile tool for more nuanced causal inference in modern DiD applications.

authors.name: Hugo Gobato Souto, Francisco Louzada Neto

papers.title: Learned Controllers for Agile Quadrotors in Pursuit-Evasion Games
papers.summary: We study one-versus-one (1v1) quadrotor pursuit-evasion, where a pursuer and an evader are trained with reinforcement learning (RL). Direct adversarial RL tends to be unstable because opponent policies change during training, causing non-stationarity, forgetting, and strategy cycling. We propose Asynchronous Multi-Stage Population-Based training, inspired by Policy-Space Response Oracles (PSRO). Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains responses against previously learned opponents held fixed during each stage. The uniform variant, AMSPB-U, samples opponents equally, while AMSPB-P combines hard prioritized fictitious self-play (PFSP) with uniform exploration to emphasize currently difficult opponents. In cross-evaluations against learned opponents, both variants improve pursuit-evasion balance over latest-opponent training. AMSPB-P scores highest while retaining competence against earlier strategies. Across varied starting positions and after larger-arena retraining, both population variants retain higher average success across the two roles than latest-opponent training. Hardware experiments with two 10 cm, approximately 40 g Crazyflie brushless quadrotors demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer against baseline controllers and learned adversaries across 42 flights. Recorded flights include captures of evaders reaching robust peak speeds of 3.31 m/s and accelerations of 17.95 m/s^2, with pursuer flight speeds up to 4.87 m/s.

authors.name: Alejandro Sanchez Roncero, Yixi Cai, Olov Andersson, Petter Ogren

papers.title: Structure and asymptotic preserving deep neural surrogates for uncertainty quantification in multiscale kinetic equations
papers.summary: The high dimensionality of kinetic equations with stochastic parameters poses major computational challenges for uncertainty quantification (UQ). Traditional Monte Carlo (MC) sampling methods, while widely used, suffer from slow convergence and high variance, which become increasingly severe as the dimensionality of the parameter space grows. To accelerate MC sampling, we adopt a multiscale control variates strategy that leverages low-fidelity solutions from simplified kinetic models to reduce variance. To further improve sampling efficiency and preserve the underlying physics, we introduce surrogate models based on structure and asymptotic preserving neural networks (SAPNNs). These deep neural networks are specifically designed to satisfy key physical properties, including positivity, conservation laws, entropy dissipation, and asymptotic limits. By training the SAPNNs on low-fidelity models and enriching them with selected high-fidelity samples from the full Boltzmann equation, our method achieves significant variance reduction while maintaining physical consistency and asymptotic accuracy. The proposed methodology enables efficient large-scale prediction in kinetic UQ and is validated across both homogeneous and nonhomogeneous multiscale regimes. Numerical results demonstrate improved accuracy and computational efficiency compared to standard MC techniques.

authors.name: Wei Chen, Giacomo Dimarco, Lorenzo Pareschi

papers.title: Fair Contracts in Principal-Agent Games with Heterogeneous Types
papers.summary: Fairness is desirable yet challenging to achieve within multi-agent systems, especially when agents differ in latent traits that affect their abilities. This hidden heterogeneity often leads to unequal distributions of wealth, even when agents operate under the same rules. Motivated by real-world examples, we propose a framework based on repeated principal-agent games, where a principal, who also can be seen as a player of the game, learns to offer adaptive contracts to agents. By leveraging a simple yet powerful contract structure, we show that a fairness-aware principal can learn homogeneous linear contracts that equalize outcomes across agents in a sequential social dilemma. Importantly, this fairness does not come at the cost of efficiency: our results demonstrate that it is possible to promote equity and stability in the system while preserving overall performance.

authors.name: Jakub T{\l}uczek, Victor Villin, Christos Dimitrakakis

papers.title: Controllable Generative Trajectory Prediction via Weak Preference Alignment
papers.summary: Deep generative models such as conditional variational autoencoders (CVAEs) have shown great promise for predicting trajectories of surrounding agents in autonomous vehicle planning. State-of-the-art models have achieved remarkable accuracy in such prediction tasks. Besides accuracy, diversity is also crucial for safe planning because human behaviors are inherently uncertain and multimodal. However, existing methods generally lack a scheme to generate controllably diverse trajectories, which is arguably more useful than randomly diversified trajectories, to the end of safe planning. To address this, we propose PrefCVAE, an augmented CVAE framework that uses weakly labeled preference pairs to imbue latent variables with semantic attributes. Using average velocity as an example attribute, we demonstrate that PrefCVAE enables controllable, semantically meaningful predictions without degrading baseline accuracy. Our results show the effectiveness of preference supervision as a cost-effective way to enhance sampling-based generative models.

authors.name: Yongxi Cao, Julian F. Schumann, Jens Kober, Joni Pajarinen, Arkady Zgonnikov

papers.title: Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills
papers.summary: As the world becomes increasingly saturated with AI-generated content, disinformation, and algorithmic persuasion, critical thinking - the capacity to evaluate evidence, detect unreliable claims, and exercise independent judgment - is becoming a defining human skill. Developing critical thinking skills through timely assessment and feedback is crucial; however, there has not been extensive work in educational data mining on defining, measuring, and supporting critical thinking. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of measuring "subskills" that underlie critical thinking. We ground our work in an authentic task where students operationalize critical thinking by writing argumentative essays. We developed a coding rubric based on an established skills progression and completed human coding for a corpus of student essays. We then evaluated three distinct approaches to automated scoring: zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and supervised fine-tuning, implemented across three large language models (GPT-5, Llama 3.1 8B, and ModernBERT). Fine-tuning Llama 3.1 8B achieved the best results and demonstrated particular strength on subskills with highly separable proficiency levels with balanced labels across levels, while lower performance was observed for subskills that required detection of subtle distinctions between proficiency levels or imbalanced labels. Our exploratory work represents an initial step toward scalable assessment of critical thinking skills across authentic educational contexts. Future research should continue to combine automated critical thinking assessment with human validation to more accurately detect and measure dynamic, higher-order thinking skills.

authors.name: Marisa C. Peczuh, Nischal Ashok Kumar, Ryan Baker, Blair Lehman, Danielle Eisenberg, Caitlin Mills, Payu Wittawatolarn, Kushaan Naskar, Keerthi Chebrolu, Sudhip Nashi, Cadence Young, Brayden Liu, Sherry Lachman, Andrew Lan

papers.title: Prediction-Augmented Trees for Reliable Statistical Inference
papers.summary: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly central to scientific discovery, but translating ML predictions into rigorous scientific claims still requires statistical inference on gold-standard labeled data. A setting that has emerged across the sciences provides the analyst with a small labeled sample, a much larger unlabeled sample, and a pre-trained predictor, with the goal of constructing a confidence interval for a quantity of interest, as was formalized in Angelopoulos et al. (2023). In this ML-driven scientific discovery literature, labeled data is typically the binding constraint on precision while computation is comparatively unconstrained, motivating the design question of how additional computation can extract more inferential value from a fixed labeled set, a fixed unlabeled set, and a fixed predictor. To address this question, we propose the Prediction-Augmented Residual Tree (PART) estimator. PART takes the same inputs as the original PPI estimator and replaces its single global rectifier with locally computed rectifiers obtained from an adaptive partition of the feature space. We show that PART outperforms existing methods by producing tighter confidence intervals across real-world datasets from ecology, astronomy, and census reports, among other domains. We then describe and analyze PAQ, an estimator based on numerical quadrature techniques. Under appropriate assumptions on the input data, we show that the variance of PAQ shrinks at a rate of $O(N^{-1} + n^{-4})$, showing that there are settings where the rate of $O(N^{-1}+n^{-1})$ of existing methods can be provably broken.

authors.name: Vikram Kher, Argyris Oikonomou, Manolis Zampetakis

papers.title: Estimation of aboveground biomass in a tropical dry forest: An intercomparison of airborne, unmanned, and space laser scanning
papers.summary: Accurate aboveground biomass (AGB) estimates are needed to report forest carbon under the Paris Agreement, yet tropical dry forests (TDFs) remain among the least studied tropical ecosystems. We present a plot-level intercomparison of airborne (ALS), unmanned (ULS) and simulated spaceborne full-waveform (SLS, GEDI simulator) laser scanning for AGB estimation in ten permanent plots of Santa Rosa National Park, Costa Rica, covering early to late succession. Reference AGB (22-220 Mg/ha) was computed from the 2021 census with a documented procedure that screens diameter time series and propagates measurement, wood-density and allometric errors (plot uncertainty 3.5-14.5%). We compared ordinary least squares (OLS), a log-log model of mean canopy height fixed a priori and a single-metric model selected from the data, with support vector machine regression (SVM). Predictor selection, scaling and hyper-parameter tuning were nested within leave-one-plot-out validation. ALS gave the lowest errors: the a priori OLS model reached an RMSE of 32.3 Mg/ha (29%, R2_LOO = 0.77) and SVM 35.8 Mg/ha (32%). SVM did not improve on OLS for any platform and was significantly worse with ULS (p = 0.01). The best ULS and SLS models reached 33% and 37%; differences between platforms were not significant with ten plots. Selecting predictors on all plots before cross-validation lowered the apparent SVM error by up to 23 percentage points, and footprint coordinates, ALS point density and terrain elevation from the GEDI simulator produced spurious skill; these effects explain the higher accuracies reported in an earlier version of this work. Model errors remained at least 2.5 times larger than the field-AGB uncertainty. With small plot networks, a height-based OLS model with ALS is the most robust choice, and more and larger plots are needed before nonlinear models can be shown to add value in TDFs.

authors.name: Nelson Matti\'e, Arturo Sanchez-Azofeifa, Pablo Crespo-Peremarch, Juan-Ygnacio L\'opez-Hern\'andez

papers.title: Proximal Regret and Proximal Correlated Equilibria: A New Tractable Solution Concept for Online Learning and Games
papers.summary: Learning and computation of equilibria are central problems in game theory, theory of computation, and artificial intelligence. In this work, we introduce proximal regret, a new notion of regret based on proximal operators that lies strictly between external and swap regret. When every player employs a no-proximal-regret algorithm in a general convex game, the empirical distribution of play converges to proximal correlated equilibria (PCE), a refinement of coarse correlated equilibria. Our framework unifies several emerging notions in online learning and game theory-such as gradient equilibrium and semicoarse correlated equilibrium-and introduces new ones. Our main result shows that the classic Online Gradient Descent (GD) algorithm achieves an optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ bound on proximal regret, revealing that GD, without modification, minimizes a stronger regret notion than external regret. This provides a new explanation for the empirically superior performance of gradient descent in online learning and games. We further extend our analysis to Mirror Descent in the Bregman setting and to Optimistic Gradient Descent, which yields faster convergence in smooth convex games.

authors.name: Yang Cai, Constantinos Daskalakis, Haipeng Luo, Chen-Yu Wei, Weiqiang Zheng

papers.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Joint Source and Parameter Estimation in Advection-Diffusion Equations
papers.summary: Source inversion problems under sparse measurements for parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) are particularly challenging to solve using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), due to their severe ill-posedness and the multiple unknowns involved including the source function and the PDE parameters. Although the neural tangent kernel (NTK) of PINNs has been widely used in forward problems involving a single neural network, its extension to inverse problems involving multiple neural networks remains less explored. In this work, we propose a weighted adaptive approach based on the NTK of PINNs including multiple networks representing the solution, the unknown source, and the PDE parameters. The key idea behind our methodology is to simultaneously solve the joint recovery of these unknowns thereby using the underlying PDE as a constraint that couples multiple unknowns functional parameters, leading to more efficient use of the limited information in the measurements. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the approximation error of PINNs in a source inverse problem governed by the advection-diffusion equation (ADE) with known velocity and diffusion coefficients. In particular, we derive an error bound for the estimated source function in terms of the PINN's training error, the noise level and the discretization error. This analysis provides theoretical insight into the factors influencing the approximation accuracy. We present numerical experiments on 2D and 3D ADE using different types of measurements data reflecting practical engineering systems. Our results demonstrate the successful performance of PINNs in solving our source inversion problem and its robustness to noise in the measurements.

authors.name: Brenda Anague, Bamdad Hosseini, Issa Karambal, Jean Medard Ngnotchouye

papers.title: Better Call Graphs: A New Dataset of Function Call Graphs for Malware Classification
papers.summary: Function call graphs (FCGs) have emerged as a powerful abstraction for malware detection, capturing the behavioral structure of applications beyond surface-level signatures. Their utility in traditional program analysis has been well established, enabling effective classification and analysis of malicious software. In the mobile domain, especially in the Android ecosystem, FCG-based malware classification is particularly critical due to the platform's widespread adoption and the complex, component-based structure of Android apps. However, progress in this direction is hindered by the lack of large-scale, high-quality Android-specific FCG datasets. Existing datasets are often outdated, dominated by small or redundant graphs resulting from app repackaging, and fail to reflect the diversity of real-world malware. These limitations lead to overfitting and unreliable evaluation of graph-based classification methods. To address this gap, we introduce Better Call Graphs (BCG), a comprehensive dataset of large and unique FCGs extracted from recent Android application packages (APKs). BCG includes both benign and malicious samples spanning various families and types, along with graph-level features for each APK. Through extensive experiments using baseline classifiers, we demonstrate the necessity and value of BCG compared to existing datasets. BCG is publicly available at https://erdemub.github.io/BCG-dataset.

authors.name: Jakir Hossain, Jue Guo, Gurvinder Singh, Lukasz Ziarek, Ahmet Erdem Sar{\i}y\"uce

papers.title: Exploring the Potential of Spiking Neural Networks in UWB NLOS Identification
papers.summary: Ultrawideband (UWB) nonline-of-sight (NLOS) identification is critical for accurate localization, yet prevailing deep learning solutions impose computational demands incompatible with low-cost edge devices. This letter explores the potential of spiking neural networks (SNNs) for this task and develops a fully unsupervised SNN solution. Against supervised deep learning baselines, our approach achieves comparable accuracy (~82%) with only 4.7K synaptic operations (SOPs) per inference, representing a three-order-of-magnitude improvement in efficiency. These results establish that SNNs can serve as a viable neuromorphic alternative for edge UWB applications.

authors.name: Youdong Zhang, Xu He, Xiaolin Meng

papers.title: PCA of probability measures: Sparse and Dense sampling regimes
papers.summary: A common approach to perform PCA on probability measures is to embed them into a Hilbert space where standard functional PCA techniques apply. While convergence rates for estimating the embedding of a single measure from $m$ samples are well understood, the literature has not addressed the setting involving multiple measures. In this paper, we study PCA in a double asymptotic regime where $n$ probability measures are observed, each through $m$ samples. We derive convergence rates of the form $n^{-1/2} + m^{-\alpha}$ for the empirical covariance operator and the PCA excess risk, where $\alpha>0$ depends on the chosen embedding. This characterizes the relationship between the number $n$ of measures and the number $m$ of samples per measure, revealing a sparse (small $m$) to dense (large $m$) transition in the convergence behavior. Moreover, we prove that the dense-regime rate is minimax optimal for the empirical covariance error. Our numerical experiments validate these theoretical rates and demonstrate that appropriate subsampling preserves PCA accuracy while reducing computational cost.

authors.name: Gachon Erell, J\'er\'emie Bigot, Elsa Cazelles

papers.title: Optimal scaling laws in learning hierarchical multi-index models
papers.summary: In this work, we provide a sharp theory of scaling laws for two-layer neural networks trained on a class of hierarchical multi-index targets, in a genuinely representation-limited regime. We derive exact information-theoretic scaling laws for subspace recovery and prediction error, revealing how the hierarchical features of the target are sequentially learned through a cascade of phase transitions. We further show that these optimal rates are achieved by a simple, target-agnostic spectral estimator, which can be interpreted as the small learning-rate limit of gradient descent on the first-layer weights. Once an adapted representation is identified, the readout can be learned statistically optimally, using an efficient procedure. As a consequence, we provide a unified and rigorous explanation of scaling laws, plateau phenomena, and spectral structure in shallow neural networks trained on such hierarchical targets.

authors.name: Leonardo Defilippis, Florent Krzakala, Bruno Loureiro, Antoine Maillard

papers.title: Distribution-free certificate of similarity between distributions with blurred total variation distance
papers.summary: Classical two-sample tests aim to determine whether two distributions are equal or not based on samples from each one. Even in an distribution-free setting, well-known methods such as the permutation test can provide statistical evidence that the two distributions differ. However, failure to reject equality does not necessarily establish that they are similar. In this work, we study the complementary problem of certifying distributional similarity with finite-sample confidence, without imposing assumptions on the underlying distributions. We show, however, that for continuous distributions, any distribution-free upper confidence bound on the total variation (TV) distance must be trivial with high probability, even if the distributions are identical. Thus, certifying similarity in TV with a distribution-free guarantee is practically impossible. We therefore examine the blurred TV distance, a relaxation of TV distance that enables us to quantify similarity after applying a common blurring operation while retaining the interpretation of TV. We construct distribution-free upper and lower confidence bounds on blurred TV, establish their finite-sample validity, and examine its properties in high dimensions.

authors.name: Rohan Hore, Rina Foygel Barber

papers.title: Allure of Craquelure: A Variational-Generative Approach to Crack Detection in Paintings
papers.summary: Recent advances in imaging technologies, deep learning and numerical performance have enabled non-invasive detailed analysis of artworks, supporting their documentation and conservation. In particular, automated detection of craquelure in digitized paintings is crucial for assessing degradation and guiding restoration, yet remains challenging due to the possibly complex scenery and the visual similarity between cracks and crack-like artistic features such as brush strokes or hair. We propose a hybrid approach that models crack detection as an inverse problem, decomposing an observed image into a crack-free painting and a crack component. A deep generative model is employed as powerful prior for the underlying artwork, while crack structures are captured using a Mumford--Shah-type variational functional together with a crack prior. Joint optimization yields a pixel-level map of crack localizations in the painting.

authors.name: Laura Paul, Holger Rauhut, Martin Burger, Samira Kabri, Tim Roith

papers.title: Securing SIM-Assisted Wireless Networks via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful wave-domain technology that enables multi-stage manipulation of electromagnetic signals through multilayer programmable architectures. While SIMs offer unprecedented degrees of freedom for enhancing physical-layer security, their extremely large number of meta-atoms leads to a high-dimensional and strongly coupled optimization space, making conventional design approaches inefficient and difficult to scale. Moreover, existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques suffer from slow convergence and performance degradation in dynamic wireless environments with imperfect knowledge of passive eavesdroppers. To address these challenges, we propose a hybrid quantum proximal policy optimization (QPPO) framework for SIM-assisted secure communications that jointly optimizes transmit power allocation and SIM phase shifts to maximize the average secrecy rate under power and quality-of-service constraints. Specifically, a parameterized quantum circuit is embedded into the actor network, forming a hybrid classical-quantum policy architecture that enhances policy representation capability and exploration efficiency in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed Q-PPO scheme consistently outperforms DRL baselines, achieving approximately 15% higher secrecy rates and 30% faster convergence under imperfect eavesdropper channel state information. These results establish Q-PPO as a powerful optimization paradigm for SIM-enabled secure wireless networks.

authors.name: Le-Hung Hoang, Quang-Trung Luu, Dinh Thai Hoang, Diep N. Nguyen, Van-Dinh Nguyen

papers.title: Constrained and Composite Sampling via Proximal Sampler
papers.summary: We study two log-concave sampling problems: constrained sampling and composite sampling. First, we consider sampling from a distribution proportional to $e^{-f}$ on a convex set $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, where $f$ is convex. Using an epigraph lifting, we reduce this problem to uniform sampling up to a one-dimensional exponential tilt over a convex set in $\mathbb R^{d+1}$. We then apply the proximal sampler to the lifted distribution. We develop an unbiased implementation of its restricted Gaussian oracle by using the cutting-plane method and rejection sampling, requiring only a separation oracle for $K$ and evaluation and subgradient oracles for $f$, without relying on projections or barrier functions. Second, we study composite sampling from $e^{-f-h}$, where $f$ and $h$ are closed and convex. This structure arises naturally in Bayesian inference, where $f$ represents data fidelity and $h$ encodes prior information. By applying an epigraph lifting to $h$, we reduce composite sampling to constrained sampling in $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, allowing us to build on the approach developed in the first part. This leads to a double lifting formulation in $\mathbb R^{d+2}$, for which we implement the proximal sampler using different combinations of subgradient and proximal oracles for $f$ and $h$. We establish mixing time bounds in R\'enyi and $\chi^2$ divergences for both problems. Finally, we revisit the convergence analysis of the proximal sampler from a variational perspective. Starting from variational formulations of its two half-steps as optimization problems over probability measures, we use a dynamic formulation of entropy-regularized optimal transport to recast them as optimal control problems. This allows us to derive their governing PDEs directly through the lens of optimization, without first analyzing particle-level SDEs.

authors.name: Thanh Dang, Jiaming Liang

papers.title: NestRL: A Nested Training Regime for Mutual Adaptation in Human-AI Teaming
papers.summary: Mutual adaptation is a central challenge in human-AI teaming, as humans naturally adjust their strategies in response to an AI agent's behavior. Existing approaches attempt to approximate human behavior by diversifying training partners; however, these partners are typically static and fail to capture the adaptive nature of human teammates. When agents are trained jointly in standard multi-agent settings, they often converge to opaque coordination strategies that work only with their co-trained partners, leading to poor generalization. To model adaptive human behavior, we formulate human-AI teaming as an Interactive Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (I-POMDP). We propose NestRL, a nested training regime that learns the solution to a finite-level I-POMDP by training agents at each level against adaptive agents from the level below. This exposes agents to adaptive behavior while preventing emergence of opaque coordination strategies. We provide theoretical analysis showing that NestRL agents avoid convergence to partner-specific strategies, and validate this empirically in the Overcooked domain against state-of-the-art baselines. NestRL achieves higher task performance with both unseen adaptive agents and real human teammates, while exhibiting significantly greater adaptability over the course of interaction.

authors.name: Upasana Biswas, Durgesh Kalwar, Subbarao Kambhampati, Sarath Sreedharan

papers.title: Assessing the Impact of Speaker Identity in Speech Spoofing Detection
papers.summary: Spoofing detection systems are typically trained using diverse recordings from multiple speakers, often assuming that the resulting embeddings are independent of speaker identity. However, this assumption remains unverified. In this paper, we investigate the impact of speaker information on spoofing detection systems. We propose two approaches within our Speaker-Invariant Multi-Task framework, one that models speaker identity within the embeddings and another that removes it. SInMT integrates multi-task learning for joint speaker recognition and spoofing detection, incorporating a gradient reversal layer. Evaluated using four datasets, our speaker-invariant model reduces the average equal error rate by 17% compared to the baseline, with up to 48% reduction for the most challenging attacks (e.g., A11).

authors.name: Anh-Tuan Dao, Driss Matrouf, Nicholas Evans

papers.title: On the Stability Connection Between Discrete-Time Algorithms and Their Resolution ODEs: Applications to Min-Max Optimisation
papers.summary: We establish a connection between the stability of discrete-time algorithms (DTAs) and continuous-time dynamical systems, in particular their $O(s^r)$-resolution ordinary differential equations (ODEs). We show that exponential stability of a common equilibrium transfers to the DTA whenever the one-step error is small relative to the distance to the equilibrium and the one-step Lyapunov decay. This condition is sharp in order, and one-step consistency alone is insufficient. The result is local and allows step-size-dependent ODEs and Lyapunov functions, covering $O(s)$-resolution ODEs whose decay rate vanishes as the step size tends to zero. Asymptotic stability is not inherited in general, but a comparison criterion and a checkable compatibility condition ensure it carries over for equilibria and compact sets. For resolution ODEs, joint regularity of the update map guarantees the required error bound. We apply the framework to two-timescale gradient descent ascent (TT-GDA), generalised extragradient, two-timescale proximal point, and (regularised) damped Newton, showing that for small step sizes and suitable parameters, every saddle point with invertible Hessian is locally exponentially stable for all but TT-GDA. For degenerate saddle points, the framework yields asymptotic stability and convergence rates.

authors.name: Amir Ali Farzin, Yuen-Man Pun, Philipp Braun, Iman Shames

papers.title: Generalized Bayes for Causal Inference
papers.summary: Uncertainty quantification is central to many applications of causal machine learning, yet principled Bayesian inference for causal effects remains challenging. Standard Bayesian approaches typically require specifying a probabilistic model for the data-generating process, including high-dimensional nuisance components such as propensity scores and outcome regressions. Standard posteriors are thus vulnerable to strong modeling choices, including complex prior elicitation. In this paper, we propose a generalized Bayesian framework for causal inference. Our framework avoids explicit likelihood modeling; instead, we place priors directly on the causal estimands and update these using an identification-driven loss function, which yields generalized posteriors for causal effects. As a result, our framework turns existing loss-based causal estimators into estimators with full uncertainty quantification. Our framework is flexible and applicable to a broad range of causal estimands (e.g., ATE, CATE). Further, our framework can be applied on top of state-of-the-art causal machine learning pipelines (e.g., Neyman-orthogonal meta-learners). For Neyman-orthogonal losses, we show that the generalized posteriors converge to their oracle counterparts and remain robust to first-stage nuisance estimation error. With calibration, we thus obtain valid frequentist uncertainty even when nuisance estimators converge at slower-than-parametric rates. Empirically, we demonstrate that our proposed framework offers causal effect estimation with calibrated uncertainty across several causal inference settings. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first flexible framework for constructing generalized Bayesian posteriors for causal machine learning.

authors.name: Emil Javurek, Dennis Frauen, Yuxin Wang, Stefan Feuerriegel

papers.title: RepoLaunch: Automating Build and Management of Code Repositories across Languages and Platforms
papers.summary: Language model (LM) agents have driven substantial progress in automated software engineering (SWE), yet building and testing software repositories at scale remains a largely manual and labor-intensive bottleneck. In this work, we introduce RepoLaunch, a novel agentic framework that automatically resolves dependencies, compiles source code, and extracts test results across diverse programming languages and operating systems. RepoLaunch achieves a 78% build success rate, outperforming the Python/Linux-only prior system by 18%. To demonstrate its application, we further present a fully automated pipeline for SWE dataset creation driven by RepoLaunch, which only requires human input at the task-design stage. RepoLaunch is open-sourced, and its automated task-generation pipeline has been adopted by several recent works on agentic benchmarking and training.

authors.name: Kenan Li, Rongzhi Li, Linghao Zhang, Qirui Jin, Liao Zhu, Xiaosong Huang, Geng Zhang, Yikai Zhang, Shilin He, Chengxing Xie, Xin Zhang, Zijian Jin, Bowen Li, Chaoyun Zhang, Yu Kang, Yufan Huang, Elsie Nallipogu, Saravan Rajmohan, Qingwei Lin, Dongmei Zhang

papers.title: RL unknotter, hard unknots and unknotting number
papers.summary: We train a reinforcement learning agent to simplify hard unknot diagrams and pair it with a learned crossing selector to search for short unknotting sequences. Three examples found by the agent lead to an infinite family of prime two-bridge knots of unknotting number three whose connected sums with the figure-eight knot also have unknotting number three, and fifteen new unknotting upper bounds were found on the set of prime knots up to 13 crossings.

authors.name: Anne Dranowski, Yura Kabkov, Daniel Tubbenhauer

papers.title: A Noise Sensitivity Exponent Controls Large Statistical-to-Computational Gaps in Single- and Multi-Index Models
papers.summary: Understanding when learning is statistically possible yet computationally hard is a central challenge in high-dimensional statistics. In this work, we investigate this question in the context of single- and multi-index models, classes of functions widely studied as benchmarks to probe the ability of machine learning methods to discover features in high-dimensional data. Our main contribution is to show that a Noise Sensitivity Exponent (NSE) - a simple quantity determined by the activation function - governs the existence and magnitude of statistical-to-computational gaps within a broad regime of these models. We first establish that, in single-index models with large additive noise, the onset of a computational bottleneck is fully characterized by the NSE. We then demonstrate that the same exponent controls a statistical-computational gap in the specialization transition of large separable multi-index models, where individual components become learnable. Finally, in hierarchical multi-index models, we show that the NSE governs the optimal computational rate in which different directions are sequentially learned. Taken together, our results identify the NSE as a unifying property linking noise robustness, computational hardness, and feature specialization in high-dimensional learning.

authors.name: Leonardo Defilippis, Florent Krzakala, Bruno Loureiro, Antoine Maillard

papers.title: Overcoming the Incentive Collapse Paradox
papers.summary: AI-assisted task delegation is increasingly common, yet human effort in such systems is costly and typically unobserved. Recent work by Bastani and Cachon (2025); Sambasivan et al. (2021) shows that accuracy-based payment schemes suffer from incentive collapse: as AI accuracy improves, sustaining positive human effort requires unbounded payments. We study this phenomenon in a budget-constrained principal-agent framework with strategic human agents whose output accuracy depends on unobserved effort. Our first contribution is a general impossibility result showing that incentive collapse is not merely a limitation of simple linear payments, but arises for any payment rule based only on observed task accuracy.To overcome this barrier, we propose a sentinel-auditing payment mechanism that enforces a strictly positive and controllable level of human effort at finite cost, independent of AI accuracy. Building on this incentive-robust foundation, we develop an incentive-aware active statistical inference framework that jointly optimizes (i) the auditing rate and (ii) active sampling and budget allocation across tasks of varying difficulty to minimize the final statistical loss under a single budget. Experiments demonstrate improved cost-error tradeoffs relative to standard active learning and auditing-only baselines.

authors.name: Qichuan Yin, Ziwei Su, Shuangning Li

papers.title: LatentUM: Unleashing the Potential of Interleaved Cross-Modal Reasoning via a Latent-Space Unified Model
papers.summary: Unified models (UMs) hold promise for their ability to understand and generate content across heterogeneous modalities. Compared to merely generating visual content, the use of UMs for interleaved cross-modal reasoning is more promising and valuable, e.g., for solving understanding problems that require dense visual thinking, improving visual generation through self-reflection, or modeling visual dynamics of the physical world guided by stepwise action interventions. However, existing UMs typically rely on pixel decoding as a bridge when their visual representations for understanding and generation are disjoint, which is both ineffective and computationally cumbersome. In this paper, we introduce LatentUM, a novel unified model that represents all modalities within a shared semantic latent space, eliminating pixel-space mediation for model-internal reasoning over generated visual states. By making generated visual tokens directly interpretable to the model itself, LatentUM enables flexible interleaved cross-modal reasoning and generation. Empirically, LatentUM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Visual Spatial Planning benchmark, pushes the limits of visual generation through self-reflection and demonstrates world modeling capability by predicting future visual states in the shared semantic latent space. Code and models are available at https://github.com/SJTU-DENG-Lab/LatentUM.

authors.name: Jiachun Jin, Zetong Zhou, Xiao Yang, Hao Zhang, Pengfei Liu, Jun Zhu, Zhijie Deng

papers.title: QiMeng-PRepair: Precise Code Repair via Edit-Aware Reward Optimization
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong program repair performance but often suffer from over-editing, where excessive modifications overwrite correct code and hinder bug localization. We systematically quantify its impact and introduce precise repair task, which maximizes reuse of correct code while fixing only buggy parts. Building on this insight, we propose PRepair, a framework that mitigates over-editing and improves repair accuracy. PRepair has two components: Self-Breaking, which generates diverse buggy programs via controlled bug injection and min-max sampling, and Self-Repairing, which trains models with Edit-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (EA-GRPO) using an edit-aware reward to encourage minimal yet correct edits. Experiments show that PRepair improves repair precision by up to 31.4% under $\mathrm{fix}_1@1$, a metric that jointly considers repair correctness and extent, and significantly increases decoding throughput when combined with speculative editing, demonstrating its potential for precise and practical code repair.

authors.name: Changxin Ke, Rui Zhang, Jiaming Guo, Yuanbo Wen, Li Ding, Shuo Wang, Xuyuan Zhu, Xiong Peng, Di Huang, Zidong Du, Xing Hu, Qi Guo, Yunji Chen

papers.title: Estimating Continuous Treatment Effects with Two-Stage Kernel Ridge Regression
papers.summary: We study the problem of estimating the effect function for a continuous treatment, which maps each treatment value to a population-averaged outcome. A central challenge in this setting is confounding: treatment assignment often depends on covariates, creating selection bias that makes direct regression of the response on treatment unreliable. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage kernel ridge regression method. In the first stage, we learn a model for the response as a function of both treatment and covariates; in the second stage, we use this model to construct pseudo-outcomes that correct for distribution shift, and then fit a second model to estimate the treatment effect. Although the response varies with both treatment and covariates, the induced effect function obtained by averaging over covariates is typically much simpler, and our estimator adapts to this structure. Our optimal learning bounds are achieved without estimating the conditional treatment density, thereby bypassing a major bottleneck in existing methods. Furthermore, we introduce a fully data-driven model selection procedure that achieves provable adaptivity to both the unknown degree of overlap and the spectral decay of the underlying kernel.

authors.name: Seok-Jin Kim, Kaizheng Wang

papers.title: VoxSafeBench: Not Just What Is Said, but Who, How, and Where
papers.summary: As speech language models (SLMs) transition from personal devices into shared, multi-user environments, their responses must account for far more than the words alone. Who is speaking, how they sound, and where the conversation takes place can each turn an otherwise benign request into one that is unsafe, unfair, or privacy-violating. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on basic audio comprehension, study individual risks in isolation, or conflate content that is inherently harmful with content that only becomes problematic due to its acoustic context. We introduce VoxSafeBench, among the first benchmarks to jointly evaluate social alignment in SLMs across three dimensions: safety, fairness, and privacy. VoxSafeBench adopts a Two-Tier design: Tier1 evaluates content-centric risks using matched text and audio inputs, while Tier2 targets audio-conditioned risks in which the transcript is benign but the appropriate response hinges on the speaker, paralinguistic cues, or the surrounding environment. To validate Tier2, we include intermediate perception probes and confirm that frontier SLMs can successfully detect these acoustic cues yet still fail to act on them appropriately. Across 22 tasks with bilingual coverage, we find that safeguards appearing robust on text often degrade in speech: safety awareness drops for speaker- and scene-conditioned risks, fairness erodes when demographic differences are conveyed vocally, and privacy protections falter when contextual cues arrive acoustically. Together, these results expose a pervasive speech grounding gap: current SLMs frequently recognize the relevant social norm in text but fail to apply it when the decisive cue must be grounded in speech. Code and data are publicly available at: https://amphionteam.github.io/VoxSafeBench_demopage/

authors.name: Yuxiang Wang, Hongyu Liu, Yijiang Xu, Qinke Ni, Li Wang, Wan Lin, Kunyu Feng, Dekun Chen, Xu Tan, Lei Wang, Jie Shi, Zhizheng Wu

papers.title: Structural interpretability in SVMs with truncated orthogonal polynomial kernels
papers.summary: Support vector machines (SVMs) can yield classifiers with similar predictive performance but different internal structures, particularly in the contributions of individual explanatory variables and their interactions. We introduce Orthogonal Representation Contribution Analysis (ORCA), a post-training methodology for SVMs constructed from tensor products of truncated Christoffel--Darboux kernels. The associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) admits a finite orthonormal polynomial basis in which the regularized component of the fitted decision function has an exact expansion. Squared expansion coefficients induce an additive decomposition of its squared RKHS norm. Based on this representation, normalized Orthogonal Kernel Contribution (OKC) indices quantify the fractions of the squared RKHS norm associated with total polynomial degrees, interaction orders, and input-variable contributions, both individually and through interactions of arbitrary order. ORCA summarizes these indices through joint structural maps, variable-specific displays, and comparisons of fitted classifiers. A controlled quartet of classification problems illustrates substantial structural differences under matched predictive performance. A double-spiral experiment compares five Jacobi kernels, while an application to the Vertebral Column data illustrates the method after cross-validated model selection. ORCA provides a quantitative characterization of the internal structure of fitted SVMs, revealing differences that may remain undetected by standard predictive performance metrics.

authors.name: V\'ictor Soto-Larrosa, Nuria Torrado, Edmundo J. Huertas

papers.title: PAIR-CI: Calibrated Conditional Independence Testing for Causal Discovery with Incomplete Data
papers.summary: The standard constraint-based paradigm for causal discovery with incomplete data -- impute first, test second -- is frequently miscalibrated: any consistent conditional independence (CI) test rejects a true null with probability approaching 1 when imputation error induces spurious conditional dependence. We introduce PAIR-CI, a nonparametric CI test that restores calibration by integrating multiple imputation directly into the inferential procedure via a paired permutation design. PAIR-CI compares cross-validated models that include and exclude the candidate variable while receiving the same imputed conditioning set, so that imputation error cancels in their loss difference rather than contaminating the test statistic. A variance estimator that nests a provably consistent cross-validation estimator inside Rubin's rules yields inference that is asymptotically valid in the many-imputation limit and conservative by a derived, sign-definite mechanism -- to our knowledge, the first formal result combining these two inferential frameworks. In simulations, existing imputation-based CI tests exhibit false positive rates of 28-45% when data are missing not at random (MNAR), whereas PAIR-CI's pooled rate is at most 3.6%, exceeding the nominal 5% only in some cells with five or more conditioning variables. Integrated into the PC algorithm, PAIR-CI is stable across functional forms and missingness mechanisms, whereas every parametric pipeline we consider, including missing-value PC, has a regime in which it fails badly. On nonlinear network benchmarks it reduces structural Hamming distance by 18% (ALARM) and 11% (HAILFINDER) relative to missing-value PC and by 31-48% relative to test-wise deletion and imputation-based Fisher-$Z$ pipelines, while attaining the highest skeleton F1; when relationships are linear, a well-specified parametric pipeline remains preferable.

authors.name: Thomas S. Robinson, Ranjit Lall

papers.title: Information-theoretic Limits of Learning and Estimation
papers.summary: Information theory plays a central role in establishing fundamental limits on what any learning or estimation algorithm can -- and cannot -- achieve, regardless of computational power. This draft provides an introduction to these connections. We begin by introducing concentration inequalities along with the notions of covering and packing in metric spaces, and the associated concept of metric entropy. These tools are essential for our analysis. We then introduce the learning-theoretic framework and derive upper bounds on generalization error in terms of metric entropy, Rademacher complexity, and the VC dimension, as well as mutual information and relative entropy. Finally we discuss the minimax estimation framework and establish lower bounds on minimax risk using Fano's inequality, yielding bounds in terms of relative entropy and covering and packing numbers. A significantly revised and augmented version of this manuscript will appear as two chapters in the forthcoming third edition of Cover and Thomas's Elements of Information Theory. For questions, please contact abbas@ee.stanford.edu.

authors.name: Abbas El Gamal, Maxim Raginsky

papers.title: Test-Time Speculation
papers.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by using a fast draft model to generate tokens and a more accurate target model to verify them. Its performance depends on the $\textit{acceptance length}$, or number of draft tokens accepted by the target. Our studies show that the acceptance length of even state-of-the-art speculators, like DFlash, EAGLE-3, and PARD, degrades with generation length, reaching values close to 1 (i.e., no speedup) within a few thousand output tokens, making speculators ineffective for long-response tasks.
