papers.summary: Radio-frequency (RF) photonics enables broadband, phase-coherent sensing beyond the reach of purely electronic architectures, yet at a given optical carrier power its sensitivity is bounded by the standard quantum limit of the optical readout. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that this limit can be surpassed in both passive and active RF imaging modalities by encoding RF signals onto a bright phase-squeezed optical carrier and recovering them via balanced homodyne detection, while the RF front end, illumination, and image reconstruction remain classical. A unified measurement model shows that phase squeezing reduces the variance of the additive readout noise by a single factor $g$, yielding peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) gains of up to $2G$, where $G\equiv10\log_{10}(1/g)$: between $G$ and $2G$ for deterministic targets in active imaging when the classical noise of the echoes is negligible against the readout noise, and set by the ratio of scene noise to readout noise in passive imaging. We validate the model in an experiment in the 5--20 MHz band, in which synthesized RF scenes are replayed through a physical squeezed-light receiver. With 3 dB of squeezing, the PSNR improves by about 6 dB, close to $2G$, in the readout-noise-dominated regime of both modalities, and the model predicts the measured gains without free parameters. These results identify where squeezed-light readout benefits RF-photonic imaging: wherever the optical readout noise, rather than the scene or the RF front end, dominates the image error.

authors.name: Visuttha Manthamkarn, Haowei Shi, Shuaifeng Guo, Christopher M. Jones, Quntao Zhuang, Zheshen Zhang

papers.title: Machine Learning the $GW$ Self-Energy Operator for Real Materials
papers.summary: Machine learning of $GW$ in solids has largely focused on prediction of scalar quasiparticle energy corrections. Here, we introduce a phase-aware many-body transformer that predicts the full $\mathbf{k}$-resolved complex self-energy matrix. As a proof of principle, we apply the model to predict quasiparticle energies before and after diagonalization of the quasiparticle Hamiltonian, obtaining a test set mean absolute error (MAE) of 29 meV for a dataset of 1745 2D materials in the static COHSEX approximation and 60 meV for a more limited dataset of 433 materials calculated within a plasmon-pole model. COHSEX pretraining followed by finetuning reduces this MAE to 42 meV. The predicted matrices also accurately reproduce QP wavefunctions.

authors.name: Xian Xu, Bowen Hou, Chengyan Zhang, Diana Y. Qiu

papers.title: Geometric tracking of a halo CME using full-circle wide-field views from PUNCH
papers.summary: We tracked the large, geoeffective halo coronal mass ejection (CME) of 2025-May-31 across the very wide field of view of the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission, as a proof of concept for data-informed forecasting of CME arrival times at Earth. using simple point-and-click measurement of the front location as far as 47 degrees away from the Sun itself, we constrained an analytic "ludicrous ice-cream cone" geometric model with just three parameters: position angle, off-Earth-Sun angle, and propagation speed. We show that the model is sufficient to capture the bulk envelope of the CME, and also insufficient to capture the complexity of the CME's evolution. We generated simulated arrival-time forecasts for the CME by extrapolating the constant-velocity propagation to determine the time of impact with Earth. These "retro-forecasts" converged to within 30 +/- 15 minutes of the actual arrival time, 8 hours prior to arrival. The convergence was marked by a clear inflection point in the curve of predicted-arrival-time vs time-of-forecast. We conclude that continuous wide-field tracking is sufficiently powerful to enable even crude models to substantially improve arrival-time forecasting precision, and discuss future work required both to validate this single-event result and to extend it to more sophisticated analyses.

authors.name: Craig E. DeForest, Kieran A. Russell, Samuel Van Kooten, Heather A. Elliott, Maher A. Dayeh, Sarah E. Gibson, Anna Malanushenko, David F. Webb, Ronnie Killough, Jillian Redfern, William L. Wells, Matthew N. Beasley, Glenn T. Laurent, Nick R. Waltham, J. Marcus Hughes, Daniel B. Seaton, Ritesh Patel, Chris Lowder, Derek A. Lamb, Alec R. DeForest

papers.title: Population structure of the velocity distribution in normal shock waves: Gaussian representations, Mach-number similarity, and prediction
papers.summary: Normal shock waves are commonly described as mixtures of upstream and downstream Maxwellians. Discrete-velocity solutions of three relaxation models up to Mach 12 and direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) of hard-sphere and variable-hard-sphere gases up to Mach 25 are used to examine the population structure, Mach-number similarity and upstream precursor of their velocity distributions. Three anisotropic Gaussian populations reproduce the streamwise reduced distributions of the Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook (BGK) model and of DSMC to within 4\% up to Mach 12, and of DSMC to within 6\% at Mach 25, whereas two Maxwellians incur errors up to 50\% (BGK) and 37\% (DSMC). Collision histories identify the hard-sphere beam with unscattered stream molecules, which carry half of the peak viscous stress; the other populations are effective descriptions, not collision classes. Above Mach 5, Rankine--Hugoniot-scaled distributions are nearly Mach-independent, with corrections linear in $1/M^2$, consistent with the scaled kinetic equation. At equal normalised density, Mach 8 and 12 give the heat flux and stress at Mach 25 within 1\%, comparable to the accuracy of the reference; with one moment equation for position, physical-space profiles follow within 5\%. Comparing three prediction methods shows that the accuracy comes from the scaling; the Gaussian form adds compactness. Ahead of the shock, the mass of upstream-moving molecules decays as a stretched exponential with effective exponent 0.68--0.87. Collisions regenerate upstream-moving molecules, which explains a decay slower than free-flight survival; a linear cascade model with a downstream-Maxwellian source and no input from the shock interior reproduces the decay rates within 1.2\%.

authors.name: Ehsan Roohi

papers.title: Demographic dynamics of the Japanese astronomy and astrophysics publication community during 1996-2025
papers.summary: We investigate the demographic evolution of the Japanese astronomy and astrophysics publication community during 1996-2025 using bibliometric data from 23,274 publications in major journals in the field. The number of active Japan-affiliated authors increased from approximately 600 in the late 1990s to more than 2,000 by the early 2020s, while annual publication output reached approximately 1,400 by 2025. Participation was highly heterogeneous, with 46% of authors observed in only one publication year within the study period and a smaller core showing long observed participation periods. We define the Community Renewal Rate (CRR) as a community-level measure of renewal, calculated as the fraction of active authors not observed during a specified preceding interval. The 5-year CRR typically remained near one quarter of the active community, with annual values ranging from approximately 21% to 33%, indicating persistent renewal despite substantial community growth. An order-of-magnitude comparison suggests that newly entering students account for only part of the renewal-author population. The community therefore expanded while sustaining both continuity through authors with long observed participation periods and renewal through recurring changes in active membership.

authors.name: Hideaki Fujiwara

papers.title: Collective coupling of over 100 individually trapped atoms to a single cavity mode
papers.summary: Coupling optical tweezer arrays to high-finesse cavities provides a shared optical interface for neutral-atom registers. Scaling this interface to large tweezer arrays requires placing many traps within the coupling region of a single cavity mode while maintaining uniform trapping and site-resolved detection. Here we match a two-dimensional array of 192 optical tweezers to the coupling profile of a millimeter-scale Fabry-Perot cavity. To improve trap uniformity in the array generated by crossed acousto-optic deflectors, we combine optimization with optical feedback and atomic fluorescence feedback, achieving a mean cesium loading probability of approximately 58%. In each trial, fluorescence imaging determines whether each individual tweezer site is occupied, allowing the cavity transmission spectra to be grouped by atom number. The grouped spectra exhibit resolved normal-mode doublets, and the group with 120 imaged atoms yields an effective collective coupling of $G_{\mathrm{eff}}/(2\pi) = 21.30 \pm 0.23$ MHz. A model based on the calculated coupling profile and measured site loading probabilities predicts that the mean squared coupling per occupied site changes little between 97 and 120 atoms. The fitted collective coupling is therefore consistent with square-root scaling with atom number despite the spatial variation in single-atom coupling. These results provide an experimental basis for studying photon-mediated many-body dynamics and developing cavity-assisted readout and optical links between neutral-atom registers.

authors.name: Shijun Guan, Guansheng Teng, Zhiguo Huang, Zhihui Wang, Pengfei Yang, Pengfei Zhang, Gang Li, Tiancai Zhang

papers.title: Quantum geometric spectroscopy with Schr\"{o}dinger cat states
papers.summary: We propose a spectroscopic approach that reads out the quantum geometry of matter from the quantum decoherence of Schr\"{o}dinger-cat light, in the same way that optical absorption reads out the energy structure of matter. For a cat-state probe comprising a superposition of two coherent states, the interbranch coherence of the outgoing light encodes the overlap between the matter states driven by the two branches. We show that, when the electromagnetic fields of the two branches differ only slightly, cat-branch decoherence is quantified by dynamical quantum geometry, which characterizes infinitesimal displacements on the matter-state manifold. For frequency-selective kitten probes of equilibrium matter, we further establish a partition law for the quantum geometric tensor between light and matter, enabling optical readout of matter quantum metric and Berry curvature through, for example, the brightening of a stellar zero in the outgoing Husimi function. For nonequilibrium matter in a pure state, short-pulse cat probes also provide a time-resolved witness of multipartite entanglement through the transient quantum metric, which can be extracted from homodyne measurements of the outgoing light. By turning cat-state decoherence, conventionally regarded as a loss of quantum information, into a carrier of information about matter, this approach establishes a spectroscopic principle that directly probes quantum-state geometry and fluctuations alongside conventional response-based spectroscopy.

authors.name: Shohei Imai, Marcelo F. Ciappina

papers.title: Quantum Sensor of Mechanical Vibrations
papers.summary: We report the use of a single trapped-ion motional mode as a probe of mechanical vibrations of the Paul trap structure. By exciting vibrations of the trap using an ultrasonic transducer mounted outside the vacuum chamber and probing the ion motion through motional sideband interactions, we observe a clear resonance response of the axial mode. We further demonstrate detection of trap vibrations with amplitudes as low as 0.6 picometers. These measurements show direct coupling between macroscopic mechanical motion and trapped-ion dynamics, providing a route toward vibration sensing using quantum control of motional states.

authors.name: Mu Young Kim, H. C. J. Gan, Nigel Benjamin Lee Junsheng, Dzmitry Matsukevich

papers.title: Unconventional Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect beyond Magnetization Scaling Driven by Pulse-Field-Induced Metamagnetism in Fe$_2$Mo$_3$O$_8$
papers.summary: First-order phase transitions often proceed through metastable states and complicated phase coexistence, yet such nonequilibrium processes are obscured in bulk measurements. The magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) probes the local off-diagonal optical response, offering access to local magnetic dynamics beyond bulk measurements. Here, we investigate the magnetic-field-induced antiferromagnetic (AFM)-ferrimagnetic (FRM) transition in the polar insulator Fe$_2$Mo$_3$O$_8$ using pulsed-field MOKE measurements extended for the first time up to 60 T and down to 1.4 K. The MOKE response exhibits unexpected and huge nonmonotonic transient behavior across the metamagnetic phase transition. The MOKE behavior does not show any scaling with the bulk magnetization, pointing to an MOKE analogue of the unconventional anomalous Hall effect. This is a new class of off-diagonal response emerging exclusively at the boundary between competing magnetic orders. At low temperatures, MOKE profiles are highly reproducible in detail, whereas at elevated temperatures they depend strongly on magnetic-field history and pulse protocol, suggesting changes in the driving mechanism of the phase transition. We infer that the excess MOKE anomaly originates from AFM-FRM phase interfaces in real space. Our results, extending MOKE into the 60 T regime, establish pulsed-field magneto-optics as a novel probe capable of uncovering transient and hidden field-induced phenomena through unconventional off-diagonal optical responses.

authors.name: Soichiro Yamane, Sota Nakamura, Shuya Suzuki, Atsutoshi Ikeda, Masaki Kondo, Takashi Kurumaji, Kentaro Ino, Keisuke Matsuura, Fumitaka Kagawa, Yoshinori Tokura, Masashi Tokunaga, Shingo Yonezawa

papers.title: Adsorbate-Free Screening of Dissociative Water Adsorption on Nickel Nanoparticles via Graph Neural Networks
papers.summary: Dissociative water adsorption is a key step in heterogeneous and electrochemical catalysis, but on finite Ni nanosystems the OH$^*$ and H$^*$ fragments can occupy many combinations of surface sites, making exhaustive density functional theory (DFT) screening impractical. We introduce a graph neural network (GNN) framework with an adsorbate-free representation: candidate O- and H-binding sites are defined by sets of Ni atoms (\textit{anchors}), and each site pair is encoded as a graph constructed solely from these anchors and their local Ni environment. Using only MACE-relaxed bare Ni geometries as input, separate GNNs predict the DFT-reference adsorption energies of OH$^*$+H$^*$ configurations and whether the proposed binding sites would be retained upon DFT relaxation, eliminating the need to construct or relax adsorbates during screening. Trained across Ni nanoclusters and Ni(111)/Ni(100) surfaces, the energy model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.031 eV on the internal validation set and demonstrates transferability to unseen Ni$_{55}$, Ni$_{91}$, and Ni$_{130}$ clusters and larger surface cells, particularly for relative-energy ranking, although quantitative accuracy varies across systems. These independent tests also support the retention classifier's use as a conservative filter for selecting configurations likely to preserve their proposed binding sites. Application to Ni nanoparticles containing up to $\sim$3000 atoms identifies favorable co-adsorption motifs and shows that lower O-site coordination generally stabilizes the dissociated state, whereas H-site coordination has a weaker influence. The framework thus offers an efficient route to screening adsorption energetics, with potential extensions to other metals and adsorbate combinations.

authors.name: Marta Monti, Alec Noppe, Olivier Lugier, Maria B. Brands, Bernd Ensing

papers.title: Reduced Density Matrices from Renormalization-Group Flows
papers.summary: We reconstruct complete one- and two-body reduced density matrices (RDMs) by a single collective backward evolution along the in-medium similarity renormalization-group flow. Benchmarks show improved accuracy and physical consistency over conventional elementwise evolution. In neutron matter, two-body RDMs reveal spin-triplet dominance in interaction-dependent Fermi-sea depletion trends. Meanwhile, the forward-backward energy difference provides an internal diagnostic of many-body truncation errors, whose quantification remains challenging in nuclear $ab\ initio$ calculations.

authors.name: X. Zhen, Z. Y. Meng, J. C. Pei, F. R. Xu

papers.title: Detecting False Self-Consistency in Density-Functional Calculations
papers.summary: Density-functional calculations feed materials databases and machine-learning models, and are declared converged when energy changes and residuals fall below thresholds. We show that these criteria, and even the agreement of independent optimizers, can accept a state from which the energy still descends or whose Hamiltonian is inconsistent with the energy. A variational formulation of self-consistency in the space of Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians yields a descent probe that exposes lower states accessible from a returned solution, and a frozen-orbital Janak test detects such an inconsistency. Both apply to any code without modification. In VASP, a UO$_2$ PBE+$U$ calculation converges 1.46 eV above a lower state, and CoO and FeO converge as metals 0.8-0.9 eV above insulating states. In a census of 339 converged calculations on tungsten-free Materials Project structures, recomputed with a modified static protocol, 57 (16.8%) show energy decreases above the threshold, 49 without an initial energy rise exceeding the tolerance.

authors.name: Mohsen Sotoudeh

papers.title: High-order Crank-Nicolson method via diagonal Pad\'e factorization
papers.summary: We present a numerical method to solve the time-dependent Schr\"{o}dinger equation at arbitrary order of accuracy in the time step, particularly well suited for tridiagonal Hamilton operators. The method is based on a factorization of the diagonal Pad\'{e} approximants of the matrix exponential into products of linear factors, which preserves tridiagonal matrix structure at every time step and yields a propagator of order 2q in the time step at a cost of O(qN) operations. The propagator is exactly unitary by construction, and at lowest order q=1 it reduces to the standard Crank-Nicolson algorithm. We further extend the method to any Hamiltonian admitting a decomposition into a sum of tridiagonal or diagonal operators via high-order split-operator techniques (McLachlan, 2022), retaining O(qN) scaling at each time step. We also analytically show and numerically verify that the precision is dictated by the split-operator method. This covers a broad range of physically relevant cases, including higher-dimensional systems, higher-order spatial discretizations, and non-separable potentials.

authors.name: Lou Freschi, Camille L\'ev\^eque, J\'er\'emie Caillat, Richard Ta\"ieb, Jonathan Dubois

papers.title: How Elasticity and Chiral Damping Shape Domain-Wall Creep
papers.summary: Asymmetric domain-wall expansion in the creep regime provides an experimentally accessible probe of the interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (iDMI) and, in principle, chiral damping. However, severe discrepancies with complementary measurement techniques and the lack of a model describing the full experimental phenomenology of the creep of chiral domain walls, limits the application of these measurements. Here, using a symmetry decomposition of the velocity curve, we derive an analytical model describing the coupled influence of domain-wall stiffness and chiral damping in the creep regime. Their interplay generates the antisymmetric distortion that shifts the velocity minimum away from the DMI field. Applied to Co-based magnetic multilayers, the model yields iDMI values consistent with BLS and flow-regime benchmarks and identifies the reasons for the longstanding discrepancy. The model provides insights for possible strategies to measure chiral damping via creep dynamics of domain walls.

authors.name: Adriano Di Pietro, Alessandro Magni, Stefania Pizzini, Giovanni Gandini, Frowin D\"orr, Yasser Shokr, Mustafa Erkovan, Gianfranco Durin, Silvia Tacchi, Marco Madami, Giovanni Carlotti, Emily Darwin, Alexandra J. Huxtable, Christopher H. Marrows, Brian J. Hickey, Vito Puliafito, Michaela K\"upferling

papers.title: Bias Conditioning and Long-Range Electrostatics for Consistent Machine-Learning Potentials of Electrified Interfaces
papers.summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) of electrified interfaces need the bias as input, but it is unclear whether a scalar electrode charge suffices and whether short-range models capture the non-local response. We add charge and field conditioning to short- and long-range MLIPs. State-of-the-art field-conditioned short-range models overpolarize thick water films nearly twofold and miss work-function shifts at stepped Pt. Our long-range model captures both, needs only the electrode charge at metals as input, and reproduces ab initio simulations of the Pt(111)--water interface.

authors.name: Lucas B. T. de Kam, Patrick Rinke, Christopher J. Stein, Philip Loche

papers.title: Linear Electrostatic Instabilities Driven by Relativistic Non-Maxwellian Pair Beams
papers.summary: We investigate how non-Maxwellian momentum distributions affect the linear growth of electrostatic instabilities driven by relativistic pair beams, motivated by the lack of a universally accepted analytical description of blazar-induced pair beams. Different beam distributions are used to describe relativistic pair beams in analytical studies and particle-in-cell simulations. A systematic comparison is therefore needed to determine how the beam distribution influences the instability growth rates. We formulate the relativistic electrostatic response in the weak-beam limit for an anisotropic $\kappa$-type distribution and compare the resulting growth rates with those obtained for Gaussian and Maxwell--J\"uttner distributions. We require $\kappa>3/2$ for a finite root-mean-square momentum spread. For the parameters considered, the $\kappa$-type distributions yield higher maximum growth rates than the Gaussian distribution, even when their mean momenta and momentum spreads are the same. The fastest-growing modes correspond to parallel propagation for the $\kappa$ and Gaussian distributions, whereas the Maxwell--J\"uttner distribution exhibits its maximum for oblique propagation for a mildly relativistic beam. An additional calculation for a highly relativistic pair beam with $\kappa=2$ finds an oblique maximum of the electrostatic growth rate. The beam momentum distribution influences the linear growth of electrostatic instabilities under the conditions investigated.

authors.name: Suman Dey

papers.title: Observing Earth's ionospheric irregularities from the Moon
papers.summary: Radio signals that propagate through the Earth's ionosphere carry information about possible irregular plasma structures. Such irregularities manifest themselves as amplitude signatures that depend on the propagation and observation geometry [1, 2]. Conventional ground and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) measurements sample these effects close to Earth. Here we present a systematic characterization of terrestrial ionospheric irregularities using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) amplitude observations from the lunar surface, at distances of approximately 356,000-398,000 km from Earth's surface [3]. Using nearly 93 h of 1-Hz lunar-surface observations of GPS L1/L5 and Galileo E1/E5a collected by the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE), we reconstruct the propagation and scanning geometry to characterize the spatiotemporal signatures of amplitude and phase fluctuations. At lunar distance, the Fresnel scale approaches its finite-source limit, extending the observations to a propagation regime beyond conventional near-Earth configurations. Detrended receiver-reported carrier-to-noise density ratios (${\delta}C/N_0$) reveal pronounced polar amplitude fluctuations at both frequency bands, also visible in the original measurements. Within the regions and local times sampled, large fluctuations occur in about 30% of valid one-minute polar windows, compared with less than 5% in either the equatorial or mid-latitude band. These findings support using the lunar surface as a vantage point for studying Earth's polar ionospheric irregularities and testing how propagation and scanning relative to the magnetic field shape their amplitude signatures. Future lunar observations could extend this approach to long-term monitoring of Earth's ionospheric irregularities

authors.name: Rong Yang, Zhihong Li, Andrea Nardin, Alex Minetto, Fabio Dovis, Claudio Cesaroni, Luca Spogli, Lucilla Alfonsi, Xirui Miao, Yuquan Ma, Wei Gao, Li-Ta Hsu, Xingqun Zhan

papers.title: A Hierarchically Compressed Immittance Operator Formulation for Fast Statics-to-Full-Wave Electromagnetic Simulation with the Boundary Element Method
papers.summary: The boundary element method allows the electromagnetic simulation of three-dimensional problems with a two-dimensional discretization, using a surface integral representation of Maxwell's equations. For applications involving broadband simulations or multiscale geometries, the well-known low-frequency breakdown of conventional integral equation formulations must be addressed, while ensuring that dielectric, semiconducting, and lossy metallic regions are modeled rigorously, including the skin effect. In this work, a new boundary element formulation based on an immittance operator is proposed, where the underlying integral equations are inherently valid from statics to the full-wave regime. To enable efficient matrix assembly and solution, a hierarchical matrix compression strategy is devised, leveraging fast direct factorization as an intermediate step, and fast matrix-vector products for the iterative solution of the final system of equations. The proposed formulation is capable of electrostatic, magnetostatic, quasistatic, and full-wave simulations of dielectrics, semiconductors, and lossy metals. Representative numerical examples drawn from a variety of applications demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method.

authors.name: Shashwat Sharma

papers.title: Reversal of dynamical backaction and cooling below the quantum backaction limit in Floquet-driven multimode optomechanical resonators
papers.summary: Dynamical backaction describes how a driven cavity field responds with delay to mechanical motion, and can be used to cool that motion toward its quantum ground state or amplify it into self-oscillation. Control over this interaction underpins laser cooling, high-fidelity state preparation, quantum transduction, and phonon lasing. In conventional cavity optomechanics, both the sign and the magnitude of the optical damping are dictated by the laser detuning, and cooling is bounded by quantum backaction (QBA), the optomechanical analogue of the Doppler limit in cold atoms. We show, in theory and experiment, that dynamical backaction can be strongly enhanced in multimode optomechanical resonators driven by time-varying (Floquet) optical fields. A modulated drive couples a sideband-unresolved MHz mode to a sideband-resolved GHz mode through the shared cavity, replacing the QBA limit of the target mode by the occupancy of the auxiliary mode. Experimentally, we cool the MHz mode to $47 \pm 13$ phonons, about half its single-mode QBA limit and an order of magnitude below what single-tone backaction reaches at the same intracavity photon number. The character of the interaction can moreover be completely inverted at fixed laser detuning, turning cooling into amplification and vice versa, controlled solely by the modulation frequency. Floquet driving thus extends open-loop quantum control, which requires no measurement or feedback, to mechanical resonators outside the resolved-sideband regime.

authors.name: Menno H. Jansen, Roel Burgwal, Ewold Verhagen

papers.title: Large-scale Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials in LAMMPS
papers.summary: Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics (MCMD) simulations are widely used to study the properties of materials at the mesoscale. Simulations with hundreds of thousands of atoms usually rely on empirical potentials because MCMD with machine-learning interatomic potentials is impractical at this scale in existing implementations. Here, we introduce a hybrid MPI/OpenMP scheme for MCMD with Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) potentials in LAMMPS. Monte Carlo moves are evaluated from local energy changes and carried out in parallel over MPI ranks, while molecular dynamics is parallelized over OpenMP threads. At a fixed number of CPUs, the wall time of the Monte Carlo moves decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks. Larger simulation cells also reduce the statistical errors of free energy calculations because thermal fluctuations decrease with system size. We demonstrate the scheme by calculating free energies of the HCP and BCC phases in the strongly anharmonic Hf--Ti system and by simulating zirconium segregation in a nanocrystalline copper sample of 670,000 atoms. For Cu--Zr, an ACE potential and an empirical potential predict similar grain boundary compositions but different amounts of zirconium dissolved in the grains. The scheme makes MCMD simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials practical at the length scales of microstructure.

authors.name: Lorenzo Piersante, Anirudh Raju Natarajan

papers.title: Deterministic nonlinear domain engineering algorithm with variable sub-coherence-length domains
papers.summary: We present a new and improved deterministic algorithm that calculates the poling domains for the implementation of arbitrary phase-matching functions (PMF) in quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystals for parametric down-conversion photon sources. In contrast to previous work, the algorithm presented here makes full use of the limits of the fabrication process, such as the minimum feature size and resolution of the lithographic process underpinning the poling procedure. This minimizes the tracking error to the target electric field and improves the accuracy in reaching the desired PMF. We give a tutorial on how to calculate the target function for arbitrary PMFs and run the algorithm. We also demonstrate the procedure on a relevant application in quantum sensing, where we use a quadratic phase on the PMF to implement a broadband photon spectrum while maintaining high nonlinearity across the crystal. The designed crystal is experimentally tested, and the result matches expectations.

authors.name: Michael Schlosser, Tommaso Faleo, Gregor Weihs, Robert Keil, Stefan Frick

papers.title: Interaction Landscapes of Structurally Distorted Toroidal Classical Spin Textures
papers.summary: We develop a classical discrete magnetostatic model of localized magnetic moments arranged in a toroidal texture, where the moments are represented by static current loops and study the behavior of the magnetic dipole-dipole interaction under several types of structural deformations. The purpose is to disentangle effects due to geometric and magnetic deformations, including elliptical, lopsided, alternating, and tilted configurations. In particular, we investigate how distortions modify the toroidal moment and the interaction energy between pairs of toroidal structures. The resulting interaction landscapes exhibit characteristic symmetry patterns and anisotropies that are highly sensitive to the underlying deformation. As a separate proof-of-concept comparison, first-principles calculations on a molecular spin-toroidal system reveal qualitatively similar orientation-dependent behavior. The calculated interaction is microscopically the conventional pairwise magnetic dipole-dipole interaction between localized moments arranged in a spin-toroidal texture; the toroidal moment characterizes the collective texture and should not be interpreted as introducing an additional elementary interaction term. Our results provide a platform for exploring orientation-dependent interactions of spin-toroidal textures in molecular magnets and related nanoscale magnetic systems that are essential to understand the role of toroidal order.

authors.name: Henry Pommer, Arkamita Bandyopadhyay, Jamal Berakdar

papers.title: A database of optical and thermal-radiative behaviour of materials under solar radiation
papers.summary: Solar-matter interactions are important in many scientific and engineering applications. Modeling them needs consistent optical and thermal-radiative properties over the full solar spectrum. Here we present SpaderOptics, a database for 21 materials: metals, oxides, semiconductors, polymers, ceramics, and carbon. It compiles wavelength-dependent refractive indices and extinction coefficients from the literature. Each literature source is kept separate, together with its original conditions. One physics-based calculation chain turns these data into reflectivity, transmissivity, absorptivity, and emissivity for different incidence angles, slab thicknesses, and temperatures. Combined with the Air Mass Zero (AM0) solar spectrum, the properties give absorbed, reflected, and transmitted solar flux for concentrated sunlight. Equilibrium temperatures are given for both a theoretical lumped body and for a slab body, in which thermal conduction is considered. All data are limited to the solid state, up to a material-specific upper temperature limit. Currently, the database applies to extraterrestrial (AM0) sunlight only. A graphical App is also provided for exploring and visualizing the database.

authors.name: Vasiliki E. Alexopoulou, Nikolaos Karalis, Konstantinos Asimakopoulos, Andrei Totu, Constantin Sandu, Paul-Peter Sotiriadis

papers.title: Quantum adiabatic and diabatic optimization: A Hilbert space engineering strategy with Rydberg arrays
papers.summary: Neutral-atom arrays provide a versatile platform for encoding combinatorial optimization problems with arbitrary graph connectivity [Nguyen et al., PRX Quantum 4, 010316 (2023)]. Although the dynamics of individual encoding gadgets has been studied [Bombieri et al., PRX Quantum 6, 020306 (2025)], understanding annealing bottlenecks in larger networks remains challenging. We investigate how engineering the Hilbert-space geometry controls quantum annealing in a family of blockaded-chain models motivated by these encodings. While boundary terms encode the target maximum independent set problem, the bulk geometry induces an auxiliary optimization problem associated with independent sets of cliques. Spectrally, the energetics of the quantum system can be approximated by physically derived clique weights. When the target problem and the auxiliary problems are consistent, the low-energy modes lie predominantly within the target subspace. This spectral structure motivates a diabatic annealing strategy that exploits target-compatible excited states, as tested on the diamond-chain graph family. These results provide a framework for predicting annealing bottlenecks, and demonstrate Hilbert-space engineering as a strategy for improving neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols.

authors.name: Rui Lin

papers.title: Tuning long-range interactions in Sr Rydberg atoms: the effect of series perturbations
papers.summary: We investigate the effect of series perturbation on the second-order dipole-dipole interactions between strontium atoms in the $5sns({^1}S_0)$ and $5snp({^1}P_1)$ Rydberg states as a means of engineering long-range interactions between atoms. The series perturbation in these atoms enables modifying the strength and the sign of the interaction by varying the principal quantum number $n$ of the Rydberg electron. We utilize experimentally available data to estimate the importance of perturber states, and find that the van der Waals interaction between two strontium atoms in the $5snp({^1}P_1)$ states shows strong peaks that deviate from the anticipated hydrogenic $n^{11}$ scaling. We identify this to be the result of the perturbation of $5snd({^1}D_2)$ intermediate states by the $4d^2({^1}D_2)$ and $4dn's({^1}D_2)$ states in the $n<20$ range. This demonstrates that divalent atoms offer a unique advantage for generating substantially stronger or weaker inter-atomic interactions than those that can be achieved using alkali metal atoms. This is due to the highly perturbed spectra of divalent atoms and other multivalent atoms that can persist up to high $n$. Such irregularities can be especially useful in engineering asymmetric Ry blockade requiring the simultaneous presence of both ``weak'' and ``strong'' interactions.

authors.name: Turker Topcu, Andrei Derevianko

papers.title: A unified framework for net effects in signed social and ecological networks
papers.summary: With improvements in data resolution and quality, researchers can now represent complex systems as signed, weighted, and directed networks. In this article, we introduce a framework for measuring net and indirect effects without simplifying these information-rich networks. It captures both direct and indirect interactions, the effect of the whole network on a node, and conversely, the effect of a node on the entire network, while accommodating the complexity of signed, weighted, and directed links. Our taxonomy unifies and extends existing approaches and measures from network science, computational social science, and ecological networks. We demonstrate its value in ecological systems, where net and indirect effects are critical yet difficult to quantify. Using generalized Lotka-Volterra dynamics, we find a strong correlation between negative net effects and species extinction. We further apply the framework to a real-world social network, where it identifies informative rankings that illuminate influence propagation and power dynamics.

authors.name: Carlos G\'omez-Ambrosi, Violeta Calleja-Solanas

papers.title: Gravitational lensing due to charged galactic wormhole
papers.summary: We propose the back reaction to the charged galactic wormhole spacetime based on Yoshiaki Sofue's exponential dark matter density profile to find exact solutions. The charges act as an additional component to the static wormhole, which is primarily formed by the galactic dark matter density. Unlike traditional mass-based models, this solution incorporates charge effects within a realistic dark matter distribution, revealing unique interactions between dark matter, electromagnetic fields, and spacetime curvature. This study confirms the criteria for wormhole formation, designating it the "Charged Galactic Wormhole," and offers a new framework for investigating galactic structures, with potential observational signatures that deepen our understanding of dark matter and spacetime. Later, the proper radial distance and the embedding surface were also analyzed. Furthermore, the deflection of light around a charged galactic wormhole was investigated, along with a comprehensive review of the resulting image. The deflection of massive objects (charge less) near charged galactic wormholes is studied using the Gauss-Bonnet and Rindler-Ishak methods, with a detailed comparison of the results from both approaches. Additionally, in both the Rindler-Ishak (RI) and Gauss-Bonnet (GB) methods, when v tends to 1 i.e. when particle's velocity comparable to the speed of light , the results from these approaches converge, producing the same outcome as strong gravitational lensing.

authors.name: Md Khalid Hossain, Farook Rahaman

papers.title: A Novel Non-Stationary Bias-Correction Framework for Hurricane Risk Assessment under Climate Change
papers.summary: Conventional hurricane track generation methods typically depend on biased outputs from Global Climate Models (GCMs), which undermines their accuracy in the context of climate change. We present a novel non-stationary bias correction framework, developed for and applied to the North Atlantic basin, that adaptively accounts for evolving biases in GCM outputs. The framework combines dimensionality reduction with data-driven surrogate modeling to learn the nonlinear evolution between historical and projected GCM climate states, allowing the bias correction to evolve with changing climate conditions. The learned relationship is subsequently applied to a reanalysis-based historical baseline to generate bias-corrected environmental fields under future climate scenarios. Using the empirical Weibull plotting approach, we calculate return periods for wind speed and rainfall across selected North American coastal cities. Our results reveal substantial differences in projected hurricane hazards with and without bias correction, highlighting the importance of accounting for evolving GCM biases in climate-risk assessment and resilience planning. This work highlights the necessity of adaptive techniques for accurately assessing future climate impacts, offering a critical advancement in hurricane risk modeling and resilience planning.

authors.name: Reda Snaiki, Teng Wu

papers.title: Threshold Properties in Degenerate Distributed Feedback Lasing
papers.summary: We investigate threshold properties in degenerate distributed feedback (DDFB) lasing in a double-grating photonic structure that operates near a degenerate band edge (DBE) with the potential to support robust single-frequency lasing. The DBE is an exceptional point degeneracy (EPD) of fourth order involving four coalescing Bloch eigenmodes. We also provide an analytical demonstration that, for a four-mode system, a quartic flat Bloch dispersion implies the coalescence of the four eigenvectors into a single eigendirection, without explicitly calculating them. Unlike previous studies based on coupled-mode theory, here the realistic double grating is studied using a full-wave method. A DDFB photonic cavity operating close to the DBE frequency is shown to display a large quality factor that scales with the fifth power of the cavity length. Upon the inclusion of gain, the DDFB cavity displays a low lasing threshold with the exceptional scaling as the inverse of the fifth power of the double-grating length, i.e., $\alpha_{D,th} \propto 1/N^5$, where $N$ is the number of waveguide unit cells making the mirrorless cavity. These results suggest the potential for compact, single-frequency lasing using a mirrorless cavity with minimal device footprint. The DDFB laser is very attractive for various applications including communications, sensing, and spectroscopy.

authors.name: Albert Herrero-Parareda, Nathaniel Furman, Filippo Capolino

papers.title: Low-energy nuclear recoil calibration of the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment with a photoneutron source
papers.summary: The LZ experiment is a liquid xenon time-projection chamber (TPC) searching for evidence of particle dark matter interactions. In the simplest assumption of elastic scattering, many dark matter models predict an energy spectrum which rises quasi-exponentially with decreasing energy transfer to a target atom. LZ has recently reported evidence for coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CE$\nu$NS) of $^{8}$B solar neutrinos, a signal nearly identical to that expected from a dark matter particle with a mass of about 5.5 GeV/$c^{2}$, which similarly produces nuclear recoil energies $<5$ keV$_{\text{nr}}$. This analysis details the first in situ photoneutron calibration of the LZ detector, using a custom yttrium-beryllium source that produces quasi-monoenergetic neutrons. Elastic nuclear recoils from both the dominant 152 keV and the rare 950 keV photoneutron modes are observed at rates consistent with expectation. We report the ionization yield, and the corresponding scintillation yield inferred from it, at a mean detected recoil energy of 3.1 keV$_{\text{nr}}$ and a drift field of 193 V/cm. The measurement demonstrates the ability of LZ to detect nuclear recoils near threshold and provides an independent check on the detector-response framework underlying few-GeV dark-matter and $^{8}$B CE$\nu$NS searches.

papers.title: One-dimensional phase singularities as a source of atypical local oscillations
papers.summary: In this work, phase singularities embedded in a wavepacket are shown to act as sources of atypical localized oscillations when the packet interacts with a linear system. We refer to these oscillations as chirpons, since they arise as strong variations of the instantaneous frequency (chirp). A mathematical expression is then provided to describe chirpons, and their behavior is explored through the interaction of a super-bandwidth wavepacket---containing two singularities---with a damped harmonic oscillator, a fundamental model for many physical systems. This interaction is analyzed theoretically, and the predictions are verified experimentally using a resonant electrical circuit as a realization of the oscillator. The results show that chirpons evolve in a manner fundamentally different from standard Fourier oscillations, revealing features of linear systems that are otherwise inaccessible. This introduces a new approach to analyze and characterize system responses, with potential applications in high-resolution spectroscopy and signal sensing.

authors.name: Enrique G. Neyra, Laureano A. Bulus Rossini, Fabi\'an Videla, Pablo A. Costanzo Caso, Lorena Reb\'on

papers.title: Quantum modeling of radical pair magnetic sensor based on electric dipole moment
papers.summary: Photoreduction of cryptochrome protein in the retina is a well-known mechanism of navigation of birds through the geomagnetic field, yet the biosignal nature of the mechanism remains unclear. The absorption of blue light by the flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) chromophore can alter the distribution of electrons in cryptochrome and create radical pairs with separated charges. In this study, the spin dynamics of electrons in the radical pair including its spin-orbit coupling were investigated by quantum mechanical modeling. Spin-orbit coupling is negligible relative to other terms and has no significant role in the dynamics. However, it engages the spatial states of the radical pair and make possible to study spatial related observables. Several interactions were considered in the presence of an external magnetic field, and the resulting electric dipole moment in cryptochrome was computed as the quantity emerging from this coupling. The computations show the induced electric dipole moment clearly depend on the characteristics of the applied magnetic field even after considering dissipative effects. In fact, our findings indicate that the radical pair in cryptochrome protein is a magnetic biosensor, in the sense that in the presence of the geomagnetic field, variations in spin states can influence its electric dipole moment, which may be interpreted via the bird as an orientation signal. The results can be used in the advancement of bio-inspired technologies which replicate animal magnetic sensitivity.

authors.name: Mahboobe Sehati, Ali Soltanmanesh, Shabnam Abutalebi, Abolfazl Bahrampour, Naser Haeri, Sareh Rostami, Alireza Bahrampour

papers.title: 2.5D Transformer: An Efficient 3D Seismic Interpolation Method without Full 3D Training
papers.summary: Transformer has emerged as a powerful deep-learning technique for two-dimensional (2D) seismic data interpolation, owing to its global modeling ability. However, its core operation introduces heavy computational burden due to the quadratic complexity, hindering its further application to higher-dimensional data. To achieve Transformer-based three-dimensional (3D) seismic interpolation, we propose a 2.5-dimensional Transformer network (T-2.5D) that adopts a cross-dimensional transfer learning (TL) strategy, so as to adapt the 2D Transformer encoders to 3D seismic data. The proposed T-2.5D is mainly composed of 2D Transformer encoders and 3D seismic dimension adapters (SDAs). Each 3D SDA is placed before a Transformer encoder to learn spatial correlation information across seismic lines. The proposed cross-dimensional TL strategy comprises two stages: 2D pre-training and 3D fine-tuning. In the first stage, we optimize the 2D Transformer encoders using a large amount of 2D data patches. In the second stage, we freeze the 2D Transformer encoders and fine-tune the 3D SDAs using limited 3D data volumes. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets are conducted to assess the effectiveness and efficiency of T-2.5D. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to that of full 3D Transformer at a significantly low cost.

authors.name: Changxin Wei, Xintong Dong, Xinyang Wang

papers.title: Large-scale patterns of small-scale vorticity interactions foster moist convection during cyclogenesis
papers.summary: Understanding the self-organization of small-scale moist convection at synoptic scales during tropical cyclogenesis is essential. We examine the role of vorticity interactions in dynamical organization of moist convection during cyclogenesis in the Bay of Bengal. Using time-varying complex networks, we encode local vorticity correlations between nodes (locations), only within a spatial proximity of sub-meso length scales. Links are established using short-time correlation of vorticity fluctuations. Spatial patches of high network connectivity depict regions of locally coherent vorticity dynamics. We find that various patches of high network connectivity arrange into extended structures forming identifiable large-scale patterns. Examining the co-evolution of moist thermodynamics parameters with local vorticity coherence, we discover a unique spatial correlation between the convective processes occurring at far away locations, owing to self-organization. We find that such spatial correlation are evident only for depressions that form cyclones, and not otherwise. We discover the physical mechanism of self-organization using modal analysis of network connectivity and vorticity budgets. In regions identified as most influential by the modal analysis, we find that vertical vorticity is enhanced locally as well as advected horizontally outwards to other locations. Such horizontal advection of vertical vorticity induces nonlocal interactions and couples small-scale convective processes across a large domain. We show that, vertical vorticity transported from regions of high convective potential help sustain strong updrafts and weaken convective inhibition in other regions. Thus, spatial interdependence is introduced between small-scale convective processes at different locations, thus explaining the self-organization of moist convection during cyclogenesis.

authors.name: Shruti Tandon, Apoorva Singh, B. N. Goswami, R. I. Sujith

papers.title: Logarithmic dispersion at marginal stability in collective attention
papers.summary: How cross-sectional heterogeneity evolves in nonequilibrium populations of competing, ageing units is a collective question that cannot be resolved from a representative trajectory or the ensemble mean alone. Analysis of more than two million age-aligned English Wikipedia page-view trajectories from six yearly cohorts spanning 2015-2020 shows that the variance of logarithmic attention grows linearly with $\ln t$, while the ensemble mean relaxes on the same logarithmic clock. This dispersion law recurs across all six cohorts and is systematically favoured over the tested power-law alternative; temporal increments also exhibit consistent antipersistent scaling. A complementary trajectory-level analysis reveals broad, non-Gaussian variation in effective relaxation rates, showing that this collective regularity coexists with heterogeneous observed trajectories. A minimal scale-free stochastic model combines mean relaxation with self-affine temporal fluctuations of age-dependent amplitude. Within this model class, logarithmic spreading emerges when fluctuation accumulation balances ageing attenuation, defining the marginal boundary between algebraic broadening and saturation. Together, age-resolved cross-sectional dispersion and temporal-increment scaling provide a transferable ensemble-level criterion for distinguishing amplification, marginal spreading, and saturation in other populations of competing, ageing units.

authors.name: Keisuke Okamura

papers.title: Recursive regularisation in lattice Boltzmann magnetohydrodynamics
papers.summary: Recursive regularisation (RR) improves the stability of lattice Boltzmann schemes, but its structure and limitations in magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) remain insufficiently understood. This work connects RR to central-Hermite-moment (CHM) collisions on D2Q9 and D3Q27 through a closed-form reconstruction valid for arbitrary second-order relaxation rates. The central moments of the Maxwell stress coincide, up to sign, with the recursion coefficients, providing a systematic basis for MHD collision operators. Common two-dimensional raw- and central-moment schemes thus correspond to regularisation with a unit bulk relaxation rate. In three dimensions, a CHM implementation reproduces RR to round-off, while a monomial central-moment collision differs at fourth order and produces a four- to twelve-fold larger kinetic-energy error in the tested flow. Chapman--Enskog analysis shows that, with a magnetic field, the hydrodynamic recursion reconstructs the third-order non-equilibrium with a relative error of $78$--$96\%$ ($4\%$ without a field). A local correction largely removes it, yet changes the solutions by less than their discretisation error, consistent with its Burnett-order character. Three-dimensional vortex simulations show approximately second-order convergence at $\mathrm{Re}=100$ and agree with pseudo-spectral solutions through the peak current at $\mathrm{Re}=1000$ and, with a unit bulk rate, at $\mathrm{Re}=3000$. There, single-rate RR develops a compressive instability whose onset depends on the grid, lattice Mach number and initial magnetic configuration. For the standard initial field, a unit bulk rate suppresses it at $\mathrm{Ma}=0.034$ for $N\ge128$. This improvement does not extend to BGK collisions or prevent failure at $\mathrm{Re}=10,000$. These results show that robust three-dimensional MHD simulations require regularisation and bulk dissipation to be considered together.

authors.name: Alessandro De Rosis

papers.title: Interfacial Resistance and Preferential Internal Mixing of Phase-Separated Condensates
papers.summary: Biomolecular condensates spatially organize biochemical processes. They can selectively partition molecules and enrich them well above their concentration outside. Their function depends on the exchange of molecules with their surroundings, whose kinetics are determined not only by partitioning and diffusion but also by interfacial resistance. The latter can hinder molecules from crossing the condensate boundary, thereby increasing their residence times in the condensate and promoting repeated encounters with interaction partners therein. So far, it has proven difficult to measure the interfacial resistance of condensates experimentally. Here, we combine fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) with fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) and calibrated fluorescence imaging to disentangle partitioning, interfacial resistance, and differences in diffusion inside and outside of condensates. Applying this approach to polyelectrolyte condensates across a range of salt concentrations, we find substantial, salt-dependent interfacial resistance, which causes molecules to undergo multiple rounds of internal mixing before escaping. DDX4-YFP condensates in living cells also exhibit substantial interfacial resistance, although they are more permeable than polyelectrolyte condensates with comparable partition coefficients. Our results indicate that interfacial resistance is a tunable property of condensates that can place them in distinct transport regimes, favoring distinct functions such as dynamic reaction crucibles or insulated molecular sinks.

authors.name: Oihan Joyot, Zo\'e Ferrand, Fernando Muzzopappa, Pierre Weiss, Fabian Erdel

papers.title: Hugoniot Relation for Multi-Temperature Euler Equations of Compressible Plasma Flows
papers.summary: Shock solutions for multi-temperature Euler equations are inherently ambiguous due to the loss of microscopic physical detail during model reduction and occurrence of non-conservative terms. This paper presents a detailed analytical study of shock structures in such models. We present two distinct Hugoniot relations, each corresponding to a physically admissible shock solution. Through classical analysis \`a la Courant--Friedrichs, we demonstrate that both satisfy admissibility conditions, revealing a fundamental non-uniqueness in shock structures. By relating these solutions to existing numerical schemes, the structure-preserving and vanishing viscosity approaches, we provide physically justified references for constructing and evaluating discontinuous numerical approximations. In particular, we emphasize that the Hugoniot relation is not uniquely determined by the macroscopic PDEs alone, but must be supplied from external sources such as experiments or first-principles simulations. This insight demonstrates the essential role of microscopic physics in resolving shock ambiguity and contributes to the theoretical foundation for modeling discontinuous plasma flows.

authors.name: Zhifang Du, Aleksey Sikstel

papers.title: Phase-Sum Coupling for Gradient-Flow Dynamics in Oscillator Ising Machines
papers.summary: Oscillator Ising machines are commonly viewed as dynamical systems that minimize an energy function, yet this interpretation is not generally valid for nonlinear oscillator hardware. Here, we show that conventional phase-difference coupling requires a stringent harmonic-by-harmonic quadrature condition between the oscillator waveform and its phase response. In contrast, symmetric phase-sum interactions intrinsically admit gradient-flow dynamics without this constraint. When combined with second-harmonic injection, the canonical sine phase-sum interaction recovers the Ising Hamiltonian on the binary phase manifold while defining a distinct continuous energy landscape. However, the physical realization of phase-sum coupling can introduce unwanted cross-harmonic interactions that compromise the gradient-flow structure. We derive a Nyquist-like phase-domain sampling criterion that specifies the number of coupling paths required to eliminate these interactions within a prescribed harmonic bandwidth. Guided by this result, we develop a CMOS architecture combining phase-resolved oscillator taps with second-harmonic-modulated coupling. Transistor-level simulations demonstrate an approximately fifteenfold reduction in non-gradient curl compared with conventional phase-difference coupling, while simulations of oscillator networks validate the resulting phase-sum dynamics. These results establish interaction symmetry as an additional design degree of freedom for engineering gradient-flow dynamics in nonlinear oscillator Ising machines.

authors.name: Abir Hasan, Sajib Bain, E. M. Hasantha Ekanayake, Kyle Lee, Kerem Camsari, Nikhil Shukla

papers.title: Quantum Field Approach to Relativistic Turbulence
papers.summary: The goal of this work is to apply quantum field theory methods to a typical relativistic hydrodynamic model. We shall take as representative model an Israel-Stewart framework, where the energy-momentum conservation laws for a conformal invariant fluid are supplemented by a Cattaneo-Maxwell equation for its viscous energy-momentum tensor. In these models the viscous energy-momentum tensor relaxes to its Landau-Lifshitz value on a finite time scale. We assume the parameters of the model depend on the speed of light $c$ in such a way that as $c\to\infty$ the fluid becomes an incompressible fluid obeying the Navier-Stokes equations. We show that because the relativistic model must be hyperbolic, each mode behaves as an overdamped oscillator with two decay constants, one of which diverges as $c\to\infty$. Thus for finite $c$ there are two basic patterns, one which contains only slowly decaying modes, and reproduces Kolmogorov turbulence when $c\to\infty$, and another made of fast decaying modes only. Each flow pattern is associated to definite relations among the velocity and viscous energy tensor correlators.

authors.name: Esteban Calzetta

papers.title: Symmetry-breaking and hysteretic transitions in an actively coupled optical trimer
papers.summary: We investigate the nonlinear dynamics of a non-Hermitian optical trimer consisting of three lossy waveguides with complex-valued coupling. Building on our previous analysis of its global dynamics, we adopt a site-resolved approach to elucidate the bifurcation structure and the organization of oscillatory states across the individual waveguides. We identify a hysteretic transition from reflection-asymmetric periodic states to periodic states exhibiting a combined reflection-translation symmetry. This transition involves a double-loop hysteretic regime characterized by the coexistence of multiple attractors. Analysis of the spatial intensity profiles and their Fourier spectra reveals distinct oscillatory behavior among the waveguides. In particular, in the regime with combined reflection-translation symmetry, the central waveguide exhibits a dominant spatial wavenumber approximately twice that of the edge waveguides. We further identify a third dynamical regime emerging through a pitchfork bifurcation of limit cycles, which breaks the combined reflection-translation symmetry and gives rise to two reflection-related periodic solutions. Despite this transition, the 2:1 relation between the dominant spatial wavenumbers of the central and edge waveguides persists. These results demonstrate how nonlinear interactions, complex coupling, and dissipation shape multistability, bifurcations, and site-dependent oscillations in a minimal non-Hermitian photonic system.

authors.name: Johanne Hizanidis, Konstantinos G. Makris

papers.title: Raman optical activity and helicity-dependent phonon splitting in chiral CoSi
papers.summary: Circularly polarized Raman scattering in solids provides access to two distinct phenomena: Raman optical activity (ROA), an intensity difference between circular polarization channels, and helicity-dependent frequency splitting of chiral phonons. We observe both in the chiral topological semimetal CoSi and show that they arise through two different symmetry channels, each rendering phonon components with opposite crystal angular momenta inequivalent. Doubly degenerate E phonons exhibit a large ROA, with an approximately fourfold intensity contrast between the two cross-circular channels. The sign of this ROA reverses between the front and back {111} surfaces, while its strong suppression on {110} supports the assignment to the axial electric toroidal octupole. By contrast, triply degenerate T phonons show helicity-dependent frequency splittings, whose mode-dependent signs are reproduced by the calculated dispersion of branches with opposite crystal angular momenta, thus identifying structural chirality as their source. First-principles calculations yield a pronounced E-mode intensity asymmetry in the resonant regime, reproduce the mode-dependent signs of the T-mode splittings, and account for their magnitudes within approximately 40%. These results establish circularly polarized Raman scattering as a symmetry- and angular-momentum-resolved probe of chiral and axial multipolar symmetry in solids.

authors.name: Yuki Suganuma, Gakuto Kusuno, Kohei Miyazaki, Hikaru Watanabe, Rikuto Oiwa, Ryotaro Arita, Satoshi Iwasaki, Yoshiki Yasuoka, Yusuke Kousaka, Yoshihiko Togawa, Takuya Satoh

papers.title: Bode-Fano Limits to Broadband Absorption by Small Particles
papers.summary: Subwavelength nanostructures can absorb light efficiently at resonance, but causality and passivity fundamentally limit the bandwidth over which strong absorption can be maintained. We derive Bode-Fano-type limits for electrically small scatterers dominated by a single mode, assuming linear, time-invariant materials with rational dispersion. The derivation maps electromagnetic absorption onto an equivalent impedance-matching problem and provides a constructive method for synthesizing material dispersion that approaches these bounds while satisfying the same physical constraints. Our results guide the design of passive nanoparticles for broadband absorption, with potential applications in nanoscale light harvesting and dissipation.

authors.name: Emanuele Corsaro, Andrea Al\`u, Carlo Forestiere

papers.title: Machine Learning Approaches for Improved Scalability of Metallic Magnetic Calorimeters
papers.summary: Metallic Magnetic Calorimeters are a promising tool for high-precision X-ray spectroscopy. However the signal processing and calibration pipeline required to exploit their full potential is complex and difficult to scale for large, highly pixelated detector arrays. In this work, we investigate Machine Learning methods for maXs-series detectors, focusing on pulse classification and artifact rejection as well as pulse-shape analysis and feature extraction. By combining unsupervised label auto-discovery with supervised classification and regression, we obtain robust and scalable artifact rejection for high-confidence template building. For ML-based feature extraction, our results constitute a promising proof of principle: in simulation, the ML estimator remains competitive across realistic pulse-shape and noise variation. On real detector data, the method reaches performance comparable to the hand-optimized FIR baseline before gain-drift correction, while further domain adaptation is required to match the established manual analysis pipeline. Both results represent important steps toward a fully automated and scalable data processing procedure.

authors.name: Marc Oliver Herdrich, Toni Mattis, G\"unter Weber, Daniel Aaron Schnau{\ss}-M\"uller, Johanna Hanke Walch, Thomas St\"ohlker

papers.title: Gappy Reconstruction of Bubbly Flows by Guided Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Experiments in multiphase flows are often limited in their ability to simultaneously obtain velocity measurements in different phases. At the same time, flow reconstruction from phase-limited measurements is a challenging problem due to the substantially different velocity statistics across the phases. We address this problem for buoyancy-driven bubbly flows in the pseudo-turbulence regime by using a guided diffusion model. We train the model using two-dimensional slices of the velocity field extracted from fully resolved three-dimensional direct numerical simulations. The model generates physically realistic velocity fields both unconditionally and when conditioned on the surrounding liquid flow. The reconstructed bubble-phase velocity field accurately reproduces key statistical features of the flow. We further show that a simple stacking procedure for adjacent two-dimensional slices enables a reasonable reconstruction of the three-dimensional flow inside a bubble. These results establish the potential of diffusion models to serve as generative priors for three-dimensional turbulent multiphase flows, opening a route toward the reconstruction of unobserved or experimentally inaccessible velocity fields from sparse, partial, or phase-limited measurements.

authors.name: Hridey Narula, Tianyi Li, Michele Buzzicotti, Luca Biferale, Prasad Perlekar

papers.title: Photon-conserving Raman soliton attractors in focusing and defocusing Kerr media
papers.summary: The sign of the Kerr nonlinear coefficient has long been regarded as irrelevant to the direction of the Raman-induced soliton self-frequency shift. Yet the standard generalized nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation (GNLSE) predicts a frequency shift that depends on the sign of the nonlinearity, which leads to an unphysical blue shift in the defocusing case. We resolve this inconsistency by deriving the time-domain form of the photon-conserving GNLSE (pcGNLSE) from its established frequency-domain counterpart. The derivation reveals that photon-number conservation imposes two sign modifications relative to the standard GNLSE: the Raman-shift coefficient acquires the absolute value of the Kerr nonlinear coefficient in place of its signed counterpart, and the self-steepening-Raman dissipation term likewise carries an absolute-value prefactor rather than a signed one. These two modifications jointly guarantee a universal spectral redshift and monotonically decreasing pulse energy during propagation, irrespective of the signs of the Kerr nonlinear coefficient and its frequency derivative. Applying the method of moments to the time-domain pcGNLSE with appropriate chirped ans\"atze, we derive closed-form evolution equations for five pulse parameters and establish explicit attractor conditions under which bright or dark Raman solitons propagate with constant peak power. Direct numerical integration of the pcGNLSE confirms all analytical predictions and demonstrates that the standard GNLSE fails qualitatively, predicting unphysical energy growth and spectral blueshift in the negative-nonlinearity regime. The results provide a rigorous analytical framework for Raman soliton dynamics in materials with negative third-order susceptibility, with direct implications for soliton-based devices in emerging semiconductor waveguide and microresonator platforms.

authors.name: Weiye Huang, Junhong Yang, Tao Sun, Qian Gao, Peilong Yang, Jintao Fan, G\"unter Steinmeyer, Jinhui Yuan, Chao Mei

papers.title: Gradient-Based Inverse Design of Free-Energy Landscapes with Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Free-energy surfaces govern the populations of metastable states and the barriers that control transitions between them, making their direct optimization a central challenge in molecular and materials design. In this work, we introduce Gradient-Based Free Energy Surface Optimization (GB-FESO), an inverse design framework that uses a trained conditional diffusion model as a differentiable surrogate for the ensemble distribution. After training, the diffusion model is frozen, and the conditioning variables defining the system are optimized so that the generated ensemble reproduces a prescribed target free-energy surface. The optimization is carried out by backpropagating a distribution-level loss, based on kernel density estimates of the Kullback-Leibler divergence, through a deterministic diffusion sampling trajectory. We first validate GB-FESO on one-dimensional Gaussian ensembles, demonstrating that both continuous and relaxed discrete conditioning variables can be optimized to recover target distributions, including those outside the training domain. We then apply the method to a four-particle Lennard-Jones toy peptide exhibiting multiple metastable conformational states. In this more physically motivated setting, GB-FESO successfully optimizes the interaction parameters to reproduce target free-energy landscapes in the majority of test cases, with optimization performed either in the full internal-coordinate space or in a reduced collective-variable representation. These results establish GB-FESO as a promising first step toward an ensemble-level inverse design framework for molecular systems with prescribed thermodynamic and kinetic behavior.

authors.name: Eli Zick, Dan Mendels

papers.title: Wall-bounded turbulence needs not be long
papers.summary: Experiments on the regeneration of long streaks in flows in which they had originally been damped show that their initial growth is due to the interaction of the mean shear with weak long cross-flow velocities (`rollers') that remain even when the streaks are damped. More surprisingly, turbulence also persists in simulations in which only the long rollers are damped while long streaks remain, and these flows are also able to recover when the damping is removed. Finally, simulations are presented in which both streaks and rollers longer than $\lambda_x^+\approx 600$ are damped. They survive and regenerate, and an interpretation in terms of their energy balance is provided. In contraposition to the classical minimal channels, which include infinitely long structures, these new flows do not contain any feature longer than the damping wavelength, and support a model in which wall turbulence only depends on processes for which the geometric $\lambda_x-\lambda_z$ aspect ratio is of order unity.

authors.name: Carlos Martinez Lopez, Javier Jimenez

papers.title: APHABAMAS: An analytical phantom-based scheme for assessing the accuracy of high-resolution 3D MRI motion-artifact simulations
papers.summary: Purpose: Motion compromises the utility of high-resolution 3D MRI. Deep learning-based methods have shown promise for mitigating motion-induced artifacts, but their development typically requires simulated motion-corrupted data. Several open-source tools exist for this task. They share a common formulation but implement this formulation with different algorithms. It is unclear which algorithm implements the formulation more accurately. This study aims to develop a scheme to answer this question. Methods: The essential ingredient of the desired scheme is a ground-truth reference that does not suffer from sampling-induced error. To meet this requirement, the proposed scheme, APHABAMAS, leverages a digital phantom whose image- and Fourier-domain representations can be expressed analytically under arbitrary rigid-body transformations. APHABAMAS is used to quantify sampling-induced errors of three existing algorithms under synthetic and tracking-data-derived motion trajectories at different motion severity levels. Results: All three algorithms produce distinct but visually plausible artifacts, demonstrating the need for a ground-truth reference. APHABAMAS shows that the algorithm utilizing the uniform-to-non-uniform (Type-2) Non-Uniform Fast Fourier Transform (NUFFT) provides the most consistent agreement with the ground-truth reference across motion types and severity levels. For the non-uniform-to-uniform (Type-1) NUFFT-based algorithm, agreement with the ground-truth reference deteriorates substantially with increasing motion severity. Conclusion: APHABAMAS provides a rigorous tool for assessing how accurately algorithms implement the common formulation for simulating motion artifacts in high-resolution 3D MRI. It enables accuracy-based ranking of the three assessed algorithms, thereby facilitating informed selection of the most suitable one for synthesizing motion-corrupted data.

authors.name: Tianqi Wu, Hui Zhang

papers.title: Band Engineering of Exciton Polaritons in Resonant Polaritonic Metasurfaces
papers.summary: Polaritonic metasurfaces provide a versatile platform for engineering hybrid light-matter states through the interplay of optical resonances and excitonic excitations. Yet, predictive models often remain phenomenological and rely on coupled-mode equations. Here, we develop an effective Hamiltonian framework for exciton polaritons in resonant polaritonic metasurfaces, derived from a semiclassical single-pole description of excitonic polarization and a Green's-function description of guided-mode resonances. The resulting non-Hermitian Hamiltonian rigorously incorporates resonant photonic harmonics, multiple excitonic degrees of freedom, and radiative losses. The model establishes selection rules for photonic-excitonic coupling governed by orbital multipole index and polarization and identifies one bright excitonic degree of freedom per retained guided harmonic. We apply the framework to a bulk van der Waals WS$_2$ metasurface patterned into a hexagonal lattice of triangular holes and uncover a new geometry-controlled topological transition driven by dipole-quadrupole band inversion, distinct from the conventional breathing-honeycomb-lattice transition. Full-wave simulations confirm the predicted topological phase diagram and the emergence of photonic and polaritonic edge states at a topological interface. Our results establish a theoretical multimode framework for geometry-controlled bandstructure engineering in polaritonic metasurfaces, with applications in topological, chiral, and quantum integrated photonics.

authors.name: Polina Pantiukhina, Daria Smirnova, Kirill Koshelev

papers.title: Load-induced Taylor-Aris dispersion in compliant electroosmotic pumps with viscoelastic electrolytes
papers.summary: We investigate the dispersion of a passive, neutral solute in a compliant slit, in which electroosmotic flow drives a viscoelastic electrolyte against an outlet pressure load. The electrolyte is modelled using the simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner model with an inviscid Newtonian solvent. Combining lubrication theory, Debye Huckel linearisation and a local elastic-foundation model, we determine the loaded flow and quantify solute dispersion. A central finding is that hydraulic loading fundamentally alters the thin-electric-double-layer limit of shear dispersion. It was observed that shear dispersion vanishes under free-flow conditions, but an adverse pressure gradient continues to support core shear under load, resulting in a finite dispersion plateau even without flow reversal. This plateau increases with hydraulic loading and is further enhanced by viscoelasticity at a fixed throughput fraction. For Newtonian flow, wall expansion leaves the plateau unchanged under constant-current conditions but increases it under constant-voltage conditions. At finite EDL thicknesses, opposing electroosmotic and pressure-driven shear can partially cancel, improving the plate number despite reduced throughput. The combined effects of shear dispersion, molecular diffusion and transit time produce an optimal EDL thickness at prescribed throughput. Joint optimisation shifts the optimum towards free-flow conditions and thinner EDLs for the range of parameters considered. The predicted plate numbers agree closely with Brownian-dynamics simulations for six benchmark cases. These results establish the role of hydraulic loading and wall compliance in controlling the trade-off between pressure delivery and band broadening in compliant electroosmotic pumps.

authors.name: Subhajyoti Sahoo, Ameeya Kumar Nayak, Kirti Chandra Sahu

papers.title: Reframing the coupling force of adaptive resolution simulation in terms of the Liouville-type hierarchy for open systems
papers.summary: In this work, we present a novel perspective on the coupling force employed to compensate the interface artifacts prevalent in adaptive resolution simulations (AdResS) of open many-particle systems. We show that a substantial part of this "thermodynamic force" can be framed in terms of the theoretical model of the Liouville-type hierarchy for open systems. The correspondence is made explicit for the case of a simple atomistic fluid, for which a one-dimensional integral expression is derived. This enables the analysis for dependencies of the thermodynamic force on important simulation parameters, which is taken to inspire both simplifications for the numerical calculation of the thermodynamic force and new criteria for its validation that are adequate to the interfacial nature of the problem. The theoretical claims are then verified in a simulation study of the atomistic supercritical Lennard-Jones fluid at different thermodynamic states.

authors.name: Julian F. Hille, Rupert Klein
