authors.name: Sharan Nurani Ramesh, Lea Sa{\ss}mannshausen, Axel Klawonn, Daniel Balzani

papers.title: Connectivity from activity in spiking neural networks
papers.summary: We show that a wide range of recurrent neural network models obey a simple set of equations tying synaptic connectivity and single-cell response properties to neural correlations. Our modeling framework considers networks in a stationary, asynchronous state and contains a broad class of synaptic filters, spiking nonlinearities, and random-plus-structured connectivity. The resulting equations naturally decompose into contributions from monosynaptic, disynaptic, and higher order paths through the network. We leverage this decomposition to express the effective monosynaptic connection between two neurons in terms of experimentally measurable statistics of the activity, and in particular, their high-frequency correlations. In this way, we show that it is possible to recover network connectivity from neural activity.

authors.name: Albert J. Wakhloo, Sebastian Mizera

papers.title: A Phase-field Model for Apoptotic Cell Death
papers.summary: The process of programmed cell death, namely apoptosis, is a natural mechanism that regulates healthy tissue, multicellular structures, and homeostasis. An improved understanding of apoptosis can significantly enhance our knowledge of biological processes and systems. For instance, pathogens can manipulate the apoptotic process to either evade immune detection or to facilitate their spread. Furthermore, of particular clinical interest is the ability of cancer cells to evade apoptosis, hence allowing them to survive and proliferate uncontrollably. Thus, in this work, we propose a phase-field framework for simulating intrinsic or extrinsic apoptosis induced by a cytotoxic phase, including deriving the configurational mechanics underlying such phenomena. The homogeneous analysis identifies degradation and recovery regimes under a fixed and evolving cytotoxic phase. To showcase model capabilities, we present simulations exhibiting different types of cellular dynamics produced when varying the mechanisms underlying apoptosis. The model is subsequently applied to probe different morphological transitions, such as cell shrinkage, membrane blebbing, cavity formation and fragmentation. Lastly, we compare the characteristics observed in our simulations to electron microscopy images, providing additional support for the model.

authors.name: Daniel A. Vaughan, Anna M. Piccinini, Mischa Zelzer, Etienne Farcot, Bindi S. Brook, Kris Van-der-Zee, Luis Espath

papers.title: Analyzing Memory Effects in Large Language Models through the lens of Cognitive Psychology
papers.summary: Memory, a fundamental component of human cognition, exhibits adaptive yet fallible characteristics as illustrated by Schacter's memory "sins".These cognitive phenomena have been studied extensively in psychology and neuroscience, but the extent to which artificial systems, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), emulate these cognitive phenomena remains underexplored. This study uses human memory research as a lens for understanding LLMs and systematically investigates human memory effects in state-of-the-art LLMs using paradigms drawn from psychological research. We evaluate seven key memory phenomena, comparing human behavior to LLM performance. Both people and models remember less when overloaded with information (list length effect) and remember better with repeated exposure (list strength effect). They also show similar difficulties when retrieving overlapping information, where storing too many similar facts leads to confusion (fan effect). Like humans, LLMs are susceptible to falsely "remembering" words that were never shown but are related to others (false memories), and they can apply prior learning to new, related situations (cross-domain generalization). However, LLMs differ in two key ways: they are less influenced by the order in which information is presented (positional bias) and more robust when processing random or meaningless material (nonsense effect). These results reveal both alignments and divergences in how LLMs and humans reconstruct memory. The findings help clarify how memory-like behavior in LLMs echoes core features of human cognition, while also highlighting the architectural differences that lead to distinct patterns of error and success.

authors.name: Zhaoyang Cao, Lael Schooler, Reza Zafarani

papers.title: What makes vertical federated learning work with thirteen samples? A controlled benchmark on coral thermal-stress multi-omics
papers.summary: Vertical federated learning (VFL) lets laboratories that hold different omics layers of the same samples train a joint model without sharing raw data, but it is usually developed for datasets with thousands of samples. We benchmarked VFL on a Montipora capitata thermal-stress dataset with 13 samples and 90,579 features across transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and microbiome data. The benchmark crosses two VFL backbones (a split-network model implemented in NVIDIA FLARE, and LASER-VFL) with three per-silo feature-selection strategies (gradient saliency, random, univariate t-test) and two allocations of a 1,300-feature budget, and adds a centralised elastic-net reference. All models were trained for the same number of steps and evaluated by repeated stratified 3-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation, with separate estimates of seed and data-split variability and end-to-end label-permutation tests. Plain VFL on all features classified heat stress well above chance (3-fold AUROC 0.869, 95% CI 0.838-0.895; permutation p = 0.020). Gradient-saliency selection with hand-set omics priors (0.904) could not be distinguished from plain VFL, from equal budgets or from random subsets of the same size (corrected p >= 0.56), and its selected features were no more consistent across seeds than random ones. LASER-VFL failed on all features at a learning rate of 1e-3 but matched the other methods at 1e-4. This version corrects versions 1-3 of this preprint, which reported that standard VFL performed at chance and that domain priors stabilised training; we show that those results arose because every model selected its checkpoint on a single-sample validation set, which evaluated the baseline after one optimiser step. With very few samples, evaluation choices outweighed every method choice we tested, and we give recommendations for evaluating federated models in this regime.

authors.name: Sam Victor

papers.title: Koopman Operator Analysis of EEG Microstate Dynamics Reveals a Cross-Dataset, Hearing-Level Adjusted Signature of Tinnitus
papers.summary: While major progress has been made in identifying EEG biomarkers for chronic Tinnitus, hearing loss remains as a major confound that must be accounted for in the identified effect. These markers have rarely been tested across independent datasets, a further test of robustness. We analyzed resting-state EEG microstate statistics, and developed a Koopman-operator description of the same microstate signal, carry a tinnitus-related difference that replicates across sites and survives adjustment for hearing level. Three public resting-state datasets (335 subjects; 234 tinnitus, 101 controls) were projected onto a fixed seven-map microstate template. Pooled across datasets, 2/56 microstate statistics differed consistently, and after adjustment for pure-tone average (PTA) none remained significant after FDR correction. Tinnitus subjects had a larger fraction of fast-decaying Koopman modes in all three datasets, and this difference survived PTA adjustment (pooled r=0.26, p=0.002). Microstate differences in tinnitus are substantially explained by hearing level; operator-level dynamics of the same signal retain a hearing-adjusted difference that generalizes across sites.

authors.name: Adyant Balaji, Abhinav Uppal, Min Suk Lee, Yuchen Xu, Akihiro J. Matsuoka, Gert Cauwenberghs

papers.title: High-Fidelity 3D Simulator for Synthetic fNIRS Data Generation
papers.summary: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides a noninvasive window into brain activity by measuring task-related changes in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin in the cortex. However, analyzing fNIRS data is challenging because of motion artifacts, physiological noise, and other confounding factors. This challenge is further compounded by the limited availability of annotated datasets, which hinders the development and validation of new analysis pipelines, particularly given the growing use of AI methods. Recognizing these challenges, we introduce a 3D fNIRS simulator that uses mesh-based Monte Carlo simulations to generate physiologically informed, full-head synthetic recordings with controllable spatiotemporal characteristics. Our simulator combines anatomically informed sensitivity profiles with parameterized models of hemodynamic responses, systemic physiology, and measurement artifacts. As a result, users can generate large labeled datasets with known cortical ground truth for developing and evaluating denoising algorithms, data augmentation strategies, mechanistic models, and in silico experiments. We validate key spatiotemporal and physiological properties of the simulator against experimental fNIRS data from open-source finger-tapping, pain-assessment, and surgical-skill datasets.

authors.name: Condell Eastmond, Niels Bracher, Xavier Intes, Stefan T. Radev

papers.title: An Octahedral Fibrous Constitutive Model for Heart Valve Mechanics and Function
papers.summary: Fibrous soft tissues derive their nonlinear mechanical response from networks of extracellular matrix fibers. The organization of fibers and their load-bearing characteristics give rise to strain stiffening, the reverse Poynting effect, and anisotropic mechanical behavior. Motivated by these coupled features, we develop an anisotropic hyperelastic model for fibrous biological tissues that accounts for the contribution of the fiber network under both tensile and compressive deformation in an asymmetric fashion. The model uses an octahedral arrangement of fibers embedded in a ground matrix, allowing anisotropy, fiber volume fraction, and pre-stretch to influence the material response. We calibrate the model to experimental data for mitral valve leaflets using an inverse finite element approach that is coupled to automatic differentiation to facilitate efficient parameter calibration. The calibrated model reproduces responses across biaxial, pure-shear, and constrained-uniaxial tests, while separate numerical tests demonstrate its ability to represent substantial volume reduction and the reverse Poynting effect. Using the calibrated model, we investigate how anisotropy and fiber reorientation affect valve deformation under physiological loading. In the idealized valve, the reference fiber orientation, which provided greater radial compliance, yielded complete leaflet coaptation. Prescribed local fiber reorientation redistributed leaflet stress but did not compromise coaptation. Swapping the preferred material directions throughout the leaflets, by contrast, prevented closure in the simulated valve. Finally, we examine how fiber pre-stretch and collagen volume fraction affect leaflet strain and contact, finding a stronger response to changes in pre-stretch over the parameter ranges studied.

authors.name: Nishan Parvez, Prashant K. Purohit, Wensi Wu

papers.title: Predator-associated cues promote host riding, and coupling to mobile hosts improves survival in an epizoic limpet
papers.summary: A host with multiscale movements may be difficult for a small animal to intercept or predict. Boarding turns that moving target into a source of locomotion. The snail Tegula nigerrima previously showed statistical signatures consistent with near-critical locomotor dynamics over limited ranges. We examined how the facultative epizoic limpet Lottia tenuisculpta approaches and boards this host, and whether host mobility improves rider survival. Crab-associated waterborne cues increased riding (19/80 without cues versus 42/76 with cues) and visible host--limpet distance closure. Paired trajectories of eventual riders captured both animals' projected movement toward one another during a nominal ten-minute window ending at the movement-analysis reference frame. Normalised by each animal's shell size, the limpet's projected contribution exceeded the host's in 22/58 pairs. A complementary exploratory assay compared each limpet's cumulative path length on an assigned surface with its no-mucus baseline at a common observation time. Log-transformed ratios varied less among individuals in gastropod-mucus groups than in the no-mucus group. Across the observed frequency range, a matched-trial comparison estimated a 1.21-fold cue-present to cue-absent amplitude ratio (95% recording-date bootstrap interval: 0.97--1.59); the treatment difference in high-frequency spectral slope remained uncertain. Survival was higher on mobile than fixed hosts, with shells occupied in both treatments (posterior median hazard ratio, fixed versus mobile: 2.1). These findings connect the behavioural formation of host--rider coupling to a survival benefit from host mobility, illustrating how one animal gains access to the multiscale locomotion of another.

authors.name: Ryo Nakayama, Katsushi Kagaya, Keita Harada, Tomoyuki Nakano

papers.title: Mechanistic bridges from receptors to whole-brain dynamics: promise and limits of master-equation mean-field models
papers.summary: Drug and disease perturbations often arise at molecular, synaptic or cellular scales, yet are often observed in population and whole-brain signals. Which microscopic mechanisms stay explicit, interpretable and testable through tractable reductions, and what can whole-brain models claim? We follow the master-equation lineage of receptor-aware adaptive mean fields, from finite-size statistics and semi-analytical transfer functions to connectome-coupled conductance-based adaptive nodes. Re-deriving its moment equations, we correct the covariance equation, which omitted a curvature term of the same order as those kept. We compare this strategy with phenomenological neural masses, exact low-dimensional and population-density reductions, large-scale spiking models and learned or hybrid surrogates. We find that effective excitatory/inhibitory synaptic kinetics, conductance state and spike-frequency adaptation can stay manipulable across scales, enabling interpretable, pharmacology-informed perturbations with testable meso- and macroscopic effects. Yet this requires coarse-grained Markovianity, population homogeneity, quasi-stationary transfer functions, moment closure, regional uniformity and measurement-specific observation models. Moreover, first-order whole-brain models discard covariance dynamics, and macroscopic fits do not identify a unique molecular cause. In compute and memory traffic, node-local detail mainly changes prefactors, while dense global covariance propagation changes the scaling class. Cross-scale models should therefore be judged by the intervention pathways and observables they preserve, validity domain, identifiability, empirical adequacy and cost. Receptor-aware mean fields are thus neither universal nor a mere realism-cost compromise, but a transparent, tractable strategy for selected mechanistic questions, provided each reduction step is independently validated.

authors.name: Yannael Bossard, Lahna Bekri, Alain Destexhe

papers.title: Stochastic partial differential equation model for environmental DNA dynamics in river environments
papers.summary: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has emerged as a novel tool for quantifying the seasonal abundance of aquatic species in water bodies; however, its mathematical modeling is still at a germinating stage because of its mechanistic uncertainties. We propose a first-step mathematical and computational framework for the eDNA dynamics of migratory fish based on a novel stochastic partial differential equation model with a delayed source input. The model governs spatiotemporal eDNA concentration in rivers where the source comes from a stochastic differential equation for the migration dynamics of the fish. The affine nature of the model facilitates its theoretical analysis, including the guarantee of well-posedness and the closed-form derivation of the Laplace functional despite the proportionality coefficient of the multiplicative noise term being non-Lipschitz. We also propose a discretization scheme for the model that theoretically generates nonnegative numerical solutions. We finally apply the proposed model to eDNA concentration data sampled from midstream reaches of a river system and perform sensitivity analysis.

authors.name: Hidekazu Yoshioka

papers.title: Ten simple rules for non-visual, reproducible and accessible bioinformatics
papers.summary: Bioinformatics workflows rely heavily on visual representations. Quality-control plots, cell embeddings, heatmaps, genome-browser tracks, and interactive dashboards are not merely illustrations, but instruments for making analytical decisions. For blind and low-vision researchers who use screen readers, braille displays, or audio-based interfaces, these create a barrier: the evidence used to justify an analysis is often encoded in visual form, while the underlying decision remains undocumented. We argue that non-visual accessibility and computational reproducibility are closely aligned, as they both require analyses to be transparent and to record why decisions were made. We present ten simple rules for non-visual bioinformatics, covering plots as decision records, cautious use of AI-generated figure descriptions, accessible computing environments, text-first literate programming, structured data and metadata, compact object summaries, accessible publication formats, collaboration practices, shared community infrastructure, and accessibility as part of FAIR research. The intended audience is computational biologists and developers. Using single-cell RNA-seq as a running example, we show that the accessible equivalent of a plot is a structured decision record. That is, a plot companion that goes beyond storing the underlying data by also stating the purpose of the analysis and the resulting quantitative evidence and uncertainty. We argue that treating accessibility in this way makes bioinformatics more inclusive and also more transparent and auditable.

authors.name: Jacqueline G. Kientsch, Stephan C. F. Neuhauss, Izaskun Mallona

papers.title: Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design
papers.summary: De novo protein design campaigns remain bottlenecked by the inference compute time required to generate and rank candidates, limiting wider functional exploration. Here, we introduce and evaluate an epitope excision approach that truncates targets to local interface windows to accelerate both backbone diffusion and structure prediction. Across 15 targets and 3,666 designs, excised windows closely reproduced full-target binding interfaces (median C\alpha RMSD of 0.37 \AA) and made it practical to design binders against the 719-residue extracellular domain of fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) by cutting RFdiffusion and AlphaFold3 GPU time by ~ 88% in one of the epitopes. Pairing this workflow with an agentic optimization loop allowed the system to autonomously identify catalytic-site targeting strategies. Under a fixed compute budget, a human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow raised the computational hit rate from 5.06% to 9.33% while further cutting GPU hours by ~ 42%. We also found that omitting target multiple sequence alignments during refolding roughly substantially increased the apparent yield. Wet-lab validation with yeast display identified nanomolar binders from the generated designs with the HITL and the fully autonomous agent (human-out-of-the-loop, HOOTL) arms recovering more enriched designs than the PI-alone baseline. Together, target excision and agent-guided search offer a practical way to scale de novo binder design to large, therapeutically relevant proteins.

authors.name: Jun W. Kim, Artiom Myaskovsky, Oscar Donosa, Lawrence Chan, Jameson K. Rogers, Avinatan Hassidim, Yossi Matias, Annalisa Pawlosky

papers.title: Adventures in Multi-Omics I: Combining heterogeneous data sets via relationships matrices
papers.summary: In this article, we propose a covariance based method for combining partial data sets in the genotype to phenotype spectrum. In particular, an expectation-maximization algorithm that can be used to combine partially overlapping relationship/covariance matrices is introduced. Combining data this way, based on relationship matrices, can be contrasted with a feature imputation based approach. We used several public genomic data sets to explore the accuracy of combining genomic relationship matrices. We have also used the heterogeneous genotype/phenotype data sets in the https://triticeaetoolbox.org/ to illustrate how this new method can be used in genomic prediction, phenomics, and graphical modeling.

authors.name: Deniz Akdemir, Julio Isidro Sanchez

papers.title: Cell Migration Boundary Motion in Drosophila Egg Chambers: A Combined Phase Field and Chemoattractant Model
papers.summary: In the Drosophila melanogaster egg chamber, collective migration of border cells toward the oocyte is guided by spatial chemoattractant gradients, yet the distribution of these signals within the tissue remains difficult to quantify experimentally. We develop a spatially resolved mathematical framework to examine how tissue geometry shapes local chemoattractant concentrations during migration. A phase-field model represents the egg chamber architecture and is coupled to a diffusion--reaction equation with spatially heterogeneous diffusivity, restricting free chemoattractant transport primarily to extracellular space while reducing diffusion within cellular domains. Chemoattractant is secreted from the oocyte boundary and degraded throughout the domain, producing geometry-dependent concentration patterns. We further couple this chemical field to a mechanical model of cluster migration through the Tangential Interface Migration (TIM) force, which links local chemoattractant cues with contact-mediated motion along neighboring nurse-cell interfaces. Simulations show that tissue architecture and signal localization jointly influence migration speed and directional persistence. In particular, geometric bottlenecks and intersections can flatten local gradients and slow migration. This framework provides a mechanistic approach for investigating how extracellular geometry, chemical signaling, and cell--cell interactions together regulate collective cell migration in vivo.

authors.name: Naghmeh Akhavan, Alexander George, Ahmet Kaan Aydin, Michelle Starz-Gaiano, Bradford E. Peercy

papers.title: A Structural Theory of Admissible Transitions in Biological Reaction Networks
papers.summary: Biological reaction networks exhibit transient changes that cannot be understood from steady states or long-term persistence alone. We extend Chemical Organization Theory to transitions between species subsets, using stoichiometry and feasible reaction fluxes to characterize structurally admissible changes without specifying kinetic parameters. The framework distinguishes algebraic admissibility from feasibility constrained by reactant availability. We relate these transitions to reaction-based ordinary differential equations and identify an asymmetry: closure-building transitions are determined by network structure, whereas subsequent reductions can depend on the realized trajectory. Transitions to terminal organizations are characterized when the relevant species sets occur along that trajectory. An HIV-immune response model illustrates how a shared closure-building phase can precede different long-term outcomes. The framework connects continuous dynamics with discrete changes in species composition and supports structural analysis of transient pathways and organization formation in systems biology, while distinguishing structural admissibility from realization under particular kinetics.

authors.name: Stephan Peter, Bashar Ibrahim

papers.title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
papers.summary: We present a tool, KATKA, for taxonomic classification with tag arrays. Compared to Ahmed et al.'s state-of-the-art tool Cliffy ({\it Genome Research}, 2025) on the SILVA dataset from their paper and a readset similar to one of theirs, KATKA is faster, more accurate, much smaller and drastically easier to build.

authors.name: Travis Gagie, Gonzalo Navarro

papers.title: CellChain: Benchmarking Cross-Scale Evidence Use for Perturbation Reasoning
papers.summary: Recent advances in foundation models and large-scale cellular perturbation datasets have driven growing interest in using LLMs to predict and reason about cellular responses. Biological reasoning in this setting involves relating molecular mechanisms, cellular responses, and functional outcomes across scales. Evaluating foundation models therefore requires assessing not only whether their predictions are correct, but also how those predictions depend on the biological evidence provided. We introduce CellChain, an experimentally grounded benchmark comprising 590 biological cases and 2,360 matched evidence-condition instances across gene-dependency prediction, cytokine-axis identification, and drug-sensitivity ranking. CellChain links perturbation experiments and external biological resources through a provenance-aware evidence graph spanning molecular, pathway, transcriptional, and phenotypic information. Task-specific conditions vary evidence coverage, composition, or assignment while preserving questions, candidate answers, reference targets, and scoring rules. Across 18 foundation models, the highest accuracies under prespecified target-evidence conditions are 57.5%, 75.5%, and 70.8%, respectively, and broader evidence coverage does not consistently improve accuracy. On the drug-sensitivity benchmark cohort, matched reference histories outperform swapped histories by an average of 13.0 percentage points in cluster-weighted accuracy. Decision-transition analysis separates corrections, newly introduced errors, and wrong-answer switches, revealing substantial answer changes hidden by small net accuracy differences. CellChain provides controlled comparisons for attributing changes in model predictions to prespecified expansions of biological context, including changes in evidence coverage, composition, and biological assignment.

authors.name: Xue Xia, Yue Wang, Shuizhou Chen, Lang Yu, Hao Wu, Wenxuan Huang, Chengkai Yao, Zhangyang Gao, Siqi Sun

papers.title: Directional gate-error asymmetry and universal selectivity bounds in non-unital open quantum systems
papers.summary: Clifford randomized benchmarking and average gate fidelity assign a single trajectory-independent decay rate to a noisy quantum gate at leading order in the dimensionless damping exposure \varepsilon = \gamma T, concealing state-dependent transition-error asymmetries in untwirled quantum circuits. While state-dependent amplitude-damping errors are well known in open quantum systems, a trajectory-level analytical framework that bounds directional transition selectivity across arbitrary pulse shapes and Markovian environments has been lacking. Using first-order toggling-frame perturbation theory for a two-level qubit coupled to a Markovian bath, we show that the antipodal survival-error slopes \chi_+ and \chi_- along any piecewise-continuous control path depend exclusively on its time-averaged Bloch vector m and transverse residence covariance matrix G, obeying the complete-positivity cofactor bound \beta(r) \le 1. On a standard polar \sqrt{X} gate, longitudinal T_1 relaxation induces a 12.23 : 1 directional survival-error split (\kappa_{T_1} = (3\pi - 8)/(3\pi + 8) \approx 0.081767), whereas time-symmetric X rotations maintain an exact 1 : 1 balance (\kappa_{T_1} = 1). Across all completely positive Markovian generators, coupling between non-unital drift and unital diffusion enforces a selectivity bound \kappa_\star = (\pi - 2\sqrt{2})/(\pi + 2\sqrt{2}) \approx 0.052456 (19.06 : 1) for time-independent single-qubit \pi swaps. We apply this framework to Gaussian and derivative-removal-by-adiabatic-gate (DRAG) waveforms on superconducting transmons and trapped-ion qubits, extend the analysis to finite damping, pulse dwell, colored thermal baths, and qutrit leakage, and construct two-branch differential lock-in protocols that isolate directional error splits immune to first-order state-preparation and measurement errors.

authors.name: Amritash Patra

papers.title: Quantum Transitions From Integrable to Chaotic
papers.summary: The quantum integrable-to-chaotic transition is commonly pictured as the quantum counterpart of the classical Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) scenario: a phaseout transition in which a family of regular eigenstates coexists with, and gradually yields to, chaotic eigenstates. Here we show that this is not the only fundamental route from integrability to chaos in quantum systems. We identify a second elementary transition---the morphing transition---which has no classical counterpart: all eigenstates hybridize and turn chaotic concurrently, so that no regular subsequence survives at any stage of the crossover. The two transitions are spectrally distinct: the phaseout spectrum is an independent superposition of regular and chaotic subsequences with Berry-Robnik statistics and a finite short-spacing intercept $P(0)$, whereas the morphing spectrum exhibits global level repulsion with Lenz-Haake statistics and $P(0)=0$. We demonstrate both transitions, and their mixture, in three models. The results for the deformed boson model further show that the quantum phaseout scenario is conditional on a smooth quantum-classical correspondence.

authors.name: Sizhe Yan, Biao Wu

papers.title: Optimal Frobenius light cones for power-law systems in any dimension
papers.summary: We prove optimal Frobenius Lieb-Robinson bounds for power-law systems with power-law exponent $\alpha$ in any dimension $d$, in particular showing that the algebraic to linear light cone transition occurs at $\alpha=d+1$. The proof uses a spectral clipping method and concentration result to allow for running a multiscale operator-norm argument which produces the optimal Frobenius norm exponent. Additionally, we prove there is a Frobenius light cone transition from polylogarithmic to algebraic at the summability threshold $\alpha=d$, and a transition from decaying in volume to non-decaying in volume at $\alpha=d/2$.

authors.name: Laura Shou, An Le, Twesh Upadhyaya, T. C. Mooney, Alexey V. Gorshkov

papers.title: Metamorphic Testing of Quantum Software based on Stabilizer States
papers.summary: A major challenge in quantum computing is to systematically check if a quantum program implements its desired functionality. For classical programs, testing is widely used; each test case comprises a pair of sample input and expected output to be compared with the actual output. To increase the number of test cases, however, one has to solve the test-oracle problem: for each additional test input one has to know the correct output. Metamorphic testing tackles this problem by utilizing metamorphic relations between input and output domains to automatically derive new test cases from existing ones. However, adapting metamorphic testing to the quantum realm is not straightforward, since quantum states cannot be directly inspected. We propose a framework of quantum metamorphic testing (QMT) in which the metamorphic relations incorporate the measurement procedures required to assess quantum outputs. We apply our QMT framework to testing the preparation of stabilizer states, which are central to protocols like measurement-based quantum computing or quantum error correction. We utilize structural properties of stabilizer states to systematically derive measurement circuits for new test cases from existing ones. We implement this framework in Qiskit, and demonstrate that it reduces by an order of magnitude the testing run time compared to testing with randomly generated input states. We further show effectiveness by revealing synthetic program faults injected by circuit mutations, as well as a real bug in the Qiskit compiler.

authors.name: Adri\'an Mar\'in Boyero, Fynn Otto, Albert Rico, Otfried G\"uhne, Malte Lochau

papers.title: Universal Quantum Computation in a Wigner's Friend Framework
papers.summary: The Wigner's Friend thought experiment illustrates a core tension in quantum mechanics: an observer inside an isolated laboratory (the Friend) measures a definite outcome, while an external observer (Wigner) describes the laboratory as a coherent superposition. Here we show that this discrepancy, usually studied as a conflict between descriptions, has a direct computational consequence. We namely propose a protocol by which Wigner can turn the Friend's laboratory into a universal quantum computer, whereby the Friend is restricted to apply simple classical operations within the laboratory. We also experimentally implement a proof-of-principle demonstration of this protocol for single-qubit gates using single photons. By recasting the coherence between incompatible descriptions as a computational resource, we thus link the foundations of quantum measurement to quantum computation.

authors.name: Mart\'i Cladera-Rossell\'o, Sebastian Horvat, Borivoje Daki\'c, Lee A. Rozema, Philip Walther

papers.title: A Quasipolynomial Quantum Algorithm for the Vector Dihedral Coset Problem with Smooth Modulus
papers.summary: We give a quantum algorithm for the vector dihedral coset problem over $\mathbb{Z}_q^n$, in which the goal is to recover $\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{Z}_q^n$ given independent samples of the form $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(|{0,\mathbf{x}}\rangle+|{1,\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{s}}\rangle\bigr)$, for $\mathbf{x}\sim \mathbb{Z}_q^n$. When the modulus $q$ is $B$-smooth, the algorithm uses $n^{O(B^{1+o(1)}\log q)}B^{O(B^{2+o(1)}\log q)}$ samples and time. For $B = \mathrm{polylog}(n)$ and $q=\mathrm{poly}(n)$, this gives a quasipolynomial time- and sample-complexity. This extends the previously known quasipolynomial-time result for power-of-two moduli (Bonnetain, Naya-Plasencia, ASIACRYPT 2018; Bai, Jangir, Kirshanova, Ngo, Youmans, CRYPTO 2025). The algorithm proceeds by reducing the modulus one prime factor $p | q$ at a time. The key ingredient is a sieving procedure that clears the non-linear terms in the phase modulo $p$ via an algorithm of Ivanyos, Santha (TCS 2017) that finds non-zero $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{F}_p^\ell$ such that $\sum_{i \in [\ell]} u_i^d \mathbf{a}_i = 0 \mod p$ for degrees $1 \le d \le p-1$, given vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_\ell \in \mathbb{F}_p^n$ as input. The algorithm also applies to the extrapolated dihedral coset problem (EDCP) introduced by Brakerski, Kirshanova, Stehl\'e, Wen (PKC 2018), which is known to be equivalent to LWE in the polynomial sample regime. However, our result does not yield a new attack on LWE in any regime, precisely because the known reduction from LWE to EDCP provides only polynomially many clean samples, whereas our algorithm requires quasipolynomially many samples. The main algorithm was obtained in a GPT-5.6 Sol conversation prompted by the author; the author is responsible for all statements, proofs, and correctness. Concurrent work of Boucher, Fouque, Shen gives an algorithm with similar guarantees for prime-power moduli.

authors.name: Aparna Gupte

papers.title: Double-Randomized Quantum Singular Value Transformations For Early Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers
papers.summary: The Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) is an algorithmic framework which encompasses a wide range of problems, including Hamiltonian dynamics, ground state preparation, Gibbs state preparation, amplitude amplification, and matrix inversion. For many areas of scientific interest such as quantum chemistry and condensed matter, the circuit depth of the block-encoding subroutine in QSVT can be formidable, limiting the scope of problems to which QSVT can be applied on early fault-tolerant hardware. We split linear operators $A$ into a core operator $A_0$ and a tail operator $A_\epsilon$, block-encoding the normalized sum of $A_0$ and the average of $n_T$ randomly sampled terms from $A_\epsilon$. We show that using randomized block-encodings of this form allows one to lower the circuit depth of QSVT while incurring a diamond norm error that scales as $\mathcal{O}(C_P\delta^2/n_T$), where $C_P$ is a prefactor which depends on the QSVT polynomial $P$ and $\delta$ is the ratio of the $\ell_1$ norms of the coefficient vectors of $A_\epsilon$ and $A$. We then go on to show that if one samples QSVT circuits from a joint probability distribution of both random block-encodings and random polynomials (Double-Randomized QSVT), then the circuit depth savings of these two randomization techniques combine multiplicatively, with only additive error contributions. We numerically calculate error bounds for long-range Heisenberg and iron-sulfur complex Hamiltonians, showing that for a diamond norm error bound of $10^{-3}$, RBE-QSVT can reduce the number of Pauli terms needed for the block-encoding by an order of magnitude or more in several cases. This paves the way for demonstrations of QSVT on early fault-tolerant hardware.

authors.name: Joel Bierman, Pawan Poudel, Yuan Liu

papers.title: Gate tunable spin splitting for Andreev spin qubits in Ge quantum well heterostructures
papers.summary: Ge-based super-semi heterostructures are a promising platform for implementing Andreev spin qubits (ASQs). For example, they can be isotopically purified to eliminate nuclear spins that cause decoherence. However, spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which is a key ingredient for ASQs, is cubic in momentum for hole-based materials like Ge, in contrast with more-conventional ASQ materials (e.g., InAs wires), for which the SOC is linear in momentum. In this work, we study the interplay between geometrical properties like the channel width, and gate-tunable properties like the chemical potential, on ASQ operations. Intriguingly, we find that the spin splitting in a planar Ge Josephson junction does not depend on the junction width, in contrast with InAs nanowires. We explore the possibility of exploiting this property to suppress the harmful effects of charge traps. However, this prospect is spoiled by the fact that charge traps also affect the chemical potential, in addition to the channel width. Our results provide insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing spin splitting in ASQs and offer guidance for optimizing ASQs in other materials with cubic SOC.

authors.name: Avani Vivrekar, Benjamin D. Woods, Mark Friesen

papers.title: Certifying quantum generative models beyond the Fisher trace
papers.summary: Whether a trained quantum generative model has learned its target is usually decided by a diagnostic validated on a labeled benchmark, and such a diagnostic can pass that validation by recovering how the benchmark was built. We analyze Fisher-trace and kernel-based certification of the real-amplitude quantum circuit Born machine in noiseless statevector simulation. For real-amplitude circuits built from half-angle rotations, the classical Fisher information equals the quantum Fisher information almost everywhere, so its trace equals the parameter count and carries no information about fit quality. The Fisher eigenvalue rank counts the live nodes of the amplitude tree: it coincides with the label on a sparse benchmark and is uninformative on a full-support one. The pooled Wasserstein and maximum-mean-discrepancy scores move with optimizer convergence and with the scoring convention. For two bitstring defect families on which both metrics have closed forms, we compute the tolerance-mismatch window in which the discrepancy rejects generators that the transport threshold admits; it opens only at certification-grade tolerances and closes as the qubit number grows. On the Hamming cost we prove a sharp tolerance ratio above which the discrepancy vote is redundant, and we obtain the exact worst-parity minimax value over all unit-diagonal positive-semidefinite kernels, which is exponentially small in the qubit number. In a numerical campaign at the tolerances a near-term experiment can resolve, the discrepancy vote changed no verdict at a thousand shots or more. The false-pass guarantee does not extend to device noise.

authors.name: Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Kathleen Hamilton

papers.title: Hidden Momenta due to Magneto-Electric Coupling in Non-Reciprocal Media
papers.summary: From a canonical quantisation approach of macroscopic quantum electrodynamics, we derive the interaction Hamiltonian due to a dipole emitter interacting with a time-symmetry-broken topological insulator (TSB-TI), described by an axionic coupling Lagrangian. This provides an additional interaction term dependent on the magneto-electric coupling strength inherent to the TSB-TI which will modify measurements on related observables. The spontaneous decay rate is calculated in the Born-Markov approximation for a general electromagnetic Green's tensor, and then specifically for the case of a planar parallel-plate cavity.

authors.name: William S. McGregor, Niclas Westerberg, Robert Bennett

papers.title: Quantum Coloring Games on Complete Graphs
papers.summary: We study the nonlocal game where two players are both given an input ($x$ and $y$, respectively), from a set of size $n$ and, without communicating, must give outputs $a$ and $b$, respectively, from a set of size $m < n$, winning when $(x = y) \leftrightarrow (a = b)$. This can be considered a graph coloring game on the complete graph with $n$ vertices. In the simplest case, the players get random equal inputs with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and random unequal inputs otherwise. We solve this case of the game, and many others, for both classical and quantum (i.e., where the players may share finite-dimensional entangled quantum states) strategy sets, proving the value (the probability of winning) of the optimal strategies and providing explicit strategies that attain this optimum for all $n$ and $m$. Our optimal strategies are synchronous: i.e., the two players always give equal outputs when given equal inputs. These strategies remain optimal when the probability of receiving equal inputs is at least $\frac{2}{m + 2}$. Across this wide range of cases, we find that quantum strategies have an advantage over classical strategies exactly when $m$ does not divide $n$; this advantage is $O\left(\frac{m}{n^2}\right)$.

authors.name: William Bolduc, Michael Jennings

papers.title: Witnessing Magic (and other Quantum Resources)
papers.summary: Motivated by measurements of quantum magic, we study the sampling cost of resource robustness ---a quantifier for a broad class of quantum resources--- by bounding the variance of optimal robustness witnesses. We first lower bound the samples required to estimate a state's resource robustness using Cram\'er-Rao bounds. We find that the number of measurements scales at least quadratically in the robustness for highly mixed states, and at least linearly in the generalized robustness for broad families of pure states, making it difficult to measure either robustness to low absolute error when the states are highly resourceful. We then derive two complementary bounds in terms of the geometry of witnesses, one of which is tight for a class of resource theories including coherence and bipartite entanglement. An additional hurdle occurs for tracking the onset of resource robustness along state-space trajectories: the integrated witness variance along a path is at least the squared resource gain over Fisher length, indicating that a state evolution with exponential resource gain necessarily goes through states for which the robustness cannot be measured efficiently. This hurdle does not occur when estimating robustness to fixed relative, rather than absolute, error. These results suggest that the ideal witness-based resource estimation task, for general resource theories, is the estimation of generalized robustness to low relative error on highly resourceful pure states.

authors.name: Brian Barch, Luis Pedro Garc\'ia-Pintos

papers.title: Control of Non-Markovianity via Channel Exceptional Points in a Driven-Dissipative Kerr-Cat Qubit
papers.summary: Exceptional points (EPs) in open quantum systems are conventionally defined at the Liouvillian level, making them representation-dependent and often requiring auxiliary degrees of freedom. We study EPs directly at the quantum-channel level in a driven-dissipative Kerr-cat qubit, in which dissipation drives bidirectional jumps between its two basis states. Interpolating two Markovian channels yields single EPs when the endpoints straddle a spectral-phase boundary and, remarkably, double EPs within the same phase. The interpolated EPs map out a Markovian--non-Markovian phase diagram: the parameter plane separates certified non-Markovian and Markovian domains, with domain boundaries switching the channel between the two characters. Three spectral criteria certify every domain. As the evolution time advances, the domains drift, split, and partially shrink, making the switching increasingly sensitive to parameters and time. This establishes a representation-independent paradigm for classifying and switching quantum memory effects, applicable to continuous-variable, discrete-variable, and hybrid systems.

authors.name: Tian-Le Yang, Hao-Long Zhang, Pei-Rong Han, Zhen-Biao Yang, Shi-Biao Zheng

papers.title: Machine-learned active spaces enable quantum calculations of spin-state energetics of transition-metal complexes on quantum hardware
papers.summary: Multireference calculations on transition-metal complexes, on classical or quantum hardware, depend on the choice of active space. The orbitals that belong in it are those that are strongly entangled in the correlated wavefunction, but measuring this entanglement requires the very correlated calculation that the active space is meant to make affordable. Here we present SpinAware, a machine-learning model that predicts density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) single-orbital entropies and orbital-pair mutual information from the unrestricted Hartree-Fock (UHF) solution of each spin state, without any correlated calculation. Each of the 20 highest occupied and 20 lowest unoccupied orbitals is described by 60 descriptors computed from the UHF solution, among them the differences between its alpha and beta occupations and energies, its metal-d and ligand character, and its exchange coupling to the other orbitals, and a transformer predicts the entropy of each orbital in the context of all others. Trained on 3454 spin-pure DMRG calculations on mononuclear Cr-Ni complexes, the model transfers to experimentally characterized complexes with ligands, binding topologies, oxidation states and metals absent from training. Over 11 spin states it reproduces the DMRG entropy profiles with a mean absolute error of 0.027, and combining the predicted entropies with the predicted mutual information gives a candidate pool that contains 99% of the DMRG-active orbitals of the benchmark spin states while keeping, on average, only 15 of the 40 orbitals. Natural-orbital occupation scans then select compact active spaces from this pool for a nickel and a cobalt complex. Sample-based quantum diagonalization with samples from IBM quantum processors reproduces the exact CASCI energies of these spaces to within 0.3 kcal/mol and their spin-state gaps to within 0.10 kcal/mol for up to 32 qubits.

authors.name: Muhammad Arsalan Ali Akbar, Thomas D. K\"uhne, Sabre Kais, Werner Dobrautz

papers.title: Constrained Adiabatic Quantum Programming
papers.summary: To find a $k$-clique in a graph, adiabatic quantum computation (AQC) evolves a quantum system from the minimum of an initial cost function to the minimum of a problem cost function that penalizes non-cliques. Existing AQC languages fix the initial cost function, so the search ranges over all $2^n$ subsets of the $n$ vertices, although only the subsets of size $k$ can be answers. We present ENQ+, an AQC language in which the programmer writes both cost functions. Data constraints define the problem cost function. Relational constraints, a new construct, declare the moves the search may make between configurations and define the initial cost function. For the clique, a single relational constraint, which exchanges a chosen vertex with an unchosen one, confines the search to the subsets of size $k$. ENQ+ thereby turns constrained quantum annealing, which physicists set up by hand for individual problems, into a programming construct. We give ENQ+ a semantics in many-world configuration (MWC) graphs, whose nodes are configurations and whose edges are moves, and derive from it a step-wise semantics of adiabatic evolution. We prove that a run stays within the component of the MWC graph that contains its initial state, and that a run from an approximate initial state still reaches the answer, with probability equal to its squared overlap with the exact one. We compile ENQ+ to quantum circuits, prove the compilation correct with respect to the semantics, and use ENQ+ to program the Three-Dimensional Matching, Hamiltonian Cycle, and Traveling Salesperson problems.

authors.name: Liyi Li, Mahir Anand, James Bryan Graves, Amr Sabry

papers.title: Accurate qLDPC decoding under real-time constraints
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires reconciling the computational demands of accurate decoding with the stringent timing constraints of real-time error correction. We present Spatiotemporal Covariance-Optimized Parallel Ensemble (SCOPE), a physics-informed framework for real-time decoding of quantum low-density parity-check codes (qLDPC). By exploiting the spatial symmetries of bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes and the temporal regularity of repeated syndrome extraction, SCOPE uncovers a spatiotemporally covariant decoding structure and organizes the circuit-level problem into a layered decoding strategy. We further compress the high-dimensional evolution of belief propagation (BP) into a low-dimensional dynamical representation, revealing distinct signatures of successful and failed decoding and enabling early detection of unpromising trajectories. Guided by these dynamical signatures, SCOPE explores multiple perturbed decoding trajectories in parallel, enabling early termination and reseeding within a fixed serial iteration budget, with message-passing parameters optimized offline by simulated annealing. Circuit-level simulations of the $[[144,12,12]]$ BB code yield a logical error rate of $p_L=4.82\times10^{-10}$ at a physical error rate of $p=10^{-3}$. We further realize a pipelined two-arm memory-augmented BP (Mem-BP) core at the register-transfer level. Functional simulations at a 250 MHz clock yield a 16 ns BP iteration interval per arm and a mean input-to-result latency of 173.8 ns at $p=5\times10^{-3}$.

authors.name: Chenzewei Qing, Tengyu Zhang, Xiaoqin Luo, Xiaolu Su, Li You

papers.title: Excitation-Selective Control of Protected Subradiant Antiresonances
papers.summary: Subradiant cavity antiresonances exhibit narrow spectral features, yet controlling their nonlinear response without perturbing the protected resonance remains challenging. Here we demonstrate excitation-selective control of a subradiant antiresonance in a driven two-emitter cavity-QED system. An auxiliary collective channel leaves the antisymmetric single-excitation state unaffected while shifting the doubly excited state, introducing tunable excitation anharmonicity without altering the linear antiresonance. This separation enables control of two-photon excitation pathways and photon correlations. Independently, a spatial coupling phase tunes optical access to the subradiant state without changing its intrinsic decay rate. We find that the interferometric phase information per incident photon is optimized when cavity-induced readout approximately matches intrinsic subradiant decay, while steady-state atomic entanglement peaks at an intermediate coupling phase. We further extend phase-selective optical control to collective subradiant modes in correlated emitter arrays. These results establish collective symmetry and spatial mode matching as distinct controls of nonlinear photon correlations, optical phase information, and atomic entanglement.

authors.name: Jing Tang, Yuangang Deng

papers.title: Scalable and Interpretable Quantum Mixture of Experts for High-Dimensional Spatio-Temporal Data
papers.summary: Quantum Mixture of Experts (QMoE) architectures offer a promising path toward scalable quantum machine learning, yet existing approaches remain largely confined to low-dimensional benchmarks and often rely on naive input partitioning that disrupts feature dependencies. We address these gaps by introducing Feature-Partitioned QMoE, which partitions high-dimensional spatio-temporal inputs into functionally coherent feature groups and assigns each group to a dedicated quantum expert. We further propose a hierarchical interpretability framework that leverages the modular structure of QMoE to produce circuit-level gating analysis, per-expert gradient saliency, and heterogeneity-based subtype discovery. Applied to ADHD classification from resting-state fMRI (N=4,458, ABCD Study, 180 brain ROIs, 363 timepoints), the proposed Theory-Driven QMoE achieves performance comparable to matched-capacity classical and quantum baselines while enabling circuit-attributable interpretation. The framework identifies FDR-corrected ADHD-associated biomarkers in executive-control and anterior default-mode networks and reveals three neurobiologically meaningful ADHD subtypes. These results position Feature-Partitioned QMoE as a scalable and interpretable methodology for applying quantum machine learning to high-dimensional biomedical data.

authors.name: Junghoon Justin Park, Anna Jung, Kyumin Lee, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Huan-Hsin Tseng, Shinjae Yoo, Jiook Cha

papers.title: Advancing Quantum Reinforcement Learning with Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search and Adaptive Non-local Observables
papers.summary: Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL) using variational quantum circuits (VQCs) is constrained by fixed measurement protocols and hand-designed circuit ans\"atze. Adaptive Non-local Observables (ANO) and Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search (DiffQAS) address these issues independently, but to our knowledge have not been combined or compared in a single QRL framework. We present an ablation of ANO and DiffQAS within the Quantum Time-series Transformer (QTSTransformer), evaluated on a 2 x 2 factorial design across six environments--two classic-control tasks and four Atari 2600 games. Three findings emerge. First, the quantum agent outperforms a matched classical transformer baseline on five of six environments, with absolute scores ranging from 360.0 vs 304.0 (MarioBros) to 17.2 vs 2.5 (Breakout), while using approximately 12.5x fewer transformer parameters on the four Atari environments (more modestly so on the two classic-control tasks). Second, ANO and DiffQAS provide complementary benefits: ANO yields the largest gain on continuous-state CartPole (347.7 vs 223.2), while DiffQAS yields the largest absolute Atari gains (Breakout 17.2 vs 3.0; DonkeyKong 70.0 vs 37.0). Third, combining both innovations exhibits an asymmetric interaction: ANO-dominant tasks tolerate DiffQAS, whereas DiffQAS-dominant tasks degrade when ANO is added. These results provide design guidance for QRL agents: select between ANO and DiffQAS according to whether the bottleneck is the measurement basis or the gate topology, rather than applying both indiscriminately.

authors.name: Junghoon Justin Park, Kyumin Lee, Anna Jung, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Huan-Hsin Tseng, Shinjae Yoo, Jiook Cha

papers.title: Quantum Dynamics of Dynamics
papers.summary: Quantum channels (in discrete time) and Gorini--Kossakowski--Sudarshan--Lindblad (GKSL) master equations (in continuous time) are the central tools of open quantum systems, but they rest on memoryless approximations (Born, Markov, secular) that fail in many physically relevant settings, most notably non-Markovian dynamics. There, tracking the state alone is insufficient: interventions at intermediate times disturb the environment, so multi-time correlations carry physical information that the state evolution cannot capture. The framework of higher-order quantum operations addresses this by treating controllable operations as \textit{inputs} to a process that maps operations to operations, so that the primitive object is a quantum \textit{dynamics} rather than a quantum \textit{state}. Here, we derive the most general continuous-time, CP-divisible evolution of such an object, the \textit{quantum comb master equation} (QCME), which governs the quantum ``dynamics of dynamics''. Its GKSL-like generator includes encoder--decoder correlation terms coupling distinct temporal interventions. A generalized Born--Markov coarse-graining derivation identifies microscopic conditions for this structure. The QCME yields time-local evolution equations for two-time correlators beyond reduced-state dynamics and extends to more times. We show correlations between Schr"odinger- and Heisenberg-picture evolutions inaccessible to independent GKSL equations, describe quantum-channel evolution motivated by process tomography, and obtain time-local equations for linear response functions and OTOCs under environmental influences.

authors.name: Takano Taira, Hiroyasu Tajima, Philip Taranto

papers.title: Complete Hypergraph States as a Resource for Robust Quantum Metrology
papers.summary: Hypergraph states extend graph states by incorporating many-body interactions via multi-controlled-$Z$ gates, but their metrological advantages and design principles remain elusive. We develop an analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information (QFI) of complete weighted hypergraphs with respect to the collective-spin generators $J_x$ and $J_y$, reducing to three finite binomial averages requiring $O(n|K|)$ arithmetic for a set of hyperedge orders $K$. At the entangling phase $\phi=\pi$, order-optimized $J_x$ sensing approaches the Heisenberg limit (HL), while $J_y$ oscillates between the HL and half the HL at large total number of qubits, $n$. We derive the quadratic and linear coefficients of the QFI under erasure and dephasing noise, showing that complete hypergraph states retain Heisenberg scaling for finite erased particles and dephasing probability $p<0.5$ in the asymptotic system size limit. For $J_y$ sensing, computational basis measurement, or, more simply, using Hamming weight detection, is sufficient to saturate the QFI under noiseless conditions and retain Heisenberg scaling under both noises. These results suggest that complete hypergraphs are a robust resource for practical metrological sensing tasks.

authors.name: Hoe Kin Mooi, Leong-Chuan Kwek

papers.title: Finding Low-Energy States of the Bernasconi Model via Simulated Transverse-Field Quantum Dynamics
papers.summary: The Low-Autocorrelation Binary Sequence (LABS) problem, the ground-state problem of the Bernasconi model, has a rugged landscape with deep, isolated local minima. We study real-time transverse-field dynamics initialized in these minima as a means of reaching lower-energy configurations. Using GPU statevector simulation for N = 20-30 spins, we compare the escape probability per verified quantum sample with the success rate per energy evaluation of steepest-descent kicks, random restarts and tabu search. Using the same field and sampling window across all system sizes, we find that, relative to the best classical baseline, the sampler achieves a factor of 11.9-35.2 for the deepest traps and 13.4-27.2 for the next energy tier. These ratios describe a constant-factor improvement in sample efficiency over the sizes studied. At the adopted field, broad Hamming-space spreading coexists with a strong preference for low-energy states. This regime follows a sharp increase in displacement as the field is raised. To connect this behaviour to the landscape, a short-time expansion relates the onset of escape to target distance and intermediate energies. Bounds on isotropic spin flips and on the free transverse mixer quantify the role of the Bernasconi potential in the observed transfer. At N = 28, the ground-state probability at t = 30 exceeds a canonical cost prediction fitted to the same mean energy by a factor of about 1.9. The cost of generating each quantum sample is assessed separately through a hardware estimate, which places a direct circuit implementation two to three orders of magnitude beyond present processor capabilities.

authors.name: Shaashwat Sagar Kale, Rudranil Basu

papers.title: Probing equilibrium properties with Gaussian states beyond mean-field
papers.summary: Computing equilibrium properties of interacting fermionic systems is central to many problems in condensed matter physics, yet computationally challenging. Mean-field methods tackle this problem by restricting to a tractable class of states, which, however, often fail to capture genuine many-body correlations. We illustrate this in the context of Gaussian mean-field methods by minimizing the energy variance of Gaussian states, showing that even states with the narrowest energy distributions poorly reproduce the microcanonical ensemble. To overcome this limitation, we develop a computationally efficient method to construct linear superpositions of Gaussian states whose energy variance can be systematically decreased by adding more terms to the superposition. We provide complementary results for the canonical ensemble, for which we propose a sampling algorithm based on convex combinations of Gaussian states. We benchmark our methods using the $t$--$V$ model and find that both methods greatly outperform mean-field calculations. In particular, we obtain the correct critical exponents as well as a significantly improved estimate for the critical temperature. As an independent result, we prove a quantum Berry--Esseen theorem for fermionic Gaussian states, which states that the local density of states converges to a Gaussian distribution in the thermodynamic limit without any assumptions about the spatial correlations of the state.

authors.name: Esther Cruz, J. Ignacio Cirac, Dominik S. Wild

papers.title: Coherence, Entanglement and Complementarity in Mixed Classical Light
papers.summary: The classical analogues of quantum correlations have been the subject of considerable interest in the past few years; however, all of these investigations consider the classical analogue of pure quantum mechanical states only. In this work, we study mixed classical light states and derive relations between the polarization coherence of the field and the (classical) entanglement between its degrees of freedom. We show, for a specific model of mixed states, where the purity is determined by a single parameter, how the coherence shared between polarization and entanglement shrinks as the level of purity decreases. The sum of the square of polarization and entanglement remains constant, a behaviour consistent with previous results [Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 153901 (2016)] of pure states, even though the constant for the mixed state case is now smaller in value.

authors.name: Asma Al-Qasimi

papers.title: Every three-qubit pure state admits an equal-modulus expansion in a fixed GHZ basis under local unitaries
papers.summary: In general, local unitary transformations alone do not necessarily generate a complete orthonormal basis from a pure state. We prove that any three-qubit pure state, after suitable local unitary transformations, can be expanded in the same fixed Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger basis, and all expansion coefficients have equal modulus. Thus, eight mutually commuting product reflection operators can generate a complete orthonormal basis from an arbitrary three-qubit pure state, thereby proving the three-qubit commuting-reflection encoding conjecture. We also give two applications of this result: first, using three Bell entanglement links, a pre-specified three-qubit pure state can be deterministically distributed through joint projective measurement and local correction; second, using local random unitary operations, a known pure state can be transformed into a maximally mixed state. The mixing protocol uses a shared three-bit classical label and attains the minimum possible label entropy, even when global unitaries are allowed.

authors.name: Wei Song, Xiao-Lan Zong

papers.title: $Q$-Drive: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Control Framework for Nonlinear Vehicular Dynamics
papers.summary: In this paper, we introduce $Q$-Drive, a hybrid quantum-classical control framework for nonlinear vehicular dynamics that integrates variational quantum circuits (VQCs) with classical optimization, encoding vehicle states into a quantum Hilbert space via angle embedding, applying a trainable quantum ansatz to generate control signals, and refining circuit parameters through gradient descent to minimize tracking error and control effort. The proposed $Q$-Drive is evaluated in two settings: Single-vehicle control of nonlinear bicycle dynamics and a decoupled multi-vehicle swarm scenario with fleet sizes ranging from $N=2$ to $N=50$, demonstrating that the approach achieves exceptionally low control effort, reduced by orders of magnitude compared to classical model predictive control (MPC) and linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) benchmarks in the single-vehicle case, with average per-vehicle control effort decreasing by over 60\% from $N=2$ to $N=50$ in the swarm setting. Beyond empirical evaluation, we establish rigorous stability guarantees by constructing a composite Lyapunov function that jointly captures classical tracking dynamics and quantum-state purity. This analysis proves that the closed-loop system remains ultimately uniformly bounded under arbitrary road conditions, including inclined, rough, and curvilinear surfaces, as well as in the presence of quantum decoherence on the NISQ hardware, with explicit critical thresholds linking decoherence rates to environmental adversity. For the swarm extension, a theoretical bound is derived that shows that the average per-vehicle control effort decreases inversely with fleet size, in agreement with empirical observations. $Q$-Drive offers a promising direction for intelligent transportation systems by enabling robust, energy-efficient, and scalable vehicle control under complex real-world driving conditions.

authors.name: Muhammad Al-Zafar Khan, Safaa Alqrinawi, Jamal Al-Karaki, Omar Alhussein, Saif Al-Kuwari, Ahmed Farouk

papers.title: Dressed higher-form symmetries in mixed state quantum matter
papers.summary: We describe how to construct emergent strong higher-form symmetries in mixed quantum states that act unitarily on Hilbert space. Our construction uses (quasi-)local recovery channels from quantum error correction to some nearby simple (stabilizer) model. We prove that when the recovery is done in an appropriate (deterministic) manner, the resulting operators continue to be unitary. When applied to operators acting on topologically non-trivial sub-manifolds (loops, surfaces), the resulting unitaries inherit the logical algebra of the fixed point model. More generally, the unitarity of the emergent symmetries allows one to define emergent excitations whose statistics follow those of the fixed point limit.

authors.name: Tibor Rakovszky, Sarang Gopalakrishnan, Curt von Keyserlingk

papers.title: Linear-optical nonlocality without postselection
papers.summary: Linear optics is one of the major platforms for quantum information processing and experimental tests of quantum foundations. This motivates a thorough exploration of its capabilities and limitations. In this paper we investigate the extent to which passive linear optics, when fed with single-photon Fock states and followed by postselection-free number-resolving measurements, can demonstrate nonlocality. These resources define BosonSampling, a computational model believed to have intermediate computational power, being neither classically simulable nor quantum universal. We prove that, when restricted to only two input photons, this system also has intermediate nonlocality capabilities, achieving a violation of the CHSH inequality no higher than $1+\sqrt{2}$. Although this value has appeared frequently in the literature as achievable, to our knowledge this is the first proof that it is maximal. We show that, as we increase the number of available photons, linear optics can produce violations arbitrarily close to Tsirelson's bound of $2\sqrt{2}$. Finally, we extend the analysis to tripartite nonlocality, leveraging well-known interferometric suppression laws to show how several tripartite inequalities can be violated in this setup beyond their bipartite bounds.

authors.name: Daniel J. Brod, Ernesto F. Galv\~ao

papers.title: Quantum sine imaginary-time evolution: sequential and QSVT implementations of a probabilistic ground-state filter
papers.summary: We propose quantum sine imaginary-time evolution (QSITE), a quantum algorithm for preparing ground states of a Hamiltonian. QSITE approximates imaginary-time evolution through an exact sine filter. We give two circuit implementations of this operator: a sequential one that applies it as a concatenation of linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), reusing two ancilla qubits across steps via mid-circuit measurement, and a coherent one based on the quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). A telescoping identity shows the two prepare the same state and succeed with identical probability, differing only in how that probability can be boosted. QSITE belongs to the family of ancilla-based probabilistic imaginary-time filters and we state rigorous convergence guarantees: we prove that the QSITE operator converges uniformly to the exact ITE operator, that the prepared state converges to the ideal ITE state, and that the filter probability increases monotonically with each concatenation step. Although the construction applies to an arbitrary Hamiltonian, we specialize it to optimization Hamiltonians, and this specialization is what exposes its structure more easily. Since MaxCut eigenvalues are integers, the probability of failure is periodic in the evolution time, yielding safe zones, the first located analytically and the second numerically. For MaxCut we further show that, when the tolerated energy error is a fixed fraction of the ground-state energy, the probability of failure can be bounded below 1/2 with concatenation steps growing linearly with the number of qubits in the first safe zone. We present numerical results for random Erd\"os-R\'enyi instances with up to 24 qubits and benchmark QSITE against QAOA.

authors.name: Victor A. Penas, Tamara Bottazzi, Marcelo Losada, Diego Tielas, Federico Holik

papers.title: Latency-Preserving Rewrites and Translation Validation for Dynamic Quantum Circuits
papers.summary: A dynamic quantum circuit measures qubits during a run and chooses later operations from the outcomes. These branches make the qubits wait: the outcome must reach the classical controller, and the controller must decide. We present qlin, a compiler that reduces this waiting time. qlin moves operations out of branches without delaying the program, a property proved in Lean 4. For error-correction decoders, which branch on syndromes that are almost always zero, qlin compiles the likely syndromes into one multiway branch and keeps the original program for the rest. A cost model decides when a classically controlled gate should become a quantum-controlled gate instead. On all benchmarks, qlin checks that the compiled program computes what its source computes, and the checker is proved sound in Lean 4. At the published per-decision cost of the QICK controller (42 ns), 10 of 65 programs run at least 10% faster than the best baseline in our cost model, up to 91.2%, mostly because one multiway branch replaces a long chain of if statements. On the register-transfer logic of the QubiC controller, a compiled distance-5 repetition decoder selects its correction in 21.3 instead of 151.1 expected cycles. Timing runs on an IBM device were too noisy to confirm or reject the model's ranking.

authors.name: Rylan Malarchick

papers.title: Shallow Clifford circuits on square lattices
papers.summary: We study the depth of CZ circuits, Clifford state preparation, and Clifford unitary synthesis over the two-dimensional square lattice. A programmable circuit on a $2{\times}k$ ladder ($n{=}2k$) implements an arbitrary CZ computation in depth at most $\frac{3n}{2}{+}3$ up to reversal of both rails. This improves the best-known LNN (Linear Nearest-Neighbor)-compliant depth-$(2n{+}2)$ construction by about 25\%. For state preparation, we consider a Phase gate programmable -H-{CNOT+P}-LC- circuit and derive matching obstructions to attaining the CZ-span counting lower bound of $2\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil{-}1$ for depth by the entangling gates. For cycle connectivity $C_n$, we prove that the minimum depth is exactly $2\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil{-}1$ when $n$ is not a multiple of four and $2\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil$ when $n\,{=}\,4k$. We construct a hole-free minimum-perimeter square-lattice patch with a Hamiltonian cycle for every even size, giving optimal-depth programmable circuits to implement Clifford states for all $n\,{=}\,4k{+}2$. Exhaustive and heuristic searches address the remaining cases for $n$ up to 256, and selected values up to 1,024 qubits. The improvement against comparable state-of-the-art, an LNN-compliant depth-$(2n{+}2)$ solution, is about 50\%. Finally, combining state synthesis circuits developed in this work with a known four-diagonal-stage decomposition gives rise to a depth $4n{-}4$ for $n\,{=}\,4k{+}2$ and depth $4n$ for $n\,{=}\,4k$ implementation of arbitrary Clifford unitaries. This improves the most relevant state-of-the-art, an LNN-compliant depth $7n{-}4$ construction, by about 43\%.

authors.name: Dmitri Maslov

papers.title: Proxima: Optimizing Syndrome Extraction Circuit Scheduling for Practical Quantum LDPC Codes
papers.summary: The fault-tolerant performance of quantum error correction codes relies critically on the scheduling of parity checks in syndrome extraction circuits (SECs). For general CSS-type quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, the vast scheduling space and intricate error-propagation patterns make it computationally prohibitive to directly optimize the logical error rate (LER) or the exact circuit-level distance ($d_{\mathrm{circ}}$). To address this challenge, we introduce Proxima, a highly effective automated SEC scheduling framework guided by a distance-related metric termed proximity. Defined directly on the detector error model (DEM), proximity quantifies the minimum number of additional faults required to complete a seed fault to an undetectable logical failure, naturally capturing arbitrary circuit-level fault mechanisms and bounding $d_{\mathrm{circ}}$ from above. Proxima synthesizes a pool of valid schedules at a target depth and ranks them by evaluating proximity within small, graph-local DEM fault subsets, progressively enlarging the subset only to break ties among top-ranked candidates. Across a broad spectrum of qLDPC code families, Proxima consistently attains low circuit depths and high circuit-level distance bounds, reducing LER by 1.4--2.6$\times$ over the strongest automated baseline and up to $40\times$ over others while generalizing robustly across noise models and decoders. Furthermore, by exploiting translational symmetry via a compact monomial representation, Proxima discovers depth-8 uniform schedules for bivariate bicycle codes that surpass even IBM's depth-7 reference schedule [Nature, 2024] by 2.1--5.1$\times$, establishing the DEM-level proximity as a practical objective for fault-tolerant compilation.

authors.name: Ruiyun Zhang, Guangqi Zhao, Zhaohui Yang, Yingjian Liu, Chenghong Zhu, Anbang Wu, Jun Xia, Yuan Xie

papers.title: Fixed Points as Programs: Finite Symmetry and One-Shot State-Gate Duality in the Misty-State Calculus
papers.summary: The same quantum object can support several logically distinct descriptions: it can be an eigenstate of an operator, a fixed point of an action, a nonstabilizer resource, or a state consumed by a gate-injection protocol. We make these relations precise in the misty-state calculus. The semantic core is a normalized superposition constructor $x\star y=\operatorname{N}(x+y)$. For any finite unitary group $G$, whenever the orbit sum is nonzero, the normalized orbit cloud $\operatorname{N}(\sum_{g\in G}U_gx)$ is fixed by every element of $G$; the involutive specialization $x\star Ux$ is therefore a certified fixed-point constructor. Applied to $U=H$ and $x=|0\rangle$, it gives the nested misty state $M=\operatorname{N}\{W,\operatorname{N}\{W,B\}\}$, the $+1$ Hadamard eigenstate. This state is not a Pauli stabilizer state; it is an H-type magic state and is Clifford-equivalent to $T|+\rangle$. We then prove an exact one-shot state-gate duality. Writing $J=XZ$ and $R_\theta=e^{\theta J}$, the state $M_\theta=R_\theta|0\rangle$ can be consumed by a Clifford controlled-$J$ injection circuit to apply either $R_\theta$ or $R_\theta^{-1}$ to arbitrary data. Whenever $R_\theta^2$ is free, feed-forward makes the implementation deterministic. At $\theta=\pi/8$, $R_\theta^2=HZ=XH$ is Clifford, so one copy of $M$ implements one exact use of the non-Clifford gate $R=e^{\pi J/8}$; conversely one use of $R$ prepares $M$ from $|0\rangle$. We formulate this as a pair of sound semantic certificates, $\operatorname{Fix}(U)$ and $\operatorname{Prog}(R)$, and separate the resulting finite symmetrization mechanism from the genuinely recursive fixed-point role of the $Y$ combinator, while identifying the exact $S$-combinator sharing pattern in $x\star Ux$. The result is a small, auditable semantics in which invariance and consumable program resources coexist without being conflated.

authors.name: Dan-Adrian German, Tony Newton

papers.title: The Cost of Quantum State Conversion
papers.summary: Which losses in quantum-state preparation can better control remove, and which are imposed by the available resources? We determine the least entropy production for converting known full-rank states using fresh thermal auxiliaries of fixed size and bounded energy range, with arbitrary driven joint control. For every reachable target, the asymptotic infimum is the decrease of a computable function of the state's spectrum. Explicit finite protocols approach this limit, including at saturated resource constraints. The result therefore supplies an attainable benchmark for state preparation, rather than only a lower bound. Reusable memory changes both reachability and the cost without enlarging any fresh auxiliary. A uniform memory gives an exact rescaling of the resource parameter; all memory states preparable from it under the same constraint have the same reachable targets and asymptotic costs. Externally supplied biased memories can do better, revealing a preparation resource distinct from dimension.
